Leadership wants to discover which cloud apps are in use and to enforce DLP and sharing policies inside the sanctioned SaaS apps themselves. Which of the following solutions BEST meets these requirements?
quizOptions: A) A next-generation firewall (NGFW) enforcing application control at the data center perimeter
B) A cloud access security broker (CASB) connected to the sanctioned SaaS apps
C) A secure web gateway (SWG) that blocks uncategorized and high-risk websites
D) A web application firewall (WAF) placed in front of the corporate website
detail.explanation: A CASB sits between users and cloud services, often through API connections to the SaaS apps, giving shadow IT discovery and cloud DLP. A secure web gateway filters web traffic but does not enforce policy inside SaaS apps, a WAF protects your own web applications, and an NGFW only sees traffic that crosses it.

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: CBC is a mode of operation for block ciphers where each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using an initialization vector for the first block. This chaining ensures identical plaintext blocks don't produce identical ciphertext.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to recognize CBC as a block cipher mode (often paired with AES) and the role of the IV in preventing pattern leakage between blocks.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures a legacy VPN appliance to use AES in CBC mode with a properly randomized IV for every session. A security review later confirms that encrypting the same repeated data block, like a file header, produces completely different ciphertext each time, preventing pattern analysis.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer encrypts two identical messages with the same key and the same initialization vector in CBC mode and gets identical ciphertext, which reveals that the messages match. Which of the following changes would BEST fix this weakness?
quizOptions: A) Increase the key length from 128 bits to 256 bits
B) Use a new random initialization vector for each message
C) Add a message authentication code to the end of each message
D) Switch the cipher mode to ECB so that blocks are independent
detail.explanation: CBC hides repeated plaintext only when the IV is unique and unpredictable for every message. ECB would leak patterns even more, a longer key does not change the deterministic output for a repeated IV, and a MAC adds integrity rather than confidentiality.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

expansion: Counter Mode Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol
definition: CCMP is the encryption protocol used in WPA2 that combines AES in counter mode for confidentiality with a CBC-MAC for data integrity. It replaced the weaker TKIP protocol used in the original WPA standard.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know CCMP is AES-based and used by WPA2, contrasted with TKIP (used by WPA) and the newer GCMP used by WPA3.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan audits the office wireless network and finds several older access points still configured for WPA with TKIP. He reconfigures them to use WPA2 with CCMP instead, giving the network AES-grade encryption and integrity checking rather than the weaker RC4-based TKIP scheme.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's access points still use WPA with TKIP. The team must move to an encryption protocol based on AES that also provides message integrity, but the existing hardware supports WPA2 and not WPA3. Which of the following settings should the team configure?
quizOptions: A) WPA3 with SAE
B) WEP with a 128-bit key
C) WPA with TKIP and a longer passphrase
D) WPA2 with CCMP
detail.explanation: WPA2 uses CCMP, which combines AES counter mode for confidentiality with CBC-MAC for integrity, and the hardware supports it. WPA3 is not supported, WEP is broken, and a longer passphrase does not make TKIP any stronger.

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: A state-level privacy law that grants California residents rights over their personal information, including the right to know what data is collected, request deletion, and opt out of the sale of their personal data to third parties.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize CCPA as a US state-level counterpart to GDPR; know that it applies based on California residency and business revenue or data thresholds, and grants rights like opting out of data sale rather than the EU's broader consent-based model.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company sells customer data to advertising partners and discovers many customers are California residents. Priya builds a Do Not Sell My Personal Information opt-out mechanism on the company website to comply with CCPA's requirement that California consumers can opt out of data sales.
detail.quizQuestion: A U.S. company with customers in both California and Germany is mapping its privacy obligations. Which of the following statements is MOST accurate?
quizOptions: A) GDPR applies only to companies headquartered in the EU, so a U.S. company's German customers are outside its scope
B) CCPA applies only to healthcare organizations and gives patients the right to see their protected health information
C) CCPA lets California residents see, delete and opt out of data sales, while GDPR protects EU residents more broadly
D) Both laws require opt-in consent for all data collection and neither one gives individuals a right to request deletion
detail.explanation: CCPA is a state-level law giving California residents access, deletion and opt-out-of-sale rights, much like a U.S. counterpart to GDPR. GDPR applies to the personal data of EU residents wherever the organization is based, and HIPAA, not CCPA, is the healthcare law.

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: CCTV is a video surveillance system that uses cameras to monitor and record activity in and around a facility, typically viewed only by authorized personnel rather than broadcast publicly. It is a core physical security control used for deterrence, detection, and after-the-fact investigation.
examContext: SY0-701 groups CCTV with other physical security controls like fencing, lighting, and guards; know that CCTV is primarily a detective control (and a deterrent) rather than a preventive one, since it records but does not stop an intrusion by itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya installs CCTV cameras covering every entrance to the data center and the badge-reader doors so that any unauthorized access attempt is captured on video. When a badge is later found to have been used at an unusual hour, the recorded footage lets the security team confirm whether it was the legitimate badge holder or someone else.
detail.quizQuestion: A warehouse suffers repeated after-hours thefts. The security manager installs visible cameras that record to a video recorder and alert the guard on motion. Which of the following BEST classifies this control?
quizOptions: A) Preventive, because it stops intruders from entering the warehouse at night
B) Compensating, because it replaces the need for locks on the warehouse doors
C) Corrective, because it restores normal operations after a theft has occurred
D) Detective, because it records activity, and deterrent, because it is visible
detail.explanation: Cameras record and alert, which is detective, and their visibility discourages attempts, which is deterrent. They do not physically stop anyone, so they are not preventive, and they neither repair damage nor substitute for another control.

definition: A CERT is a team of experts designated to respond to and coordinate handling of computer security incidents, often operating at a national or sector level. The original CERT at Carnegie Mellon became the model that many organizational and national response teams are based on.
examContext: SY0-701 references CERT/CSIRT as incident response teams; know the terms are largely interchangeable depending on an organization's naming convention, and understand their coordinating role during incidents.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company experiences a ransomware outbreak that spreads beyond their internal capability to contain, so they escalate to the national CERT for coordinated guidance and threat intelligence on the specific ransomware strain. The CERT's indicators of compromise help Chen's team identify and isolate every infected host within hours.
detail.quizQuestion: A national government wants a central team that coordinates the response to major computer security incidents across many organizations and shares alerts about emerging threats. Which of the following BEST describes this team?
quizOptions: A) A change advisory board that approves modifications to infrastructure
B) A computer emergency response team operating at the national level
C) A security operations center that monitors the network of a single company
D) A network operations center that monitors the availability of WAN links
detail.explanation: A CERT coordinates incident response, often nationally or for a sector, and shares threat information. A company SOC serves one organization, a CAB reviews changes, and a NOC monitors performance and uptime rather than security incidents.

definition: CFB is a mode of operation for block ciphers that turns them into a self-synchronizing stream cipher by XORing plaintext with encrypted feedback from the previous ciphertext block. It allows encryption of data that isn't a multiple of the block size without needing extra padding.
examContext: SY0-701 may test CFB as one of several block cipher modes (alongside ECB, CBC, GCM, CTM); remember that CFB and similar feedback modes turn a block cipher into a stream-like cipher, unlike ECB which encrypts each block independently and insecurely.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is configuring a legacy serial-communication application that streams data in small, irregular chunks rather than fixed blocks, so he selects CFB mode for the AES cipher instead of a mode that requires full blocks. This lets the application encrypt each small chunk as it arrives without waiting to pad it out to a full block size.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer must encrypt variable-length sensor messages with a block cipher without padding the final block. The design uses a mode in which the plaintext is XORed with encrypted output that is fed back from the previous ciphertext block, producing a self-synchronizing stream cipher. Which of the following modes does this describe?
quizOptions: A) Counter Mode (CTR), which encrypts an incrementing counter value
B) Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), which pads the final block to a full block
C) Electronic Code Book (ECB), which encrypts every block independently
D) Cipher Feedback (CFB), which feeds earlier ciphertext back into the cipher
detail.explanation: CFB uses the previous ciphertext as feedback and works like a self-synchronizing stream cipher, so no padding is needed. CTR also avoids padding but uses a counter instead of feedback, CBC needs full blocks, and ECB has no chaining at all.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: CHAP is an authentication protocol that verifies a user's identity using a three-way handshake and a hashed challenge value, so the password itself is never sent across the link. It improves on simpler protocols by protecting against replay attacks through periodic re-challenges.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to contrast CHAP with PAP: PAP sends credentials in cleartext while CHAP never transmits the actual password, only a hashed response to a random challenge, and repeats the challenge periodically during the session.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria disables PAP on the company's remote-access server because it sends passwords in plaintext, and configures CHAP instead so that only a hashed challenge-response crosses the link. During a penetration test, the tester captures the handshake traffic but cannot recover any usable password from it.
detail.quizQuestion: A legacy dial-in service authenticates users with PAP, and an audit found passwords readable in packet captures. The team wants a PPP authentication method that never sends the password over the link and re-challenges the user during the session. Which of the following should replace PAP?
quizOptions: A) PAP, carried inside an IPsec tunnel between the dial-in client and the server
B) A pre-shared key configured identically on every dial-in client and on the server
C) CHAP, which answers a random challenge with a hashed response and repeats it
D) PAP, with the password hashed once on the client before it is sent to the server
detail.explanation: CHAP proves knowledge of the password with a hashed response to a random challenge and repeats the challenge during the session, so the password never crosses the link. A single hash would be replayable, tunneling PAP still transmits the password, and a shared key is not per-user authentication.

definition: CI/CD is a software development practice that automates building, testing, and deploying code changes frequently and reliably. Security must be built into the pipeline, often called DevSecOps, so vulnerabilities are caught before code reaches production.
examContext: SY0-701 references CI/CD pipelines in the context of secure DevOps practices, including automated security testing integrated directly into the build and deployment process.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya integrates an automated static application security testing tool directly into the company's CI/CD pipeline so every code commit is scanned for vulnerabilities before it can be merged. A developer's commit introducing a SQL injection flaw is automatically blocked from deployment, long before it would have reached production.
detail.quizQuestion: A team ships code to production several times a day through an automated pipeline. After a breach traced to a vulnerable open-source library, the CISO wants vulnerabilities caught before code reaches production without slowing releases. Which of the following is the BEST approach?
quizOptions: A) Require a manual penetration test of the whole application and a management review before every release
B) Move to one release per year so that a long security review can be completed before each release
C) Run a vulnerability scan of the production servers once each quarter and track the findings in tickets
D) Add automated security tests, such as static analysis and dependency scanning, as pipeline stages
detail.explanation: Building automated security checks into the pipeline (DevSecOps) catches flaws such as vulnerable dependencies on every build, without slowing delivery. Manual tests and yearly releases remove the speed, and quarterly production scans find problems only after deployment.

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

items.name: User provisioning
items.detail: Automatically create, change and remove accounts as people join, move and leave.

items.name: Resource provisioning
items.detail: Spin up servers, networks and cloud resources from code (infrastructure as code).

items.name: Guard rails
items.detail: Automated limits that stop risky actions before they happen.

items.name: Security groups
items.detail: Automatically apply and adjust network access rules.

items.name: Ticket creation and escalation
items.detail: Alerts automatically open tickets and escalate them if unanswered.

items.name: Enabling / disabling services and access
items.detail: Quickly turn services or accounts on or off, such as disabling a compromised account.

items.name: Continuous integration and testing
items.detail: Automatically build and test code on every change to catch problems early.

items.name: Integrations and APIs
items.detail: Connect tools so they share data and trigger each other (SOAR playbooks).

definition: The CIA triad is the foundational security model describing the three goals every control should support: keeping data confidential (only accessible to authorized parties), ensuring its integrity (unaltered and trustworthy), and maintaining its availability (accessible when needed). Nearly every security control maps back to protecting one or more of these three properties.
examContext: SY0-701 opens with the CIA triad as the core security model; be ready to classify a given control or attack by which leg of the triad it primarily affects (e.g., ransomware mainly threatens availability, while a data breach threatens confidentiality).

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is asked to justify a new backup and replication strategy to management, so he explains it in terms of the CIA triad: encryption protects confidentiality, checksums protect integrity, and redundant failover servers protect availability. This framing helps leadership understand why all three investments are necessary rather than redundant.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator who is authorized to view vendor payment records quietly changes the bank account numbers on several of them so that invoices are paid to a different account. No records were deleted or exposed publicly, and the system stayed online. Which of the following was MOST directly violated?
quizOptions: A) Non-repudiation, because the administrator can deny having made the changes
B) Integrity, because the data was changed without authorization
C) Confidentiality, because an insider accessed records that should have been restricted
D) Availability, because the payment system could no longer be trusted to process invoices
detail.explanation: The defining harm is that trustworthy data was altered, which is a loss of integrity. The administrator was allowed to view the records, so confidentiality was not the issue, the system stayed online, and non-repudiation is not a leg of the CIA triad.

definition: A method for allocating IP addresses and routing that replaces rigid class-based addressing with flexible-length subnet masks, expressed as slash notation such as /24, allowing more efficient use of address space and route aggregation.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to read and apply CIDR notation, like 10.0.0.0/24, to determine subnet size and understand how it enables route summarization, reducing the size of routing tables across large networks.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria needs to subnet a /16 network into smaller segments for different departments without wasting address space on rigid class boundaries. Maria uses CIDR notation to carve out precisely sized subnets like /26 and /27 for each department, matching the number of devices in each group efficiently.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer must carve a subnet from 192.168.10.0 for a branch office that needs 100 host addresses and wants to waste as few addresses as possible. Which of the following CIDR blocks is the BEST choice?
quizOptions: A) 192.168.10.0/24, which provides 254 usable host addresses
B) 192.168.10.0/26, which provides 62 usable host addresses
C) 192.168.10.0/25, which provides 126 usable host addresses
D) 192.168.10.0/27, which provides 30 usable host addresses
detail.explanation: A /25 leaves 7 host bits, giving 2^7 minus 2 = 126 usable addresses, the smallest block that fits 100 hosts. A /26 (62) and a /27 (30) are too small, and a /24 (254) works but wastes more addresses.

definition: The CIO is the senior executive responsible for an organization's overall information technology strategy, infrastructure, and systems, aligning IT investments with business goals. In security governance, the CIO is typically a key stakeholder who balances security initiatives against budget, operations, and business needs.
examContext: SY0-701's governance objective expects you to recognize executive roles like the CIO as part of the oversight and accountability structure, often the person a CISO or security team escalates risk decisions to when they exceed the security team's authority.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's security team identifies a critical vulnerability that would require taking a revenue-generating system offline for emergency patching, so Sam escalates the risk decision to the CIO rather than making the call unilaterally. The CIO weighs the business impact against the security risk and approves a scheduled maintenance window within 24 hours.
detail.quizQuestion: A security manager finds a critical risk that would need $2 million of new infrastructure to fix, far above the security team's authority. The manager must escalate to the executive who owns the company's internal IT infrastructure, systems and technology budget. Which of the following roles is the MOST appropriate?
quizOptions: A) The database administrator, who manages and secures the company databases
B) The data protection officer, who oversees privacy regulation compliance
C) The chief technology officer, who directs product technology and innovation
D) The chief information officer, who runs internal IT operations and systems
detail.explanation: The CIO is responsible for IT strategy, infrastructure and systems and is where risk decisions beyond the security team's authority are escalated. The CTO focuses on product technology, the DPO on privacy compliance, and a DBA on databases.

definition: A CIRT is the designated group responsible for detecting, responding to, and recovering from cybersecurity incidents within an organization. The term is functionally synonymous with CSIRT in most organizations.
examContext: SY0-701 may use CIRT and CSIRT interchangeably; recognize both refer to the internal team that executes the incident response plan.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is named the lead of her company's newly formed CIRT, and she writes the on-call rotation so a qualified responder is always reachable within fifteen minutes of an alert. When a malware infection is detected at 2 a.m., the rotation ensures someone begins containment immediately rather than waiting until morning.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's monitoring tools detect ransomware spreading across file servers. The incident response plan names an internal group that carries out containment, eradication and recovery. Which of the following is this group?
quizOptions: A) The network operations center that monitors the availability of WAN links
B) The computer incident response team that executes the incident response plan
C) The change advisory board that approves modifications to infrastructure
D) The data protection officer who advises on privacy regulations
detail.explanation: A CIRT, or CSIRT, is the designated team that detects, responds to and recovers from incidents by executing the response plan. A NOC watches uptime, a CAB approves changes, and a DPO advises on privacy law.

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: A nonprofit organization that publishes the CIS Critical Security Controls and CIS Benchmarks, which are widely adopted, prioritized best-practice guidelines and configuration standards for securing operating systems, applications, and network devices.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize CIS Benchmarks as a common source for secure configuration baselines, also called hardening guides, referenced when auditing or hardening systems, often used alongside STIG and NIST guidance.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria needs to harden a fleet of newly provisioned Linux servers before they go into production. Maria applies the CIS Benchmark for the specific Linux distribution, disabling unnecessary services and enforcing secure configuration settings that align with an industry-recognized baseline.
detail.quizQuestion: A security engineer needs prescriptive, step-by-step configuration guidance for hardening a new Linux server build, published by a nonprofit community and widely used as a secure baseline. Which of the following sources BEST meets this need?
quizOptions: A) The NIST Cybersecurity Framework, which describes high-level security functions
B) The OWASP Top 10, which lists the most critical web application risks
C) CIS Benchmarks, which give detailed secure configuration settings for specific systems
D) ISO/IEC 27001, which defines requirements for an information security management system
detail.explanation: CIS Benchmarks are detailed, prescriptive hardening guides for operating systems, applications and devices. The NIST CSF and ISO 27001 operate at the program level, and the OWASP Top 10 is about web application risks rather than server configuration.

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A CMDB is a centralized repository that stores information about an organization's IT assets, their configurations, and the relationships between them. It supports change management and helps identify the potential impact of proposed changes or incidents.
examContext: SY0-701 connects CMDB to asset and change management; know it tracks configuration items and their dependencies, helping teams assess the blast radius of a change or incident.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team maintains a CMDB that maps every application to the specific servers, databases, and network devices it depends on. When a critical patch requires rebooting a shared database server, Sam quickly queries the CMDB to see every downstream application that will be affected and schedules a maintenance window accordingly.
detail.quizQuestion: Before applying a patch to the central authentication server, the change manager wants to know every application and server that depends on it so the impact of the change can be assessed. Where should the manager look FIRST?
quizOptions: A) The vulnerability scanner's report archive, which lists the known weaknesses
B) The SIEM's correlation rule set, which defines the alerts the SOC receives
C) The incident response plan, which describes how breaches are handled by the team
D) The configuration management database, which records assets and relationships
detail.explanation: A CMDB stores configuration items and the relationships between them, so it shows what depends on the authentication server. SIEM rules, scan reports and the incident response plan do not map dependencies.

definition: A CMS is a software platform used to create, manage, and publish digital content, such as a website, without requiring users to write code directly. Popular CMS platforms are frequent attack targets because outdated plugins, themes, or core software can introduce serious vulnerabilities.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CMS platforms in the context of web application vulnerabilities and patch management; remember that unpatched CMS plugins/extensions are a very common real-world attack vector requiring regular vulnerability scanning.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya runs a vulnerability scan on the company's public website and finds the CMS is running a plugin with a known SQL injection flaw three versions out of date. She schedules an emergency update and adds the CMS to the automated patch-management cycle so plugin versions no longer silently drift out of date.
detail.quizQuestion: A marketing website runs on a popular CMS. A scan shows the core software is current, but a plugin that was installed three years ago and is no longer used has a known remote code execution flaw. Which of the following actions BEST reduces the risk?
quizOptions: A) Move the whole site to HTTPS and replace the certificate with one that has a longer key
B) Remove the unused plugin and keep the remaining plugins and themes patched
C) Require longer passwords and a password manager for all CMS editor accounts
D) Back up the CMS files and database every night and store the copies offsite
detail.explanation: The weakness is an outdated component that does not need to exist, so removing it and patching the rest closes the hole. HTTPS protects traffic, strong passwords protect accounts, and backups help recovery, but none of them fix the vulnerable plugin.

definition: COOP is the process of planning how an organization's essential functions will continue during and after a disruptive event, such as a natural disaster or cyberattack. It overlaps closely with business continuity planning but is especially associated with government and critical-function continuity requirements.
examContext: SY0-701 groups COOP with BCP and DRP as resilience and recovery planning concepts; know that COOP focuses on keeping essential operations running during a disruption, which is closely related to but distinct from disaster recovery, which focuses on restoring systems afterward.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan helps a county government agency draft a COOP document identifying which services (like emergency dispatch) must keep running no matter what, and lines up an alternate site and backup staff for each one. When a flood knocks out the primary building, the agency keeps dispatch running from the pre-designated alternate site within the hour.
detail.quizQuestion: A government agency needs a plan that keeps its essential functions, such as issuing emergency alerts, running from an alternate site even if its headquarters is unavailable for weeks. Which of the following BEST describes this planning effort?
quizOptions: A) A disaster recovery plan that restores server backups
B) An incident response plan that contains malware outbreaks
C) A business impact analysis that ranks systems by cost
D) Continuity of operations planning for essential functions
detail.explanation: COOP focuses on keeping essential operations running during and after a disruption, a term especially used by government. A DRP restores IT systems afterward, a BIA is the analysis that informs plans, and an incident response plan handles security incidents.

items.name: RTO
items.detail: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable TIME to restore a service. "How long can we be down?"

items.name: RPO
items.detail: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable DATA LOSS, measured as time since the last good backup. "How much data can we lose?" It sets backup frequency.

items.name: MTTR
items.detail: Mean Time To Repair/Restore: the average time to fix a failed component or service.

items.name: MTBF
items.detail: Mean Time Between Failures: the average time a REPAIRABLE system runs between failures. A reliability measure.

items.name: MTTF
items.detail: Mean Time To Failure: the average lifespan of a NON-repairable component (it is replaced rather than repaired).

items.name: MTD
items.detail: Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest outage a business function can survive before the damage is unacceptable; RTO must be shorter than MTD.

items.name: BIA
items.detail: Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical functions and sets their RTO and RPO.

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: COPE is a mobile device deployment model where the organization owns and manages the device but allows the employee to also use it for personal purposes. It gives IT more control than BYOD while still offering employees some personal flexibility.
examContext: SY0-701 compares COPE, BYOD, and CYOD; know COPE devices are company-owned, giving IT full management rights, unlike the employee-owned BYOD model.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's company issues COPE smartphones to the sales team, fully managed through MDM but allowing employees to install personal apps and browse freely during off hours. Because the devices are corporate-owned, Alex can enforce full-disk encryption and push security patches without needing employee consent for each change.
detail.quizQuestion: A sales company buys phones, enrolls them in MDM before they are handed out, and lets employees use them for personal apps and calls as well. The company keeps the right to wipe the devices. Which of the following deployment models is this?
quizOptions: A) COBO, where the company owns the device and personal use is not allowed
B) COPE, where the company owns and manages the device but personal use is allowed
C) CYOD, where employees pick a personally owned device from an approved list
D) BYOD, where employees bring and own the devices they use for work
detail.explanation: Company-owned, company-managed devices that also allow personal use are COPE. In BYOD the employee owns the phone, CYOD describes choosing from an approved list, and COBO is company-owned for business use only.

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: Contingency planning is the broad discipline of preparing alternative actions an organization will take when normal operations are disrupted, encompassing business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response as subsets. It ensures the organization isn't caught improvising during a crisis.
examContext: SY0-701 treats contingency planning as the umbrella term under which BCP, DRP, and incident response plans all sit; if a question asks for the broadest term covering "what to do when things go wrong," CP is often the intended answer.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is tasked with building out the organization's overall contingency planning program, so he creates a hierarchy of documents: a business continuity plan for operations, a disaster recovery plan for IT systems, and an incident response plan for security events, all under one contingency planning framework. This structure ensures each specific plan is tested and nothing falls through the cracks.
detail.quizQuestion: A CEO asks for one umbrella program that covers business continuity, disaster recovery and incident response, so the organization knows what to do whenever normal operations are disrupted. Which of the following BEST describes this?
quizOptions: A) Contingency planning, the broad discipline that includes the other plans
B) Change management, which governs how approved changes are deployed
C) Disaster recovery planning, which is only one part of the overall effort
D) Business continuity planning, which is only one part of the overall effort
detail.explanation: Contingency planning is the umbrella over business continuity, disaster recovery and incident response. BCP and DRP are subsets of it, and change management is an unrelated process for approving and deploying changes.

definition: The CPU is the primary processor that executes instructions in a computer system. In security, CPU features like virtualization extensions and secure enclaves support protections such as trusted execution environments and hardware-based isolation.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CPU-level security features or vulnerabilities, such as hardware support for virtualization or side-channel exploits affecting processor caches.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan enables CPU-based virtualization extensions on the hypervisor hosts so each virtual machine runs in a properly isolated hardware-enforced boundary. This prevents a compromised VM from easily accessing memory belonging to another tenant VM on the same physical host.
detail.quizQuestion: A researcher shows that code running in one cloud virtual machine can infer secrets from another virtual machine on the same host by measuring timing differences in the shared processor cache. Which of the following BEST describes this class of vulnerability?
quizOptions: A) A SQL injection against the cloud provider's customer portal
B) A buffer overflow in the hypervisor's management interface
C) A rogue DHCP server on the provider's internal network
D) A side-channel attack against the CPU's shared cache
detail.explanation: Inferring secrets from timing and cache behavior is a hardware side-channel attack. The other options describe attacks on software memory handling, databases and network configuration, none of which involve processor caches.

definition: A CRC is a checksum algorithm used to detect accidental changes to data during transmission or storage. It catches corruption efficiently but, unlike a cryptographic hash, offers no protection against intentional tampering by a skilled attacker.
examContext: SY0-701 tests whether you know CRC is for detecting accidental data corruption, not a secure integrity control against malicious tampering, which instead requires a cryptographic hash like SHA or HMAC.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's network team notices a high rate of CRC errors on a specific switch port and traces it to a faulty cable causing bit corruption during transmission. Replacing the cable resolves the errors, illustrating that CRC is designed to catch this kind of accidental physical-layer corruption rather than deliberate tampering.
detail.quizQuestion: A vendor publishes a firmware update with a CRC-32 value so customers can verify the download. An analyst warns that this will not stop an attacker who tampers with the file. Which of the following is the BEST improvement?
quizOptions: A) Add parity bits to each block of the firmware file before it is sent to customers
B) Switch from CRC-32 to a 64-bit CRC so that the check value is much harder to forge
C) Digitally sign the firmware, or publish a SHA-256 hash over a trusted channel
D) Publish an MD5 hash on the same download page as the firmware file itself
detail.explanation: A CRC only detects accidental errors, and an attacker can recompute it. A digital signature or a cryptographic hash delivered over a trusted channel detects deliberate changes. A longer CRC or parity bits have the same weakness, and an MD5 hash next to the file can be replaced along with it.

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

definition: A CRL is a list published by a Certificate Authority identifying digital certificates that have been revoked before their scheduled expiration, such as due to key compromise. Clients check the CRL, or use the faster OCSP method, to avoid trusting a revoked certificate.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts CRL with OCSP: a CRL is a periodically downloaded list that can be stale, while OCSP provides real-time revocation status for a single certificate.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization discovers that a server's private key was exposed in a misconfigured backup, so he immediately has the CA revoke the associated certificate and publish the update to the CRL. Clients that check the CRL before the certificate's natural expiration date will now refuse to trust it.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee's laptop that holds a VPN client certificate is stolen. The security team wants the VPN gateway to reject that certificate immediately, even though it does not expire for several months. Which of the following BEST accomplishes this?
quizOptions: A) Delete the employee's original certificate signing request from the CA's records
B) Reissue the certificate to the employee with a new serial number and a longer key
C) Shorten the validity period of the CA's own root certificate so stolen certificates age out
D) Revoke the certificate at the CA so the gateway finds it on the revocation list
detail.explanation: Revocation is how a CA withdraws trust before expiry, and the gateway learns of it through the CRL (or OCSP). Changing the root's validity affects every certificate, deleting the CSR does nothing to a certificate already issued, and reissuing leaves the stolen one valid.

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: A voluntary framework published by NIST that organizes cybersecurity activities into core functions, including Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover, to help organizations assess and improve their security posture.
examContext: SY0-701 expects familiarity with the NIST CSF core functions as a common language for describing an organization's security maturity, often contrasted with prescriptive, mandatory standards like PCI DSS.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is asked to benchmark the organization's security program against an industry standard and chooses the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Chen maps existing controls to the Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover functions, revealing that the company has strong protective controls but weak detection capability.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants a voluntary, flexible framework to describe its current cybersecurity posture and target state using the functions Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, without a certification audit. Which of the following BEST meets this need?
quizOptions: A) ISO/IEC 27001, a standard against which an organization can be audited and certified
B) PCI DSS, a mandatory contractual standard for payment card data
C) NIST RMF, a process for categorizing and authorizing federal information systems
D) NIST CSF, a voluntary framework organized around five core functions
detail.explanation: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is voluntary and built on Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. ISO 27001 is certifiable, PCI DSS is mandatory for card data, and the RMF is a lifecycle process mainly for federal systems.

items.name: NIST CSF
items.detail: Voluntary framework organized into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (version 2.0 adds Govern).

items.name: NIST RMF
items.detail: The Risk Management Framework for federal systems: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

items.name: NIST SP 800-53
items.detail: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls.

items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A CSIRT is the formal team responsible for coordinating an organization's response to security incidents, from detection through recovery and lessons learned. It is the most commonly used term for this function in both enterprise practice and the exam.
examContext: SY0-701 frequently uses CSIRT as the standard term for the incident response team; know its responsibilities span the full incident response lifecycle, not just technical remediation.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's CSIRT runs a post-incident lessons-learned meeting after containing a phishing-driven breach, documenting that the initial alert was missed for six hours due to an alert-fatigue issue in the SIEM. They adjust alert thresholds afterward, directly reducing detection time for the next similar incident.
detail.quizQuestion: During a ransomware outbreak, executives ask who will lead the technical response, coordinate with legal and communications, and run the post-incident review. Which of the following groups BEST fits this role?
quizOptions: A) The computer security incident response team
B) The security operations center staff whose role is limited to alert triage
C) The change advisory board that approves modifications to infrastructure
D) The internal audit committee that reviews compliance with policy
detail.explanation: A CSIRT coordinates the whole incident lifecycle, from detection through recovery and lessons learned. SOC triage is only the front end, a CAB approves changes, and an audit committee reviews compliance rather than responding to incidents.

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: The CSO is the senior executive responsible for the organization's overall security strategy, which may include both physical security and information/cyber security depending on the company's structure. The CSO sets security policy direction and represents security risk to the rest of executive leadership.
examContext: SY0-701's governance objective expects you to know that executive roles like the CSO (sometimes split into a CISO for cyber-specific duties) own ultimate accountability for security risk decisions and policy approval.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security team presents a risk register showing several unaddressed high-severity findings, and the CSO uses that report to secure additional budget and headcount from the board. With executive backing from the CSO, Maria's team hires two more analysts to close the remediation backlog.
detail.quizQuestion: A board wants a single executive accountable for both physical security, such as guards and access control, and cybersecurity, who will also present security risk to the rest of the executive team. Which of the following roles BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) The chief technology officer
B) The data protection officer
C) The chief information officer
D) The chief security officer
detail.explanation: A CSO owns the overall security strategy, which can span physical and cyber security, and represents security risk to leadership. The CIO runs IT, the CTO leads technology direction, and the DPO focuses on privacy compliance.

definition: A CSP is a company that offers cloud computing services such as infrastructure, platforms, or software over the internet, like AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. Security responsibilities are divided between the CSP and the customer according to a shared responsibility model that varies by service type.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily tests the shared responsibility model: in IaaS the customer manages more of the stack, while in SaaS the CSP manages nearly everything except data and access.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team assumes their CSP automatically encrypts all stored data, but an audit reveals that encryption at rest for their storage buckets was actually an opt-in setting they never enabled. She updates the configuration and documents the shared responsibility boundary clearly for the rest of the team going forward.
detail.quizQuestion: A company runs its web application on virtual machines in a public cloud (IaaS). A breach is traced to an unpatched operating system on one of the web servers. Under the shared responsibility model, which party is responsible for the missing patch?
quizOptions: A) The hypervisor vendor, because virtualization isolates each guest operating system
B) The customer, because it manages the guest operating system and applications in IaaS
C) Both parties equally, because the model divides every task evenly between them
D) The cloud provider, because it owns the physical hardware that hosts the virtual machines
detail.explanation: In IaaS the provider secures the physical infrastructure and virtualization layer, while the customer manages the operating system, applications and data. The responsibility is split by layer, not evenly, and the hypervisor vendor does not patch customer guests.

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: A CSR is a message sent to a Certificate Authority to request a digital certificate, containing the applicant's public key and identifying information. The CA validates the request and issues a signed certificate in response.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the order of operations: generate a key pair, create a CSR, submit it to a CA, then receive the signed certificate back.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam generates a new public/private key pair for a web server and creates a CSR containing the server's domain name and organization details. He submits the CSR to a public CA, which verifies domain ownership and returns a signed certificate that Sam installs on the server.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator has generated a new key pair on a web server and needs a certificate from a public CA. Which of the following should the administrator send to the CA?
quizOptions: A) A self-signed certificate that the CA will countersign to convert into a trusted one
B) A certificate signing request with the public key and the server's identifying information
C) A certificate revocation list that contains the server's domain name and public key
D) The server's private key, so the CA can sign it and return a matching certificate to install
detail.explanation: The CSR carries the public key and identity details, and the CA validates it and returns a signed certificate. The private key must never leave the server, a CRL lists revoked certificates, and a CA issues its own signature rather than converting a self-signed one.

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: CSRF is a web attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into submitting an unwanted request to a site where they're already logged in, exploiting the trust that site places in the user's browser session. Anti-CSRF tokens embedded in forms prevent this by verifying the request genuinely originated from the legitimate site.
examContext: SY0-701 tests CSRF as distinct from XSS: CSRF abuses the trust a site has in an authenticated user's browser, while XSS abuses the trust a user has in a site's content; know anti-CSRF tokens as the standard mitigation.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria discovers that her banking application's fund-transfer form has no hidden token, meaning a malicious webpage could silently submit a transfer request using a logged-in victim's session cookie. She adds a unique anti-CSRF token to the form that the server validates on submission, blocking forged cross-site requests.
detail.quizQuestion: A user logged in to an online banking site clicks a link in an email. The link silently submits a funds transfer request to the bank, which processes it because the browser sends the user's session cookie automatically. Which of the following would BEST prevent this attack?
quizOptions: A) Anti-CSRF tokens that are validated on every state-changing request
B) Parameterized queries for every database call in the application
C) A longer lifetime for the session cookie so users reauthenticate less often
D) Output encoding of all user-supplied data displayed in web pages
detail.explanation: CSRF works because the site trusts any request that carries the user's cookie, so a secret per-request token proves the request came from the real form. Output encoding stops XSS, parameterized queries stop SQL injection, and a longer cookie lifetime makes the exposure worse.

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: A CSU is a hardware device that connects a company's internal digital network to an external WAN circuit (often paired with a DSU), terminating the line and providing diagnostics and signal conversion. It sits at the network's demarcation point with the telecom provider.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CSU/DSU as part of WAN connectivity and the network demarcation point; know it sits between the customer's router and the carrier's line, a boundary that matters when troubleshooting whose responsibility a connectivity failure is.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam is troubleshooting an intermittent WAN outage and traces the problem to the CSU at the network's demarcation point rather than the internal router. Because the CSU is owned by the carrier, Sam opens a ticket with the ISP instead of trying to fix it internally, saving hours of wasted effort.
detail.quizQuestion: A company leases a digital WAN circuit from a carrier. A device at the customer's premises terminates the carrier's line, converts the signal for the customer's router, and marks where the carrier's responsibility ends. Which of the following is this device?
quizOptions: A) A CSU/DSU at the demarcation point
B) A VPN concentrator that terminates remote-access tunnels
C) A wireless access point that bridges clients to the LAN
D) A layer 3 switch that routes between internal VLANs
detail.explanation: A CSU/DSU terminates the carrier's digital circuit and sits at the demarcation point, which helps decide whether a fault is the carrier's or the customer's. The other devices serve remote users, internal routing and wireless access.

definition: Counter Mode (CTR, sometimes written CTM) turns a block cipher into a stream cipher by encrypting successive values of an incrementing counter and XORing the result with the plaintext. It allows blocks to be encrypted and decrypted in parallel, making it fast for high-throughput applications.
examContext: SY0-701 may list CTM alongside GCM, CBC, and ECB as cipher modes; remember that counter mode's parallelizability makes it popular in high-speed network encryption, and that GCM combines counter mode with built-in authentication.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya needs to encrypt a very high-throughput data feed between two data centers and chooses a cipher running in Counter Mode specifically because it can encrypt multiple blocks in parallel across CPU cores. This lets the link sustain full line-rate speed without the encryption becoming a bottleneck.
detail.quizQuestion: A network appliance must encrypt 10 Gbps of traffic with AES and can process blocks in parallel on many cores. The design calls for a mode that turns the block cipher into a stream cipher by encrypting an incrementing counter, with no padding. Which of the following modes BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) Cipher Feedback (CFB), which feeds earlier ciphertext back into the cipher
B) Electronic Code Book (ECB), which encrypts every block independently
C) Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), which chains each block to the previous ciphertext
D) Counter mode (CTR), which encrypts successive counter values
detail.explanation: Counter mode encrypts a counter and XORs the result with the data, so blocks can be processed in parallel and no padding is needed. CBC and CFB depend on earlier ciphertext and cannot encrypt blocks in parallel, and ECB, though parallel, leaks patterns.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: The CTO is the senior executive responsible for an organization's overall technology direction and innovation strategy, often focused on product and engineering technology choices rather than day-to-day IT operations. The CTO works alongside the CIO and CSO to ensure new technology adoption doesn't outpace security review.
examContext: SY0-701's governance objective expects you to distinguish the CTO's technology-strategy focus from the CIO's IT-operations focus and the CSO's security focus, since exam scenarios sometimes test which executive owns a particular type of decision.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's engineering team wants to adopt a new third-party API for the company's flagship product, and the CTO requires a security review to be completed before approving the integration. The CTO's insistence on involving the security team early catches a data-handling issue before the API ever reaches production.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is launching a new cloud-based product. The executive who directs product technology and engineering choices must work with the other executives so that new technologies get a security review before adoption. Which of the following roles is this?
quizOptions: A) The chief financial officer, who controls the budget and financial reporting
B) The chief security officer, who owns the security strategy and policy direction
C) The chief technology officer, who directs innovation and product engineering
D) The chief information officer, who runs internal IT operations and infrastructure
detail.explanation: The CTO is responsible for technology direction and engineering choices for products. The CIO runs internal IT operations, the CSO owns security strategy, and the CFO handles finance.

definition: CVE is a standardized naming system that assigns unique identifiers to publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities, making it easier to reference and track them consistently across tools and organizations. Each CVE entry typically includes a description and references to patches or advisories.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs CVE with CVSS (severity scoring) and NVD (the database hosting CVE details); know a CVE ID follows the format CVE-YEAR-NUMBER.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's vulnerability scanner flags a web server and references CVE-2023-44487 in its report, letting him quickly look up the exact flaw, affected versions, and available patch. Because the identifier is standardized, every tool in his stack references the same vulnerability consistently.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan report lists a finding labeled CVE-2024-12345. Which of the following BEST describes what this identifier represents?
quizOptions: A) A unique standard name for one specific publicly known vulnerability
B) A category of software weakness, such as improper input validation
C) A severity score from 0 to 10 that is assigned to the vulnerability
D) A report listing every unpatched system in the whole environment
detail.explanation: A CVE ID names one specific public vulnerability so tools and teams can refer to it consistently. The severity score is CVSS, the weakness category is a CWE, and a list of unpatched systems comes from a scan report.

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: CVSS is a framework for rating the severity of a vulnerability on a scale from 0 to 10, based on factors like attack vector, complexity, and impact. It helps organizations prioritize which vulnerabilities to patch first.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to interpret a CVSS score range, such as 9.0-10.0 being Critical, to prioritize remediation; know it's a scoring framework, not a vulnerability database itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team has fifty open vulnerabilities but limited patching time this week, so she sorts them by CVSS score and tackles the 9.8-rated remote code execution flaw first, deferring a 3.1-rated low-impact information disclosure issue. This prioritization ensures the most exploitable risk is closed first.
detail.quizQuestion: A scan finds 300 vulnerabilities, but the team can patch only 20 this week. They want to start with the most severe, using a standard score based on attack vector, complexity and impact. Which of the following BEST describes the approach?
quizOptions: A) Sort by CVE identifier and begin with the lowest identifier numbers
B) Sort by CWE category and begin with the weaknesses that are listed first
C) Sort by publication date and begin with the oldest published findings
D) Sort by CVSS score and begin with the Critical findings from 9.0 to 10.0
detail.explanation: CVSS rates severity from 0 to 10, so it is the standard way to prioritize patching, with 9.0 to 10.0 as Critical. CVE numbers, CWE categories and publication dates do not say how severe or exploitable a flaw is.

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: A community-developed catalog of common software and hardware weakness types, such as buffer overflows or improper input validation, that serves as a standardized classification system for describing security vulnerabilities at the root-cause level.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference CWE alongside CVE; remember that CVE identifies specific known vulnerabilities in specific products, while CWE categorizes the underlying type of weakness, the root cause, that can lead to vulnerabilities.
