detail.practicalScenario: Priya is reviewing a static code analysis report that flags a function as vulnerable to CWE-89, SQL Injection. Priya uses the CWE classification to understand the root-cause weakness pattern and trains developers to use parameterized queries to eliminate that entire class of defect across the codebase.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer finds that several recent vulnerabilities in the company's applications share one root cause: user input is used without validation. Which of the following would BEST help the team classify and track this type of weakness across all of its products?
quizOptions: A) The Common Weakness Enumeration, which catalogs types of software weakness
B) The National Vulnerability Database, which hosts details for each CVE entry
C) CVE identifiers, which name individual vulnerabilities in specific products
D) CVSS base scores, which rate the severity of each vulnerability
detail.explanation: CWE classifies the underlying type of weakness, such as improper input validation, which is what the team wants to track across products. CVE names specific flaws, CVSS scores severity, and the NVD stores the details of CVE entries.

items.name: Base / Temporal / Environmental
items.detail: Base = intrinsic traits (attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact on CIA). Temporal = exploit maturity and fix availability. Environmental = adjustments for YOUR organization.

items.name: CVE vs CVSS vs CWE vs NVD
items.detail: CVE is the unique ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is its severity score. CWE is the category of weakness. NVD is the US database that publishes CVE entries with CVSS scores.

definition: CYOD is a mobile device deployment model where employees select a device from a company-approved list, which the organization then owns or manages. It balances user choice with the ease of IT support and security standardization.
examContext: SY0-701 differentiates CYOD, which offers choice from an approved, company-owned list, from BYOD (any personal device) and COPE (company-issued with personal use allowed).

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's IT department offers new hires a choice of three approved smartphone models under a CYOD program, all pre-enrolled in MDM before being handed out. This lets employees pick a device they like while ensuring IT only has to support a small, consistent set of hardware configurations.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to simplify mobile support by letting employees choose from three company-purchased phone models that are enrolled in MDM before they are handed out. Personal devices are not allowed. Which of the following deployment models is this?
quizOptions: A) COBO, where the company issues one device for business use only
B) COPE, where the company issues one device and personal use is allowed
C) BYOD, where employees bring and own the devices they use for work
D) CYOD, where employees choose from an approved list of company devices
detail.explanation: Choosing a company-owned device from a short approved list is CYOD. BYOD uses employee-owned devices, COPE and COBO do not involve choosing, and COBO prohibits personal use.

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: DAC is an access control model where the owner of a resource decides who is granted access and what permissions they have. It's flexible but can lead to inconsistent security since individual users control permissions rather than a central policy.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts DAC, where the resource owner decides access, with MAC's system-enforced labels and RBAC's role-based assignments; know DAC is the default model in most file systems like Windows NTFS.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam creates a shared folder on a file server and, as its owner, grants read-write access to two colleagues directly through the file properties dialog. Because this is DAC, Sam personally controls who can access the folder rather than a central security team setting the policy.
detail.quizQuestion: The owner of a project folder on a Windows file server, using standard NTFS permissions, gives a coworker read access without involving IT. Which of the following access control models is in use?
quizOptions: A) Discretionary access control, where the resource owner decides who gets access
B) Rule-based access control, where fixed rules apply to every user
C) Role-based access control, where permissions come from the user's job role
D) Mandatory access control, where system-enforced labels decide access
detail.explanation: When the owner of a resource decides who may access it, as with NTFS file permissions, the model is DAC. MAC uses labels set by the system, RBAC grants permissions by role, and rule-based control applies the same rules to everyone.

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: A DBA is the person responsible for managing, maintaining, and securing an organization's databases, including configuring access permissions, performance tuning, and backups. Because DBAs often hold powerful privileged access to sensitive data, their accounts are a high-value target and a key focus of least-privilege and separation-of-duties controls.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference the DBA role in the context of privileged account management and separation of duties; remember that DBA accounts should be covered by just-in-time or just-enough access policies and session auditing like any other privileged account.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex, the DBA for a healthcare application, is required to request temporary elevated access through the company's privileged access management tool instead of holding standing admin rights to the patient database at all times. This just-in-time approach means Alex's full database privileges are only active during an approved maintenance window, not around the clock.
detail.quizQuestion: An audit finds that a database administrator can change production data, approve their own access requests, and delete the audit logs of their own activity. Which of the following would BEST address the risk?
quizOptions: A) Move the database server to its own VLAN behind a dedicated internal firewall appliance
B) Separate duties so others handle approvals and logs, and record the DBA's sessions
C) Encrypt the production database with a stronger algorithm and a longer encryption key
D) Require the DBA to change the account password every 30 days and use a longer passphrase
detail.explanation: The problem is concentrated privilege with no independent oversight, so separation of duties and session auditing are the fix. Password rotation, stronger encryption and network segmentation do not stop an authorized administrator from abusing access.

definition: A DDoS attack floods a target system or network with traffic from many compromised devices, known as a botnet, simultaneously overwhelming its resources and making services unavailable to legitimate users. It's distinguished from a simple DoS attack by its distributed, multi-source nature.
examContext: SY0-701 tests DDoS mitigation strategies like traffic scrubbing, rate limiting, and content delivery networks; know the 'distributed' element comes from a botnet of many infected hosts across different networks.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's e-commerce site goes offline during a flash sale after receiving traffic from tens of thousands of distinct IP addresses simultaneously, far more sources than any single attacker could control directly. He enables a cloud-based scrubbing service that filters the botnet traffic before it reaches the origin server, restoring availability within minutes.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's web server is overwhelmed by traffic from 40,000 compromised IoT cameras around the world, and the traffic saturates the company's internet link. Which of the following would BEST keep the site available?
quizOptions: A) Block the offending source addresses with rules on the company's edge firewall
B) Add more processor cores and memory to the web server and scale up its database
C) Use a cloud DDoS scrubbing or CDN service that filters the traffic upstream
D) Enable HTTPS with HSTS on every page of the site so all visitor traffic is encrypted
detail.explanation: A volumetric attack fills the internet link before it reaches the firewall or server, so the traffic must be absorbed upstream by a scrubbing service or CDN. Edge filtering and a bigger server cannot help once the link is full, and HTTPS does not change availability.

items.name: DoS vs DDoS
items.detail: DoS comes from a single source; DDoS is distributed across many compromised devices (a botnet), so it cannot be stopped by blocking one IP.

items.name: Volumetric
items.detail: Saturates bandwidth (UDP or ICMP floods).

items.name: Protocol
items.detail: Exhausts connection-state resources, such as a SYN flood against a firewall or server's state table.

items.name: Application layer
items.detail: Low bandwidth but expensive requests (HTTP floods, Slowloris) that tie up the web application.

items.name: Amplification
items.detail: A small spoofed request makes a third-party server (open DNS, NTP or memcached) send a much larger reply to the victim.

items.name: Reflection
items.detail: The attacker spoofs the VICTIM's IP as the source so that innocent servers send their responses to the victim, hiding the real attacker.

items.name: Defenses
items.detail: Rate limiting, CDN or scrubbing services, SYN cookies, WAF, RTBH (remotely triggered black hole) routing, and over-provisioned capacity.

definition: DEP is an operating system security feature that marks certain memory regions as non-executable, preventing malicious code injected into those regions, such as via a buffer overflow, from running. It works alongside ASLR as a core memory-exploit mitigation.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs DEP with ASLR as OS-level exploit mitigations; know DEP specifically blocks code execution from data-only memory regions like the stack or heap.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security baseline enforces DEP on every workstation, so when a malicious document attempts to execute shellcode it had injected into a data buffer, the operating system blocks the execution attempt outright. The exploit fails even though the buffer overflow vulnerability itself was never patched.
detail.quizQuestion: A security engineer enables a feature that marks the stack and heap as non-executable. An exploit that injects shellcode into a buffer now fails with an access violation when the injected code tries to run. Which of the following features was enabled?
quizOptions: A) Code signing, which verifies the publisher of an executable
B) ASLR, which randomizes the memory locations used by a process
C) DEP, which prevents code from executing in data-only memory regions
D) TPM sealing, which ties encryption keys to the measured boot state
detail.explanation: DEP blocks execution from memory areas meant only for data, so injected shellcode cannot run. ASLR hides where things are rather than blocking execution, TPM sealing protects keys, and code signing verifies who published a program.

definition: DES is a legacy symmetric block cipher with a 56-bit key that is now considered cryptographically weak and can be broken by brute force with modern computing power. It has been replaced by AES for virtually all modern security uses.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize DES, and its variant 3DES, as deprecated or weak algorithms that should not be used in new systems, in contrast to the current standard, AES.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan finds a legacy payment application still encrypting card data with DES due to code written over two decades ago. He flags it as a critical finding in the security assessment, since the 56-bit key can now be brute-forced in hours, and schedules a migration to AES.
detail.quizQuestion: An audit of a legacy payment application finds that it encrypts card data using DES with a 56-bit key. Which of the following is the BEST recommendation?
quizOptions: A) Replace DES with RC4, because it is a stream cipher that supports much longer keys
B) Keep DES but switch to ECB mode so each block is encrypted independently
C) Replace DES with AES, because a 56-bit key can be brute forced with modern hardware
D) Keep DES but rotate the key daily so attackers have less time to break it
detail.explanation: A 56-bit key is small enough to be exhausted quickly, so DES must be replaced with AES. Daily rotation does not help when a key can be broken in hours, RC4 is itself broken, and ECB leaks patterns and makes things worse.

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

definition: A key exchange algorithm that allows two parties to establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel without ever transmitting the key itself, forming the mathematical foundation for many secure communication protocols.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange algorithm, not an encryption or signing algorithm, and that it underlies protocols like IPsec and TLS; also know it is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks unless combined with authentication.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex is designing a VPN configuration and needs two endpoints to agree on a session encryption key without ever sending that key across the network. Alex configures the IPsec tunnel to use Diffie-Hellman key exchange so both sides derive the same shared secret independently, keeping the key itself off the wire entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: Two branch offices must establish a shared secret over the internet before building a VPN tunnel. They have no prearranged secret, and the key itself must never travel across the link. Which of the following does this?
quizOptions: A) A SHA-256 hash of the shared password, which produces a fixed-length digest
B) An HMAC calculation, which uses a pre-shared key to authenticate data
C) A Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which derives the same secret on both sides
D) An RSA digital signature, which proves who created a message
detail.explanation: Diffie-Hellman lets two parties compute the same secret from public values, so the key is never transmitted. Signatures prove origin, an HMAC needs a secret that is already shared, and a hash does not establish a key between strangers.

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and other network configuration settings, like DNS servers and the default gateway, to devices joining a network. A rogue DHCP server can redirect clients to malicious DNS servers or gateways as part of a man-in-the-middle attack.
examContext: SY0-701 may test DHCP snooping as a switch security feature that blocks rogue DHCP servers from handing out malicious configuration information to clients on the network.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya notices several workstations receiving IP configurations that point to an unfamiliar DNS server not managed by IT. She traces it to a rogue DHCP server an employee accidentally connected to the network and enables DHCP snooping on the switches so only the authorized server's responses are trusted going forward.
detail.quizQuestion: Several users on one VLAN suddenly receive a default gateway of 192.168.5.250, which belongs to an unauthorized laptop, and their traffic is being intercepted. Which of the following switch features would BEST prevent this from happening again?
quizOptions: A) BPDU Guard on the user-facing access ports to block rogue switches
B) Dynamic ARP inspection on the access ports to drop forged ARP replies
C) Port mirroring on the uplink to copy the traffic to a protocol analyzer
D) DHCP snooping, with only the uplink port configured as a trusted port
detail.explanation: DHCP snooping drops DHCP offers that arrive on untrusted ports, so a rogue server cannot hand out a malicious gateway. BPDU Guard protects spanning tree, dynamic ARP inspection validates ARP packets, and port mirroring only copies traffic for analysis.

definition: DHE is a key exchange method that generates a brand-new, temporary Diffie-Hellman key pair for every session instead of reusing the same key pair repeatedly. This provides perfect forward secrecy, meaning that even if a key is later compromised, past encrypted sessions remain safe.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize DHE and its elliptic-curve variant ECDHE as the mechanisms that provide forward secrecy in TLS handshakes, a key differentiator from static/non-ephemeral key exchange.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the company's web servers to prefer TLS cipher suites that use DHE for key exchange instead of static RSA key exchange, specifically to gain forward secrecy. Months later, when an old server's private key is exposed during a breach, previously captured encrypted traffic still cannot be decrypted because each session used its own ephemeral key.
detail.quizQuestion: A web server uses a static RSA key exchange. The threat model assumes an adversary records all TLS traffic today and might steal the server's private key next year. Which of the following changes would BEST protect the confidentiality of today's recorded sessions?
quizOptions: A) Enable HSTS so that browsers always connect to the site over HTTPS instead of HTTP
B) Replace the server certificate with one that has a longer RSA key and a newer signature hash
C) Switch to ephemeral Diffie-Hellman cipher suites so that every session uses a unique key
D) Reduce the lifetime of the session cookies to fifteen minutes and require frequent re-authentication
detail.explanation: Ephemeral key exchange (DHE or ECDHE) creates a fresh key per session, so a later theft of the server's long-term key cannot decrypt recorded traffic. A longer certificate key still protects the same static exchange, and cookie lifetime and HSTS do not change how session keys are derived.

definition: DKIM is an email authentication method that adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages, allowing the receiving mail server to verify the message wasn't altered in transit and actually came from the claimed sending domain. It works alongside SPF and DMARC to reduce email spoofing and phishing.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know DKIM, SPF, and DMARC as the three complementary email-authentication protocols; DKIM specifically focuses on message integrity and sender verification through a digital signature in the email header.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures DKIM signing on the company's outbound mail server so every email is cryptographically signed with a private key, and publishes the matching public key in DNS. When a competitor's mail server receives a forged email claiming to be from Chen's company, the DKIM signature check fails and the message is flagged as suspicious.
detail.quizQuestion: A receiving mail server must verify that a message was not altered in transit and that the sending domain authorized it, using a signature in the message header that is checked against a public key published in the sender's DNS. Which of the following does this?
quizOptions: A) DMARC, which tells receivers how to handle messages that fail authentication
B) SPF, which lists the IP addresses that are allowed to send mail for the domain
C) DKIM, which signs messages and publishes the verification key in a DNS record
D) S/MIME, which signs and encrypts messages with a certificate issued to each sender
detail.explanation: DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to each message that receivers verify with a key published in DNS, proving integrity and domain origin. SPF checks the sending server's address, DMARC sets policy using the SPF and DKIM results, and S/MIME uses individual user certificates rather than a DNS-published domain key.

items.name: A / AAAA
items.detail: Map a hostname to an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.

items.name: CNAME
items.detail: An alias that points one name at another name.

items.name: MX
items.detail: Names the mail servers for a domain, with priorities.

items.name: NS
items.detail: Names the authoritative name servers for the zone.

items.name: PTR
items.detail: Reverse lookup: IP address to hostname.

items.name: TXT
items.detail: Free-form text. Used for domain verification and for email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).

items.name: SOA
items.detail: Start of authority: zone metadata such as the serial number and refresh timers.

items.name: SRV
items.detail: Locates a service, giving host and port.

items.name: DNSSEC
items.detail: Signs records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity (defeats cache poisoning). It does NOT encrypt queries.

items.name: DoH / DoT
items.detail: DNS over HTTPS / TLS: encrypt DNS queries for privacy.

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: A DLL is a file containing code and data that multiple programs can use simultaneously on Windows systems. Attackers exploit DLL injection or DLL hijacking to run malicious code within the context of a legitimate, trusted process, helping it evade detection.
examContext: SY0-701 tests DLL injection as a technique where malicious code is loaded into a legitimate process's memory space to inherit its permissions and evade security tools watching for suspicious standalone processes.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's EDR tool flags that a trusted system process has loaded an unsigned library from a temporary folder, a classic sign of DLL injection. Investigation reveals malware was using this technique to run its code under the identity of a legitimate Windows process, avoiding suspicion from basic process monitoring.
detail.quizQuestion: An EDR alert shows that a signed, legitimate PDF reader loaded an unfamiliar DLL from a user-writable folder and then began making outbound connections to an unknown host. Which of the following techniques MOST likely explains this behavior?
quizOptions: A) DLL hijacking, which places a malicious library where a trusted app loads it
B) A logic bomb, which triggers malicious code when a specific date or event occurs
C) A backdoor account, which gives an attacker direct login access to the host
D) Session hijacking, which steals a valid session token from a user's web browser
detail.explanation: Loading an unexpected library into a trusted process lets malicious code inherit that process's trust and permissions, which is DLL hijacking or injection. A logic bomb needs a trigger condition, a backdoor account is a login path rather than code in a process, and session hijacking targets web session tokens.

definition: DLP is a set of tools and policies that detect and block unauthorized transmission or exposure of sensitive data, such as credit card numbers or personal information leaving the network via email or USB. It enforces data handling policy automatically rather than relying on user discretion.
examContext: SY0-701 tests DLP's role in preventing data exfiltration, including scanning outbound email and removable media transfers for sensitive patterns like PII or payment card data.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys a DLP solution that scans all outbound email for patterns resembling Social Security numbers and credit card numbers. When an employee accidentally attaches a spreadsheet full of customer PII to an external email, the DLP system automatically blocks the send and alerts the security team.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to stop employees from emailing spreadsheets that contain customer credit card numbers and from copying those files to USB drives, without depending on employees to follow policy. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A DLP solution with content inspection rules on the email gateway and on the endpoints
B) Full-disk encryption on every laptop so that stolen devices cannot be read by anyone
C) A weekly SIEM report that lists the USB devices inserted on each computer in the office
D) A web application firewall placed in front of the customer-facing portal and its login page
detail.explanation: DLP inspects content for patterns such as card numbers and blocks the transfer automatically at the email gateway and endpoint. Disk encryption protects lost devices, a WAF filters web attacks, and a weekly report detects after the fact rather than preventing the leak.

expansion: Domain Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance
definition: DMARC is an email security policy standard that tells receiving mail servers what to do when a message fails SPF or DKIM checks (such as quarantine or reject it) and provides reporting back to the domain owner about authentication failures. It ties SPF and DKIM together into an enforceable, monitored policy.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM by adding enforcement (reject/quarantine/none) and reporting; a common exam distinction is that SPF/DKIM verify, while DMARC decides what happens on failure and reports back to the sender domain.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam publishes a DMARC record for the company's domain set to "reject," so that any email failing both SPF and DKIM checks is blocked outright instead of just flagged. Within weeks, the DMARC aggregate reports reveal a third party had been spoofing the company's domain for phishing, and the policy was already stopping those messages from reaching victims.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's domain is being spoofed in phishing emails sent to its customers. SPF and DKIM records are already published, yet receiving servers still deliver the spoofed messages, and the security team has no visibility into how often it happens. Which of the following should the team publish NEXT?
quizOptions: A) An S/MIME certificate for every employee mailbox so outbound messages are signed by each sender
B) A DMARC record with a quarantine or reject policy and an address for reports
C) A DKIM key with a longer key length and a shorter rotation interval for the signing selector
D) A second SPF record that lists every additional server authorized to send mail for the domain
detail.explanation: SPF and DKIM only verify. DMARC tells receivers what to do when those checks fail (none, quarantine or reject) and sends reports back to the domain owner. A domain may publish only one valid SPF record, and S/MIME protects individual messages rather than setting domain policy.

definition: A DMZ is a network segment that sits between an internal trusted network and an untrusted external network, like the internet, hosting public-facing servers such as web or mail servers. It limits the exposure of the internal network if a public-facing server is compromised.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize the DMZ as a buffer zone protected by firewalls on both sides, isolating internet-facing services from the sensitive internal LAN.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria redesigns the network so the public web server sits in a DMZ bounded by two firewalls, one facing the internet and one facing the internal LAN. When the web server is later compromised through a vulnerability, the attacker cannot pivot directly into the internal network because the second firewall blocks unauthorized traffic between the zones.
detail.quizQuestion: A company hosts a public web server and a mail relay alongside its internal file servers. The architect wants the public servers reachable from the internet, but a compromise of one of them must not give direct access to the internal LAN. Which of the following designs BEST achieves this?
quizOptions: A) Place the public servers in a DMZ with firewalls controlling traffic from the internet and from the internal network
B) Place the public servers behind a NAT device on the same subnet as the internal file servers and printers
C) Place the public servers on the internal VLAN and allow only ports 80 and 443 through the edge firewall to them
D) Place the public servers outside the firewall, directly on the internet, with host-based firewalls enabled on each
detail.explanation: A DMZ (screened subnet) isolates internet-facing servers between two sets of firewall rules, so a compromised public server still cannot reach the internal LAN directly. A flat internal network, a server with no perimeter firewall, and NAT on the same subnet each leave the internal hosts exposed.

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.

definition: DNAT is a technique that rewrites the destination IP address of incoming packets, commonly used to forward external traffic to an internal server hosted behind a firewall or router. It allows a public-facing service to use a private internal IP address.
examContext: SY0-701 may differentiate DNAT, which translates inbound destination addresses, often for port forwarding to internal servers, from standard NAT/PAT used for outbound traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures DNAT on the perimeter firewall so that traffic arriving on the public IP's port 443 is automatically forwarded to an internal web server's private address. External users never see or need to know the internal addressing scheme used behind the firewall.
detail.quizQuestion: A small company needs customers on the internet to reach an internal web server at 10.0.5.20 over TCP 443, using the firewall's single public IP address. Which of the following BEST accomplishes this?
quizOptions: A) A static route that sends traffic for 10.0.5.20 toward the internet gateway
B) A source NAT rule that translates internal addresses to the public IP for outbound traffic
C) A destination NAT rule that forwards the public address on port 443 to 10.0.5.20
D) A DHCP reservation that always assigns 10.0.5.20 to the web server
detail.explanation: DNAT rewrites the destination of inbound packets, which is how a public address and port are mapped to a private server. Source NAT or PAT handles outbound traffic, a static route only chooses a path, and a DHCP reservation keeps the server's address constant without publishing it.

items.name: Static NAT
items.detail: One-to-one fixed mapping between a private and a public address. Used to publish an internal server.

items.name: Dynamic NAT
items.detail: Private addresses are mapped to a pool of public addresses on demand.

items.name: PAT (NAT overload)
items.detail: Many private hosts share ONE public IP, distinguished by port numbers. What home routers do.

items.name: DNAT / port forwarding
items.detail: Destination NAT: rewrites the destination of inbound traffic so an outside client can reach an internal service.

items.name: Security note
items.detail: NAT hides internal addressing but is NOT a firewall; it provides no real protection by itself.

definition: DNS translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses that computers use to locate each other on a network. Because it is foundational to how users reach websites, DNS is a frequent attack target for poisoning, hijacking, and tunneling.
examContext: SY0-701 covers DNS attacks like cache poisoning and tunneling for data exfiltration, along with the DNSSEC mitigation that adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya notices unusually large and frequent DNS queries to an external domain from a single workstation, which turns out to be malware using DNS tunneling to exfiltrate stolen data past the firewall. She blocks the domain and implements DNS query monitoring to catch similar behavior going forward.
detail.quizQuestion: A SOC notices a workstation sending thousands of DNS TXT queries with long, random-looking subdomains to a single external domain. The volume of queries matches the size of a large file that is missing from a file server. Which of the following is MOST likely occurring?
quizOptions: A) A DHCP starvation attack against the local network
B) A zone transfer from the authoritative name server
C) DNS cache poisoning of the internal resolver
D) Data exfiltration through DNS tunneling
detail.explanation: Encoding data into long subdomains and sending it in many queries is DNS tunneling, a way to move data past controls that allow DNS. Cache poisoning inserts forged answers, a zone transfer copies a zone's records, and DHCP starvation exhausts address leases.

definition: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records, allowing resolvers to verify that responses have not been tampered with and genuinely originate from the authoritative source. It protects against DNS spoofing and cache poisoning attacks.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know DNSSEC provides integrity and authentication for DNS data but does not encrypt DNS queries themselves, a separate concern addressed by protocols like DNS over TLS.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen enables DNSSEC on his organization's domain so resolvers can cryptographically validate that DNS responses for the company's website truly came from the authoritative name server. A later attempted cache-poisoning attack against an ISP's resolver fails because the forged response doesn't carry a valid signature.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants resolvers to be able to verify that DNS answers for its domain really came from its authoritative servers and were not modified, but it does not need to hide the queries themselves. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) DNSSEC, which signs DNS records so resolvers can validate them
B) A longer TTL on all DNS records to reduce the number of cache misses
C) DNS over TLS, which encrypts queries between the client and the resolver
D) A split-horizon design with separate internal and external DNS zones
detail.explanation: DNSSEC provides integrity and authentication for DNS data through digital signatures, without encrypting queries. DNS over TLS hides queries but does not prove the answers are genuine, and a longer TTL or split-horizon zones do not authenticate responses.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: A DoS attack attempts to make a system or service unavailable to legitimate users, typically by overwhelming it with traffic or exploiting a resource-exhaustion flaw, originating from a single source. It differs from a DDoS attack, which uses multiple distributed sources.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes a single-source DoS from a multi-source DDoS; know both primarily target the availability leg of the CIA triad.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam traces a service outage to a single host repeatedly sending malformed packets designed to crash a vulnerable application. Because all the malicious traffic originates from one IP address, he simply blocks that address at the firewall, immediately restoring the service.
detail.quizQuestion: A single attacker sends a stream of malformed requests to a web application's search function from one IP address. Each request makes the server consume a large amount of memory until the application stops responding. Which of the following BEST describes this attack?
quizOptions: A) A denial of service attack that exhausts server resources from a single source
B) An amplification attack that abuses open DNS resolvers to multiply traffic
C) A SQL injection attack that crashes the database behind the application
D) A distributed denial of service attack that uses a botnet of compromised hosts
detail.explanation: One source exhausting a server's resources with crafted requests is a DoS attack. A DDoS uses many sources, amplification relies on third-party servers sending larger replies to a spoofed victim, and SQL injection targets database queries rather than memory.

items.name: DoS vs DDoS
items.detail: DoS comes from a single source; DDoS is distributed across many compromised devices (a botnet), so it cannot be stopped by blocking one IP.

items.name: Volumetric
items.detail: Saturates bandwidth (UDP or ICMP floods).

items.name: Protocol
items.detail: Exhausts connection-state resources, such as a SYN flood against a firewall or server's state table.

items.name: Application layer
items.detail: Low bandwidth but expensive requests (HTTP floods, Slowloris) that tie up the web application.

items.name: Amplification
items.detail: A small spoofed request makes a third-party server (open DNS, NTP or memcached) send a much larger reply to the victim.

items.name: Reflection
items.detail: The attacker spoofs the VICTIM's IP as the source so that innocent servers send their responses to the victim, hiding the real attacker.

items.name: Defenses
items.detail: Rate limiting, CDN or scrubbing services, SYN cookies, WAF, RTBH (remotely triggered black hole) routing, and over-provisioned capacity.

definition: A DPO is the individual responsible for overseeing an organization's data privacy strategy and ensuring compliance with privacy regulations such as GDPR. The DPO acts as a liaison between the organization, regulators, and individuals regarding how personal data is collected, used, and protected.
examContext: SY0-701's governance and compliance objectives expect you to recognize the DPO as the accountable role for privacy regulation compliance (like GDPR), distinct from a CSO who owns broader security risk.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya, the company's DPO, is notified of a data breach involving customer personal information and determines within hours that GDPR's 72-hour notification requirement applies. She coordinates with legal and the security team to draft the regulator notification before the deadline, avoiding a compliance violation.
detail.quizQuestion: A company that processes the personal data of EU residents must appoint someone who monitors GDPR compliance, advises on data protection impact assessments, and acts as the contact for regulators and for individuals exercising their rights. Which of the following roles is this?
quizOptions: A) The data protection officer
B) The data custodian
C) The chief information security officer
D) The data processor
detail.explanation: The DPO is the accountable role for privacy regulation compliance and the liaison to regulators and individuals. The CISO owns broader security risk, a custodian handles technical storage, and a processor is a party that handles data on a controller's behalf.

items.name: Data owner
items.detail: A senior person ACCOUNTABLE for a dataset. Decides its classification and who may access it.

items.name: Data controller
items.detail: Decides WHY and HOW personal data is processed (GDPR term). Carries the primary legal responsibility.

items.name: Data processor
items.detail: Processes personal data ON BEHALF of the controller, following its instructions (a payroll or cloud vendor).

items.name: Data custodian
items.detail: Handles the TECHNICAL side: storage, backups, access controls and protection.

items.name: Data steward
items.detail: Looks after data QUALITY and the correct labeling and use of data under policy.

items.name: Data subject
items.detail: The individual the personal data is about.

items.name: DPO
items.detail: Data Protection Officer: oversees privacy compliance (GDPR).

definition: The set of policies, tools, and procedures an organization uses to restore critical IT systems, data, and operations after a disruptive event such as a natural disaster, cyberattack, or hardware failure, typically guided by RTO and RPO targets.
examContext: SY0-701 ties DR to business continuity concepts such as BCP, RTO, and RPO; know that DR specifically focuses on restoring IT infrastructure and data after a disruption, often tested through tabletop exercises and failover drills to alternate sites.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's company suffers a ransomware attack that encrypts the primary data center's file servers. Because Jordan had built and tested a DR plan with an offsite replicated backup site, the team fails over operations to the secondary site and restores critical services within the organization's defined recovery time objective.
detail.quizQuestion: A fire destroys a company's primary data center. The recovery team must restore databases, servers and network services at an alternate site to meet a 4-hour RTO and a 1-hour RPO. Which of the following BEST describes the discipline guiding this effort?
quizOptions: A) Incident response, which contains and eradicates an active attacker
B) Business continuity, which keeps every part of the business operating
C) Disaster recovery, which restores IT systems and data after a disruption
D) Change management, which approves and schedules modifications to systems
detail.explanation: Restoring IT systems and data against RTO and RPO targets is disaster recovery. Business continuity is the broader effort to keep the whole business running, incident response deals with security incidents, and change management governs planned modifications.

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: A set of access control technologies used by content owners to restrict how digital media and software can be copied, shared, or used after distribution, enforcing licensing terms through encryption and usage restrictions.
examContext: SY0-701 discusses DRM in the context of protecting intellectual property and controlling data use after it leaves the organization's direct control; contrast it with IRM, which applies similar concepts to enterprise documents rather than commercial media.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company licenses a training video library to external partners and needs to prevent partners from redistributing the videos freely. Sam implements DRM on the video platform so each license ties playback to an authorized device and expires automatically after the contract term ends.
detail.quizQuestion: A software vendor wants to limit how many devices a customer can install its media-authoring application on, and to stop users from copying the licensed audio library that ships with it. Which of the following technologies BEST addresses this?
quizOptions: A) Data loss prevention that scans outbound email and web uploads for sensitive content
B) Information rights management that controls who can open internal company documents and files
C) Full-disk encryption that protects the data on a customer's laptop if the device is stolen
D) Digital rights management that enforces license terms through encryption and usage restrictions
detail.explanation: DRM controls how commercial software and media can be copied and used after distribution. DLP watches for data leaving a network, IRM applies similar controls to enterprise documents rather than commercial media, and disk encryption protects data on a lost device.

definition: A DRP details the specific technical steps and procedures for restoring IT systems, data, and infrastructure after a disruptive event, such as failing over to a backup data center. It is a more technical, IT-focused subset of the broader business continuity plan.
examContext: SY0-701 differentiates DRP, which restores IT/technical systems, from BCP, which keeps the overall business running; know DRP execution is measured against RTO and RPO targets.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's data center suffers a power failure, and her team follows the DRP's documented steps to fail over database replication to the secondary site within the defined RTO. Because the plan was tested quarterly, every engineer already knew their exact role, and recovery finished faster than the target window.
detail.quizQuestion: A company keeps both a business continuity plan and a disaster recovery plan. Which of the following would MOST likely be found in the disaster recovery plan rather than in the business continuity plan?
quizOptions: A) Step-by-step procedures for restoring the database cluster at the standby site
B) Manual paper workarounds for taking customer orders while systems are unavailable
C) Alternate work locations and call trees for staff who cannot reach the main office
D) Succession plans that name who takes over each executive role during an emergency
detail.explanation: A DRP is the technical, IT-focused plan for restoring systems and data, such as restoring a database at a standby site. Work locations, succession plans and manual workarounds keep the business operating and belong to the broader business continuity plan.

items.name: RTO
items.detail: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable TIME to restore a service. "How long can we be down?"

items.name: RPO
items.detail: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable DATA LOSS, measured as time since the last good backup. "How much data can we lose?" It sets backup frequency.

items.name: MTTR
items.detail: Mean Time To Repair/Restore: the average time to fix a failed component or service.

items.name: MTBF
items.detail: Mean Time Between Failures: the average time a REPAIRABLE system runs between failures. A reliability measure.

items.name: MTTF
items.detail: Mean Time To Failure: the average lifespan of a NON-repairable component (it is replaced rather than repaired).

items.name: MTD
items.detail: Maximum Tolerable Downtime: the longest outage a business function can survive before the damage is unacceptable; RTO must be shorter than MTD.

items.name: BIA
items.detail: Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical functions and sets their RTO and RPO.

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: DSA is a public-key cryptographic algorithm used specifically for creating and verifying digital signatures, providing authentication and non-repudiation, though it is not used for encryption. It has largely been supplemented by RSA and ECC-based signature schemes in modern systems.
examContext: SY0-701 may list DSA alongside RSA and ECC as digital signature algorithms; know DSA is signature-only, unlike RSA, which can also perform encryption.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team needs to digitally sign software updates so customers can verify authenticity before installing, but has no need to encrypt the update files themselves. They select DSA for generating the signing keys, since the requirement is purely for verifiable, non-repudiable signatures rather than confidentiality.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer needs an algorithm that is used only to create and verify digital signatures on software releases, with no ability to encrypt data. Which of the following algorithms fits this description?
quizOptions: A) RSA, which can both sign data and encrypt it with a public key
B) Diffie-Hellman, which lets two parties agree on a shared secret key
C) DSA, which can create and verify signatures but cannot encrypt data
D) AES, which encrypts bulk data quickly using a shared secret key
detail.explanation: DSA is signature-only, providing authentication and non-repudiation without encryption. RSA can also encrypt, AES is a symmetric cipher with no signing, and Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange method.

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: DSL is a technology that delivers high-speed internet access over traditional copper telephone lines, commonly used for small office or home internet connectivity. It is generally slower and less resilient than fiber or dedicated business circuits, which matters when evaluating a site's connectivity risk.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference DSL in the context of remote site or branch office connectivity and availability/resilience planning, where a single DSL line represents a single point of failure compared to redundant diverse-path circuits.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan reviews a branch office's network resilience and finds it relies on a single DSL line with no backup connection. He arranges a secondary cellular failover link so that if the DSL line goes down, the branch's point-of-sale systems can still reach the payment processor.
detail.quizQuestion: A branch office depends on a single DSL line for all of its WAN connectivity. Management says an outage would stop all sales and asks the security team to improve availability within a modest budget. Which of the following BEST addresses the risk?
quizOptions: A) Upgrade the DSL plan to a faster download speed and a larger data allowance from the same provider
B) Install a stronger next-generation firewall with intrusion prevention at the branch office edge
C) Add a second internet connection from a different provider that follows a physically diverse path
D) Encrypt all of the branch office traffic with a site-to-site VPN back to the headquarters
detail.explanation: The risk is a single point of failure, so the fix is redundancy over a different provider and path. A faster plan, a stronger firewall and a VPN do not keep the branch online when the one circuit fails.

definition: A set of security requirements established by the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council that organizations handling credit card data must follow to protect cardholder information, covering network security, access control, and encryption.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize DSS in the context of PCI DSS; any organization that stores, processes, or transmits credit card data must comply, and the standard mandates specific controls like network segmentation of cardholder data environments and regular vulnerability scanning.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's e-commerce company processes thousands of credit card transactions and must segment the network to isolate systems that handle cardholder data. Jordan implements network segmentation and quarterly vulnerability scans to satisfy PCI DSS requirements, reducing the scope of systems subject to the strictest audit controls.
detail.quizQuestion: A retailer processes online credit card payments. Auditors tell the company it must segment its cardholder data environment and run regular vulnerability scans to satisfy a security standard required by its payment processor. Which of the following standards are they describing?
quizOptions: A) FISMA, a law that requires federal agencies to run a security program
B) PCI DSS, a contractual standard for organizations that handle payment card data
C) HIPAA, a law that protects the privacy and security of patient health information
D) SOX, a law that governs financial reporting controls at public companies
detail.explanation: PCI DSS is the security standard set by the payment card industry for anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data, and it requires controls such as segmentation and regular scanning. The other options are laws for health data, public company financial reporting and federal agencies.

definition: EAP is a flexible authentication framework used in wireless networks and point-to-point connections, supporting multiple authentication methods like certificates, tokens, and passwords. It's commonly used with 802.1X for enterprise Wi-Fi authentication.
examContext: SY0-701 references EAP variants such as EAP-TLS and PEAP in the context of enterprise wireless authentication delivered through 802.1X and a RADIUS server.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the corporate wireless network to use EAP-TLS, requiring each laptop to present a client certificate rather than just a shared password before connecting. A stolen Wi-Fi password alone is now useless to an attacker, since authentication depends on possessing the issued certificate as well.
detail.quizQuestion: A company deploys WPA3-Enterprise and wants each user to authenticate with a digital certificate instead of a password. The access points will pass authentication requests to a RADIUS server. Which of the following EAP methods should be configured?
quizOptions: A) EAP-TLS, which uses certificates on both the client and the server
B) WPA3-Personal, which uses a single passphrase shared by every user
C) LEAP, a legacy Cisco method that is vulnerable to dictionary attacks
D) PEAP, which tunnels a password-based inner method inside a TLS session
detail.explanation: EAP-TLS authenticates with certificates on both sides, which removes passwords entirely. PEAP still relies on a password for the inner authentication, WPA3-Personal is not an EAP method, and LEAP is a weak legacy method.

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

definition: ECB is the simplest block cipher mode, encrypting each fixed-size block of plaintext independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks. This makes it insecure for most real data because patterns in the plaintext remain visible in the ciphertext.
examContext: SY0-701 often uses ECB as the example of a cipher mode to avoid; remember the classic exam clue is a famously visible pattern leaking through in encrypted image data, which illustrates why ECB should not be used for anything beyond trivial, single-block data.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is reviewing an application's encryption implementation and notices repeating patterns in encrypted image files, a telltale sign the developers used ECB mode. She has the team switch to GCM mode instead, which eliminates the pattern leakage and adds built-in integrity protection.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer encrypts a company logo with AES in ECB mode and notices that the outline of the logo is still visible in the encrypted image. Which of the following changes would BEST fix this problem?
quizOptions: A) Compress the image with a lossless algorithm before it is encrypted with the same key
B) Encode the encrypted output in Base64 before the image is stored or sent to other users
C) Increase the AES key length from 128 bits to 256 bits and keep using the same mode
D) Use a mode such as CBC or GCM with a unique initialization vector for each encryption
detail.explanation: ECB encrypts identical blocks to identical ciphertext, so patterns survive no matter how long the key is. Modes such as CBC and GCM with a unique IV hide the patterns. Compression and Base64 encoding do not change the mode's weakness.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: ECC is a public-key cryptography approach based on the mathematics of elliptic curves, providing equivalent security to RSA with much smaller key sizes. This makes it efficient for mobile devices and constrained environments.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know ECC offers strong security with smaller keys than RSA, making it preferred for performance-constrained devices like smartphones and IoT sensors.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan selects ECC instead of RSA for a fleet of battery-powered IoT sensors because it delivers comparable security with a fraction of the processing overhead and key size. The devices can now perform TLS handshakes quickly without draining their batteries as fast as RSA would have required.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is designing an application for battery-powered IoT sensors that must perform public-key operations. Engineers want security comparable to a 3072-bit RSA key but with smaller keys and less processing. Which of the following should they choose?
quizOptions: A) AES with a 256-bit key in Galois/Counter Mode for bulk encryption
B) RSA with a 4096-bit key and the OAEP padding scheme for encryption
C) DSA with a 1024-bit key and a SHA-1 digest for signing messages
D) Elliptic curve cryptography with a 256-bit key and a standard curve
detail.explanation: A 256-bit elliptic curve key gives roughly the strength of a 3072-bit RSA key with far less computation, which suits constrained devices. A 4096-bit RSA key is heavier, a 1024-bit DSA key is too weak, and AES is symmetric, so it does not provide public-key operations.

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: A variant of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange that uses elliptic curve cryptography instead of traditional modular arithmetic, achieving the same shared-secret negotiation with much smaller key sizes and lower computational overhead.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know ECDH provides the efficiency benefits of elliptic curve cryptography, meaning smaller keys and faster computation, applied specifically to key exchange, making it popular for mobile devices and TLS 1.3 cipher suites.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is configuring TLS settings for a mobile banking app and wants strong key exchange security without draining battery life on low-power devices. Maria selects cipher suites using ECDH instead of traditional Diffie-Hellman, achieving equivalent security with significantly smaller key sizes and faster handshakes.
detail.quizQuestion: A mobile app and its server establish a session key during a TLS 1.3 handshake. The architect wants an efficient elliptic curve method that negotiates a shared secret but does not by itself create digital signatures. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) ECDH, which negotiates a shared secret using elliptic curves
B) ECDSA, which signs messages using elliptic curves
C) DSA, which signs messages using modular arithmetic
D) RSA, which signs and encrypts using large prime factors
detail.explanation: ECDH is the elliptic curve form of Diffie-Hellman key exchange. ECDSA and DSA are signature algorithms, and RSA is a general-purpose public-key algorithm that is not an elliptic curve method.

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: ECDHE combines elliptic curve cryptography with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange, generating a fresh temporary key pair for each session using much smaller and faster elliptic curve keys than traditional DHE. It is the preferred key exchange method in modern TLS because it is both fast and provides forward secrecy.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize ECDHE as the modern, efficient standard for TLS key exchange, offering the same forward-secrecy benefit as DHE but with better performance due to smaller elliptic curve keys.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen upgrades the company's load balancers to prioritize ECDHE cipher suites over classic DHE suites, cutting the TLS handshake's CPU overhead significantly while keeping forward secrecy. Mobile app users notice the connection feels noticeably faster, especially on lower-powered devices.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's TLS configuration uses a static ECDH key. An auditor requires forward secrecy, so that a stolen long-term key cannot decrypt past sessions, with minimal performance cost on mobile clients. Which of the following changes BEST meets the requirement?
quizOptions: A) Use ECDHE cipher suites so that a new key pair is generated for every session
B) Use RSA key exchange with a 4096-bit certificate and a SHA-256 signature on the server
C) Use ECDSA certificates for authentication and disable session resumption on the server
D) Use static ECDH with a larger curve and rotate the server key once every year
detail.explanation: ECDHE generates an ephemeral key per session, which provides forward secrecy and is fast on elliptic curves. A bigger static key and yearly rotation still expose every session between rotations, RSA key exchange has no forward secrecy, and ECDSA certificates only authenticate the server.

items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: A digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curve cryptography that provides the same authentication and non-repudiation guarantees as traditional signature algorithms like DSA or RSA, but with smaller key sizes and faster performance.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know ECDSA is used for digital signatures, proving authenticity and integrity, not key exchange; contrast it with ECDH, which is used for key exchange, and note it is commonly found in TLS certificates and cryptocurrency transactions.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company is issuing new TLS certificates for its web servers and wants smaller certificate sizes with faster signing operations. Sam selects ECDSA as the signature algorithm for the certificate authority's issued certificates, reducing handshake overhead while maintaining strong authentication guarantees.
detail.quizQuestion: A software publisher wants to sign its releases with an algorithm that uses small keys, verifies quickly on mobile devices, and provides non-repudiation. Which of the following should it choose?
quizOptions: A) HMAC-SHA256, which authenticates data with a shared secret key
B) AES-GCM, which encrypts data and adds an authentication tag
C) ECDSA, which signs data using elliptic curve keys
D) ECDH, which agrees on a shared key using elliptic curves
detail.explanation: Non-repudiation needs an asymmetric signature, and ECDSA provides one with small, fast keys. ECDH is for key exchange, while AES-GCM and HMAC use shared secrets, so they cannot prove who signed.

definition: EDR is a security solution that continuously monitors endpoint activity, detects suspicious behavior, and enables rapid investigation and response, going beyond traditional signature-based antivirus. It typically provides visibility into process execution, network connections, and file changes on a host.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts EDR's behavioral, response-capable monitoring with traditional AV's signature-based detection; EDR is often a prerequisite for effective incident response on endpoints.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's EDR agent flags a process spawning an unusual child process that attempts to disable logging, a behavior no signature-based antivirus would catch. He uses the EDR console to isolate the host remotely within seconds, stopping lateral movement before the attacker can reach other systems.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst must investigate a suspicious process on a remote laptop by viewing its parent process, network connections and file changes, and then isolate the host from the network without touching the device. Which of the following tools provides these capabilities?
quizOptions: A) A network-based IDS connected to a SPAN port on the core switch
B) A vulnerability scanner that runs weekly against the corporate network
C) A traditional signature-based antivirus scanner on each laptop
D) An EDR platform with a lightweight agent installed on each endpoint
detail.explanation: EDR records endpoint activity and lets analysts investigate and respond remotely, including network isolation. A network IDS sees only traffic, signature antivirus only looks for known files, and a vulnerability scanner finds weaknesses rather than investigating processes.

definition: EF is the percentage of an asset's value that would be lost if a specific risk event occurred. It's used together with asset value to calculate the Single Loss Expectancy in quantitative risk assessment.
examContext: SY0-701 tests EF as part of the SLE formula, SLE = Asset Value x EF; know EF is expressed as a percentage of loss, not a dollar figure by itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria estimates that a successful ransomware attack on a $100,000 file server would destroy about 40% of its business value due to downtime and recovery costs, setting the exposure factor at 0.4. Combined with the asset value, this gives her the SLE figure needed for the next step of the risk calculation.
detail.quizQuestion: A building's contents are valued at $800,000. Risk analysts expect a fire to destroy $200,000 of the contents, and they expect a fire about once every ten years. Which of the following is the exposure factor?
quizOptions: A) 10 percent
B) 25 percent
D) 75 percent
detail.explanation: Exposure factor is the percentage of an asset's value lost in an event: $200,000 divided by $800,000 is 25 percent. The $200,000 figure is the single loss expectancy, not a percentage, and the once-in-ten-years estimate is the annualized rate of occurrence.

items.name: Qualitative
items.detail: Uses descriptive ratings (high / medium / low) on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix. Quick and subjective.

items.name: Quantitative
items.detail: Uses numbers and currency to calculate expected loss. More objective, but needs good data.

items.name: SLE
items.detail: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value (AV) x Exposure Factor (EF). The cost of ONE incident.

items.name: ARO
items.detail: Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.

items.name: ALE
items.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO. Compare it with the annual cost of a control to see if the control pays for itself.

items.name: Worked example
items.detail: A laptop worth $2,000 (AV) with 100% EF has an SLE of $2,000. If theft is expected once every two years (ARO 0.5), ALE = $1,000 a year, so a $300 a year tracking service is worth buying.

items.name: Assessment frequency
items.detail: Ad hoc (as needed), recurring (scheduled), one-time (for a project) or continuous (ongoing monitoring).

items.name: Key risk indicators
items.detail: Metrics that signal rising risk before an incident, such as the number of unpatched critical systems.

definition: EFS is a Windows feature that transparently encrypts individual files and folders on an NTFS volume, tied to the user's account credentials. It protects data at rest from other local users but not from an attacker who compromises the user's own login.
examContext: SY0-701 may contrast EFS, which encrypts at the file/folder level, with FDE, which encrypts an entire disk via BitLocker; know EFS keys are tied to a specific user account.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam encrypts a folder containing sensitive HR documents using EFS on a shared workstation with multiple local accounts. When a different user account logs into the same machine, that folder's contents remain unreadable because the encryption key is tied specifically to the HR user's credentials.
detail.quizQuestion: A sales rep wants specific folders on a shared Windows laptop to stay encrypted per user account, so a second user who logs in to the same laptop cannot read them even after the volume has been unlocked. Which of the following technologies BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) EFS, which encrypts individual files with keys tied to the user's account
B) A TPM, which seals keys to the measured boot configuration
C) A self-encrypting drive, which encrypts all data in the drive controller
D) BitLocker, which encrypts the entire volume with one key
detail.explanation: EFS encrypts at the file and folder level using keys tied to a specific user, so another account on the same unlocked system cannot read the files.
