Full-disk approaches such as BitLocker and self-encrypting drives protect data at rest for all users once the system is running, and a TPM stores keys rather than separating users.

items.name: Full-disk
items.detail: Everything on the drive, including the OS (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS). Protects a lost or stolen device; data is exposed once the system is unlocked and running.

items.name: Partition / volume
items.detail: One partition or logical volume is encrypted while others stay in the clear.

items.name: File / folder
items.detail: Individual files (EFS, GPG, 7-Zip AES). Protects specific data even from other users of the same machine.

items.name: Database
items.detail: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) encrypts the database files; column- or record-level encryption protects individual fields such as SSNs.

items.name: Transport / communication
items.detail: Protects data in motion: TLS, IPsec, SSH, WPA3. The data is not necessarily encrypted at the other end.

definition: EMM is a broader category of tools that combines mobile device management, mobile application management, and content management to secure and control mobile devices and the data they access. It extends beyond basic device-level controls to cover apps and content policy as well.
examContext: SY0-701 treats EMM as an umbrella term encompassing MDM and MAM capabilities; know it's about managing mobile endpoints holistically, not just enforcing device-level settings.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company adopts an EMM platform that combines device-level passcode enforcement with application-level controls restricting corporate email to an approved, containerized app. This lets her manage both the device settings and the specific apps handling sensitive data from a single console.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants one platform to enforce a passcode on managed phones, distribute and update approved apps, and control access to corporate documents on those phones. Which of the following BEST describes the solution?
quizOptions: A) Enterprise mobility management, which combines device, app and content management
B) Mobile application management used by itself, which controls only individual apps
C) Mobile device management used by itself, which controls only device-level settings
D) Network access control, which checks device health on wired switch ports
detail.explanation: EMM is the umbrella that combines MDM, MAM and content management, which covers the device, its apps and the documents. MDM or MAM alone covers only part of the requirement, and NAC controls network access rather than managing phones.

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: EOL marks the point at which a vendor stops selling or actively developing a product, though limited support may continue for a period afterward. Running EOL software carries risk because future vulnerabilities may not receive timely patches.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes EOL, where the vendor stops active development, from EOS, where the vendor stops all support entirely; both represent escalating risk of running unsupported systems.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan discovers that a critical business application depends on a database version the vendor has marked EOL, meaning no further feature updates will be released. He begins budgeting for a migration project now, well ahead of the eventual EOS date when security patches will stop entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: A vendor announces that a database product will no longer be sold or developed after December, although security patches will continue for another two years. Which of the following BEST describes the product's status in December?
quizOptions: A) Retired, because the vendor has removed all of the product's documentation
B) Fully supported, because the vendor is still releasing security patches
C) End of service, because the vendor has stopped all support and security patches
D) End of life, because the vendor has stopped selling and developing it
detail.explanation: End of life is when a vendor stops selling and actively developing a product, often with limited support afterward. End of service is later, when all support and patches stop, so the product is not yet at that point.

definition: EOS is the date after which a vendor no longer provides any support, updates, or security patches for a product. Systems running past their EOS date are considered high risk since newly discovered vulnerabilities will never be fixed.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize EOS/EOL systems as a significant vulnerability management concern, often requiring compensating controls, isolation, or a forced upgrade.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's vulnerability scan flags a firewall running firmware that reached its EOS date two years ago, meaning any newly discovered flaw in it will never be patched. She isolates the device on a restricted VLAN and accelerates its replacement, since no vendor fix will ever be coming.
detail.quizQuestion: A company runs a critical legacy application on an operating system whose vendor ended all support and security updates last year. The application cannot be migrated for 18 months. Which of the following is the BEST way to reduce risk in the meantime?
quizOptions: A) Wait for the vendor to publish an exceptional out-of-band patch for the next critical flaw found
B) Raise the complexity requirements and lockout thresholds for the application's administrator passwords
C) Isolate the system on its own segment, restrict access with strict firewall rules, and add monitoring
D) Rely on regularly updated antivirus signatures to catch exploit attempts against the old OS
detail.explanation: Unpatched flaws will never be fixed, so compensating controls such as isolation, strict access rules and monitoring reduce exposure until migration. Antivirus does not cover OS flaws, the vendor will not release patches, and stronger passwords do not stop exploitation of a vulnerability.

definition: A holistic, organization-wide approach to identifying, assessing, and managing risks across all business functions, not just IT, so that risk decisions align with overall strategic objectives and risk appetite.
examContext: SY0-701 ties ERM to the broader organizational context of risk management, where cybersecurity risk is just one category managed alongside financial, operational, and reputational risk under a unified governance structure.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's CISO wants cybersecurity risk reported in the same terms the board already uses for financial and operational risk, rather than as an isolated IT concern. Jordan integrates the security risk register into the company's ERM program, presenting cyber risk alongside supply chain and financial risks using a consistent scoring methodology the board already understands.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's risk register tracks IT risks separately from financial, operational and reputational risks, so executives cannot see which risks most threaten the company's strategic objectives. Which of the following approaches would BEST fix this?
quizOptions: A) A separate risk register for each business unit, managed by that unit's own leader
B) A larger security budget and more analysts for the information security team to hire this year
C) A deeper technical vulnerability assessment of the whole IT environment and its supply chain
D) Enterprise risk management that rates every type of risk against the same appetite and strategy
detail.explanation: ERM manages risk across the whole organization under one governance structure, so cyber risk can be compared with other risks against strategy. More technical assessment, more budget and separate registers keep risks siloed.

definition: An ERP system is an integrated software platform that manages an organization's core business processes, such as finance, HR, supply chain, and inventory, in one centralized system. Because ERP systems aggregate so much sensitive business data in one place, they are high-value targets requiring strong access controls and monitoring.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference ERP systems as an example of a large, business-critical application where role-based access control and segregation of duties (e.g., preventing one person from both creating and approving a vendor payment) are essential security requirements.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures role-based access control in the company's ERP system so that the employee who creates a new vendor record cannot also be the one who approves payments to that vendor. This segregation of duties closes a fraud loophole that an internal audit had previously flagged.
detail.quizQuestion: An auditor finds that one employee in the ERP system can create new vendors, enter invoices for them and approve payments. Which of the following controls would BEST reduce the risk of fraud?
quizOptions: A) Require the employee to use multifactor authentication when signing in to the ERP
B) Enforce role-based access with separation of duties for vendor creation and payment approval
C) Encrypt the ERP database at rest with a stronger algorithm and a longer key
D) Back up the ERP system every night to offsite storage and test the restores each quarter
detail.explanation: The weakness is one authorized person controlling every step of a payment, so separation of duties through role-based access is the fix. MFA only confirms who signed in, encryption protects stored data, and backups support recovery, none of which stop an insider from committing fraud.

definition: An ESN is a unique identifier burned into older mobile phone hardware to distinguish one physical device from another on a cellular network, a predecessor to the modern IMEI. It can be used for device tracking, fraud detection, or blocking a stolen device from the network.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference ESN alongside IMEI/SIM identifiers in the context of mobile device management and tracking lost or stolen devices; know it is a hardware-level identifier distinct from a phone number or account.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's company reports a stolen company phone's ESN to the carrier, who blacklists that identifier across the network so the device cannot be activated on any carrier using that database. This renders the stolen hardware useless even if the thief swaps the SIM card.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee's lost phone is now being used with a different SIM card. The security team wants the carrier to block the physical handset regardless of which SIM is inserted. Which of the following can be used to identify the handset?
quizOptions: A) The device's hardware identifier, such as the IMEI or ESN
B) The employee's account password for the corporate email system
C) The subscriber's phone number assigned to the old SIM
D) The issuer certificate stored on the phone's SIM card
detail.explanation: A hardware identifier such as the IMEI or ESN identifies the handset itself, so it can be blocked whatever SIM is inserted. The phone number and issuer certificate belong to the SIM, and an account password is not a device identifier.

definition: ESP is an IPsec protocol that provides confidentiality through encryption, as well as integrity and authentication, for IP packet payloads. It is the more commonly used IPsec component since it offers encryption, unlike AH.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs ESP with AH within IPsec; remember ESP provides encryption plus authentication, making it the typical choice for VPN tunnels that require confidentiality.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures a site-to-site VPN to use IPsec with ESP in tunnel mode so that both the header and payload of every packet between the two offices are fully encrypted. An attacker capturing traffic between the sites sees only unreadable ciphertext rather than the original internal IP addressing or data.
detail.quizQuestion: A company builds an IPsec VPN between two offices and requires that the traffic be encrypted as well as authenticated. Which of the following IPsec protocols must be used?
quizOptions: A) IKE used alone, which only negotiates keys and security associations
B) GRE used alone, which encapsulates traffic without protecting it
C) ESP, which encrypts the payload and provides integrity and authentication
D) AH, which authenticates packets but does not encrypt them
detail.explanation: ESP provides confidentiality through encryption in addition to integrity and authentication. AH authenticates but leaves the payload readable, IKE only sets up keys, and GRE is a tunneling protocol with no security of its own.

items.name: AH
items.detail: Authentication Header: integrity and authentication of the whole packet but NO encryption. IP protocol 51, and it breaks when NAT rewrites the header.

items.name: ESP
items.detail: Encapsulating Security Payload: encryption plus (optional) integrity and authentication. IP protocol 50. This is what provides confidentiality.

items.name: Transport mode
items.detail: Encrypts only the payload and keeps the original IP header; typically host-to-host.

items.name: Tunnel mode
items.detail: Encrypts the entire original packet and wraps it in a new IP header; typically gateway-to-gateway (site-to-site VPN).

items.name: IKE
items.detail: Internet Key Exchange: negotiates the security associations and keys (UDP 500; UDP 4500 for NAT traversal).

definition: A FACL is a list attached to a file or directory that specifies exactly which users or groups can read, write, or execute it, offering more granular control than basic owner/group/everyone permission models. It lets administrators grant specific permissions to additional users without changing the file's basic ownership.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know FACLs as a more granular alternative to standard Unix permission bits, allowing multiple distinct users or groups to have different permission levels on the same file or folder.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan needs to give one contractor read-only access to a shared project folder without changing the folder's existing owner or group permissions for everyone else. He adds a FACL entry granting that specific user read access, leaving the standard permission bits untouched for all other users.
detail.quizQuestion: On a Linux file server, a project file is owned by user alice and group dev. An administrator must give user bob read and write access and user carol read access to the same file, without changing its owner or group or adding them to dev. Which of the following should the administrator use?
quizOptions: A) A change of ownership that makes bob the sole owner of the entire file
B) A symbolic link to the file that is placed in each user's home directory
C) File system access control lists that add per-user entries to the file
D) A chmod change that grants read and write permission to all other users
detail.explanation: A FACL lets an administrator grant specific permissions to additional users or groups on a file without changing its ownership. Granting everyone access is far too broad, changing the owner removes alice's control, and a symbolic link does not grant permissions.

definition: FDE encrypts an entire storage drive, including the operating system, applications, and data, so that the contents are unreadable without the correct key or credentials. It protects data at rest if a device is lost or stolen, as long as it's powered off or locked.
examContext: SY0-701 references FDE solutions like BitLocker; know FDE protects data at rest but offers no protection once the system is unlocked and running.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam enables FDE on every company laptop, storing the recovery keys centrally in case a password is forgotten. When a sales employee's laptop is later stolen from a car, the thief cannot access any corporate data because the entire drive remains encrypted and the device is locked.
detail.quizQuestion: An executive's laptop, protected with full-disk encryption, is stolen from a conference table while the screen is unlocked. Which of the following statements BEST explains the risk to the data?
quizOptions: A) FDE protects data at rest only while the volume is locked, so an unlocked running system exposes its data
B) FDE cannot be combined with a screen lock, so the data was always exposed to anyone who held it
C) FDE encrypts only the operating system partition, so the executive's files were never protected
D) FDE keys are stored in plaintext on the drive, so a thief can simply read them and decrypt everything
detail.explanation: Full-disk encryption protects a drive that is powered off or locked, but once the system is unlocked the data is decrypted for use, so a thief with the running laptop can reach it. The other statements describe weaknesses that FDE does not have.

items.name: Full-disk
items.detail: Everything on the drive, including the OS (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS). Protects a lost or stolen device; data is exposed once the system is unlocked and running.

items.name: Partition / volume
items.detail: One partition or logical volume is encrypted while others stay in the clear.

items.name: File / folder
items.detail: Individual files (EFS, GPG, 7-Zip AES). Protects specific data even from other users of the same machine.

items.name: Database
items.detail: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) encrypts the database files; column- or record-level encryption protects individual fields such as SSNs.

items.name: Transport / communication
items.detail: Protects data in motion: TLS, IPsec, SSH, WPA3. The data is not necessarily encrypted at the other end.

expansion: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program
definition: A US government program that standardizes security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring requirements for cloud products and services used by federal agencies, allowing a single authorization to be reused across multiple agencies.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know FedRAMP specifically governs cloud service providers selling to the federal government, and that it uses a do-once-use-many-times authorization model to avoid redundant assessments across agencies.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's cloud startup wants to sell its SaaS platform to federal government agencies and learns every agency customer will require the same rigorous security authorization. Sam pursues a single FedRAMP authorization so the platform can be adopted by multiple federal agencies without repeating the full assessment process for each one.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud provider wants to sell its SaaS product to several U.S. federal agencies and would like to be assessed once, with the resulting authorization reused by many agencies. Which of the following programs provides this?
quizOptions: A) SOC 2, which gives customers an audit report on a service organization's controls
B) PCI DSS, which sets security requirements for organizations that handle payment card data
C) FISMA, which requires federal agencies to run an information security program of their own
D) FedRAMP, which standardizes the assessment and authorization of cloud services for federal use
detail.explanation: FedRAMP uses a do-once, use-many-times model for authorizing cloud services sold to the federal government. FISMA applies to the agencies' own programs, PCI DSS covers card data, and SOC 2 is an audit report that is not an authorization for federal use.

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: FIM is a security control that monitors critical files and system configurations for unauthorized changes, alerting administrators when unexpected modifications occur. It helps detect malware, tampering, or unauthorized configuration drift.
examContext: SY0-701 tests FIM as a detective control for identifying unauthorized changes to critical system or configuration files, typically using cryptographic hashes to detect any modification.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya deploys a FIM tool that calculates and stores a hash of every critical system file on the production web servers. When an attacker later replaces a legitimate system binary with a trojanized version, the FIM tool immediately detects the hash mismatch and alerts the SOC.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to be alerted whenever anyone changes system binaries, configuration files or web content on a production server outside an approved change, using cryptographic hashes of the files as the baseline. Which of the following BEST fits this requirement?
quizOptions: A) Network access control, which checks device health before granting access to the network
B) Data loss prevention, which blocks sensitive data from leaving the network by email or USB
C) A web application firewall, which filters malicious HTTP requests aimed at the web server
D) File integrity monitoring, which compares current file hashes with a trusted baseline
detail.explanation: FIM is a detective control that alerts when monitored files differ from a hashed baseline. DLP, NAC and a WAF address data leakage, device admission and web attacks, not unauthorized changes to files.

definition: A US federal law that requires federal agencies and their contractors to develop, document, and implement an information security program to protect government data and systems, with NIST providing the standards and guidelines for compliance.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to associate FISMA with federal agency security requirements and its close relationship to the NIST Risk Management Framework, which agencies use to implement FISMA's mandated controls.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya works for a government contractor that must demonstrate compliance with federal information security requirements before being awarded a new contract. Priya leads the team through implementing the NIST Risk Management Framework to satisfy FISMA requirements, documenting security controls for the agency's authorizing official to review.
detail.quizQuestion: A contractor that operates information systems on behalf of a federal agency asks which law requires it to implement an information security program guided by NIST standards. Which of the following applies?
quizOptions: A) SOX, which requires internal controls over financial reporting at publicly traded companies
B) GDPR, which governs how organizations collect and process the personal data of EU residents
C) FISMA, which requires federal agencies and their contractors to run an information security program
D) HIPAA, which requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards for protected health information
detail.explanation: FISMA requires federal agencies and their contractors to develop and implement an information security program, using NIST standards and the Risk Management Framework. The other laws cover health data, EU privacy and public company financial reporting.

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: An FPGA is a reconfigurable integrated circuit that can be programmed after manufacturing to perform custom hardware functions, including cryptographic acceleration. In security, FPGAs are used in HSMs and specialized devices for high-performance, hardware-based cryptographic operations.
examContext: SY0-701 mentions FPGAs in the context of hardware-based cryptographic acceleration and embedded or ICS security, offering reconfigurable flexibility that fixed-function chips lack.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's team builds a hardware security appliance using an FPGA to perform AES encryption at line speed for a high-throughput network link. Because the FPGA is reprogrammable, the team later updates it to support a new cipher mode without replacing the physical hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: A payment processor needs hardware that can be reprogrammed in the field to accelerate a new cryptographic algorithm without replacing the device, while still being faster than a general-purpose CPU. Which of the following components BEST fits this requirement?
quizOptions: A) An FPGA, a chip that is programmed after manufacturing for custom hardware functions
B) A GPU, a processor designed for rendering graphics and for massively parallel arithmetic
C) A TPM, a secure chip that stores keys and attests to boot integrity
D) An ASIC, a chip whose logic is fixed permanently when it is manufactured and cannot change
detail.explanation: An FPGA is reconfigurable after manufacturing, so its logic can be updated for a new algorithm while staying fast. An ASIC cannot be changed once built, a TPM stores keys rather than accelerating arbitrary algorithms, and a GPU is a fixed processor design.

definition: FRR is a biometric accuracy metric measuring how often a system incorrectly denies access to a legitimate, authorized user. A high FRR frustrates real users with repeated failed scans, so it must be balanced against the false acceptance rate, which measures how often impostors are wrongly let in.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know FRR alongside FAR and the crossover error rate as the key metrics for evaluating biometric authentication system accuracy and tuning its sensitivity threshold.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company rolls out fingerprint scanners at the data center entrance, but employees complain they're frequently denied entry even with a valid fingerprint. Chen realizes the scanner's sensitivity is tuned too aggressively, producing a high false rejection rate, and adjusts the threshold to reduce legitimate users being turned away while still catching impostors.
detail.quizQuestion: A fingerprint reader at a data center door often rejects authorized staff, who must scan several times. Management wants fewer lockouts of legitimate users but is concerned about weakening security. Which of the following statements BEST describes the problem and the trade-off?
quizOptions: A) The false acceptance rate is high; loosening the sensitivity will reduce it but may increase false rejections
B) The false rejection rate is high; tightening the sensitivity will reduce it and also reduce false acceptances
C) The false rejection rate is high; loosening the sensitivity will reduce it but may increase false acceptances
D) The crossover error rate is low; no change to the sensitivity is needed to fix the problem
detail.explanation: Rejecting authorized users is the false rejection rate. Lowering the matching threshold admits more genuine users but also lets more impostors through, so FRR and FAR trade off against each other, with the crossover error rate marking where they are equal.

items.name: Fingerprint
items.detail: Cheap and widely accepted, but can be fooled by lifted prints or fakes unless liveness detection is used.

items.name: Retina
items.detail: Scans the blood-vessel pattern at the back of the eye. Very accurate but intrusive, so uncommon.

items.name: Iris
items.detail: Scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Accurate and stable over a lifetime, and less intrusive than retina.

items.name: Facial recognition
items.detail: Convenient, but affected by lighting and angle, and spoofable with photos or masks without liveness checks.

items.name: Voice
items.detail: Affected by noise and illness; spoofable with recordings or deepfakes.

items.name: Vein / palm
items.detail: Maps the pattern of blood vessels; difficult to forge.

items.name: Gait
items.detail: A behavioral biometric based on how a person walks.

items.name: FRR (Type I)
items.detail: False Rejection Rate: a LEGITIMATE user is wrongly denied. Hurts usability.

items.name: FAR (Type II)
items.detail: False Acceptance Rate: an IMPOSTOR is wrongly allowed in. This is the dangerous one for security.

items.name: CER / EER
items.detail: Crossover (Equal) Error Rate: the point where FAR equals FRR. The LOWER the CER, the more accurate the system.

definition: FTP is a protocol for transferring files between a client and server over a network, but it transmits data, including credentials, in plaintext by default. It should be replaced by secure alternatives like FTPS or SFTP in any security-conscious environment.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize FTP as insecure, unencrypted, and running on port 21, and to prefer FTPS or SFTP instead; a classic distractor tests whether you know FTP alone offers no encryption.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's network capture tool reveals plaintext usernames and passwords being transmitted every time a legacy application connects to a file server over FTP. She migrates the application to use SFTP instead, immediately eliminating the credential exposure without changing the underlying file transfer workflow.
detail.quizQuestion: A vendor's nightly job uploads files to the company's FTP server on port 21. A packet capture shows the vendor's username and password in readable text. The vendor's software also supports SSH and TLS-based file transfer. Which of the following is the BEST fix?
quizOptions: A) Move the FTP service to a nonstandard port that scanners do not check
B) Block TCP port 20 on the firewall so that the data connection is not used
C) Require the vendor to choose a longer password for the FTP account
D) Replace FTP with SFTP or FTPS so that credentials and data are encrypted
detail.explanation: FTP sends credentials and data in plaintext, so the fix is a protocol that encrypts them: SFTP over SSH or FTPS over TLS. A new port is obscurity, a longer password is still readable in the capture, and blocking port 20 would break transfers without adding protection.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: FTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption to traditional FTP, securing the authentication and data transfer between client and server. It should not be confused with SFTP, which is a completely different protocol built on SSH.
examContext: SY0-701 tests the distinction between FTPS, which is FTP wrapped in TLS/SSL, and SFTP, file transfer over SSH; know they are not interchangeable despite the similar names.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's compliance auditor requires encrypted file transfers but the vendor's legacy software only supports traditional FTP commands wrapped in TLS, not SSH. He configures FTPS rather than SFTP, since it layers encryption onto the familiar FTP command structure the vendor software expects.
detail.quizQuestion: A partner asks for secure FTP and sends a configuration guide that tells the company to open TCP port 22 and load SSH keys. The company's server supports FTP with TLS. Which of the following statements BEST describes the problem?
quizOptions: A) FTPS authenticates with SSH keys, so the partner's guide is correct as written
B) SFTP and FTPS are the same protocol, so the server only needs a different port number
C) The guide describes FTPS, which must always use port 22 for its control channel
D) The guide describes SFTP, a different protocol, so the two are not interchangeable
detail.explanation: SFTP runs over SSH (port 22) and uses SSH keys, while FTPS is ordinary FTP wrapped in TLS with certificates. Despite the similar names they are different protocols and cannot be swapped by changing a port.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: GCM is a block cipher mode that combines the speed of counter mode encryption with a built-in authentication tag, providing both confidentiality and integrity verification in a single pass. This authenticated encryption design makes it the preferred mode for modern protocols like TLS 1.3.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize AES-GCM as a widely used authenticated encryption mode in current TLS cipher suites, valued because it detects tampering as part of encryption rather than requiring a separate integrity check like an HMAC.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria selects AES-GCM for the company's new API encryption standard specifically because it provides both encryption and tamper detection in one operation, removing the need to implement a separate HMAC check. This simplifies the code and closes a gap where a previous implementation forgot to verify integrity at all.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer is choosing an AES mode for a new API and wants one operation that provides both confidentiality and tamper detection, without adding a separate HMAC. Which of the following modes BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) ECB, which encrypts every block independently with the same key
B) GCM, which adds an authentication tag to counter mode encryption
C) CBC, which chains each block to the previous ciphertext block
D) CFB, which turns the cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher
detail.explanation: GCM is an authenticated encryption mode: it encrypts in counter mode and produces a tag that detects modification. CBC, ECB and CFB provide confidentiality only, so they would need a separate integrity check.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: A European Union regulation that governs how organizations collect, process, store, and transfer the personal data of EU residents, granting individuals rights such as data access, correction, and erasure, with significant fines for noncompliance.
examContext: SY0-701 treats GDPR as the primary example of a data privacy regulation with extraterritorial reach, since any organization processing EU residents' data must comply regardless of where the organization is based, and tests awareness of concepts like the right to be forgotten and breach notification timelines.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company processes customer data for European clients, so Sam implements a data mapping process to track where personal data is stored and builds a workflow so EU customers can request deletion of their records within the regulation's required timeframe. This keeps the company compliant and avoids the steep fines GDPR allows regulators to impose.
detail.quizQuestion: A U.S.-based online store with no offices in the EU sells to customers in France and Italy. A customer in France demands that the store delete all of her personal data. Which of the following BEST describes the store's obligation?
quizOptions: A) GDPR does not apply because the store has no offices in the EU, so it may ignore the request
B) GDPR applies because the store processes EU residents' data, so it must honor the erasure request
C) The store must honor the request only if the customer also happens to live in California
D) Only the customer's own bank is required to honor erasure requests that are made under GDPR
detail.explanation: GDPR has extraterritorial reach: any organization that processes the personal data of EU residents must comply, including the right to erasure. Having no EU office does not exempt the store, and the California law is a separate regime.

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

items.name: Fines
items.detail: Monetary penalties set by regulators (GDPR is the best-known example).

items.name: Sanctions
items.detail: Formal restrictions or penalties, including legal action or being barred from certain activity.

items.name: Reputational damage
items.detail: Loss of customer trust and negative press.

items.name: Loss of license
items.detail: Losing the right to operate, handle payment cards, or practice in a regulated field.

items.name: Contractual impacts
items.detail: Breach of contract, terminated agreements and lost business.

definition: A free, open-source implementation of the OpenPGP standard that provides encryption and digital signing for files, emails, and communications, allowing users to protect confidentiality and verify sender authenticity using public-key cryptography.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize GPG as a practical, widely used tool for implementing PGP-style asymmetric encryption and signing, commonly contrasted with S/MIME as two competing approaches to secure email encryption.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya needs to send a confidential financial report to an external auditor over email without relying on a corporate PKI deployment. Priya uses GPG to encrypt the file with the auditor's public key and digitally sign it with her own private key, so only the auditor can decrypt it and can verify it genuinely came from Priya.
detail.quizQuestion: Two researchers want to exchange files so that only the recipient can read them and the recipient can verify who sent them. They want free, open-source software that implements the OpenPGP standard and do not want to depend on a certificate authority hierarchy. Which of the following tools BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) HTTPS, which encrypts web traffic between a browser and a server
B) S/MIME, which relies on certificates issued by a trusted certificate authority
C) BitLocker, which encrypts a whole drive with a key stored in the TPM
D) GPG, which uses public-key encryption and signatures with a web of trust
detail.explanation: GPG implements OpenPGP, giving encryption and digital signatures with a decentralized web of trust. S/MIME depends on a CA hierarchy, BitLocker protects stored data on one machine, and HTTPS secures web sessions rather than files exchanged between people.

definition: A GPO is a collection of configuration settings in a Windows Active Directory environment that can be applied to users or computers to enforce security policies, such as password requirements, software restrictions, or screen-lock timeouts. GPOs let administrators centrally push consistent security configurations across thousands of endpoints at once.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference GPOs as the mechanism for enforcing baseline configurations and hardening settings across Windows domain-joined systems; know it's a centralized policy-enforcement tool, conceptually similar to MDM for mobile devices.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam creates a GPO that forces a 15-minute screen-lock timeout and a minimum 14-character password on every domain-joined workstation in the company. Within one login cycle, every existing machine automatically picks up the new setting without an administrator touching each device individually.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator must enforce a 15-minute screen lock and disable the command prompt on all 2,000 Windows computers joined to the company's Active Directory domain, and have the settings reapply if users change them. Which of the following should be used?
quizOptions: A) A logon script that runs once the first time each user signs in
B) A Group Policy Object linked to the domain or an organizational unit
C) A mobile device management profile pushed to company phones
D) A RADIUS policy on the wireless controllers that sets device rules
detail.explanation: Group Policy Objects centrally enforce settings on domain-joined computers and reapply them at regular intervals. A one-time logon script cannot keep settings enforced, RADIUS controls network access, and MDM profiles manage mobile devices.

definition: GPS is a satellite-based navigation system that provides precise location and time data to compatible receivers, commonly built into mobile devices, vehicles, and asset trackers. In security contexts, GPS data supports geofencing, device-tracking, and geolocation-based access policies, but it can also be spoofed or jammed.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference GPS in the context of mobile device management features like geofencing and remote-wipe triggers, or as an example of a signal that attackers can spoof to defeat location-based security controls.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the MDM platform to use each company phone's GPS location to automatically trigger a remote wipe if the device leaves the country without authorization. When a sales laptop-replacement phone is mistakenly left in an airport abroad, the geofencing policy wipes its corporate data before anyone can misuse it.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital's MDM automatically locks any managed tablet that leaves the campus, but a tester shows the lock can be bypassed with a cheap GPS spoofing device in a backpack. Which of the following would BEST strengthen the control?
quizOptions: A) Require employees to sign an acceptable use policy that bans the use of GPS spoofers
B) Disable location services altogether and rely on the user's password to unlock the devices
C) Combine geofencing with other signals, such as Wi-Fi network checks and device certificates
D) Increase the GPS update interval so that the tablet's location is checked only once an hour
detail.explanation: GPS signals can be spoofed, so location should be corroborated with independent signals such as the connected Wi-Fi network and device identity. Checking less often makes spoofing easier, a password does not replace location control, and a policy does not stop a technical attack.

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: A GPU is a specialized processor originally designed for rendering graphics but now widely used for highly parallel computing tasks, including password cracking and machine-learning workloads. Attackers use GPU clusters to dramatically speed up brute-force and hash-cracking attacks compared to using a CPU alone.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference GPUs in the context of password-cracking speed and why strong hashing algorithms with built-in work factors (like bcrypt or Argon2) are recommended, since they are specifically designed to resist GPU-accelerated brute-force attacks.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan is evaluating the organization's password hashing algorithm and recommends migrating from a fast, unsalted hash to bcrypt specifically because bcrypt's deliberate slowness resists the kind of massively parallel cracking attempts that a GPU cluster can perform. This single change makes a stolen password database far less practical for attackers to crack at scale.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker steals a database of unsalted SHA-1 password hashes and uses a rack of GPUs to crack most of them within hours. Which of the following changes would BEST slow this kind of attack in the future?
quizOptions: A) Require users to change their passwords every 30 days with no other change
B) Store passwords with a salted, deliberately slow algorithm such as Argon2
C) Store passwords with an unsalted SHA-256 hash instead of the SHA-1 hash
D) Encrypt the password hashes with AES and keep the key on the same server
detail.explanation: GPUs excel at computing fast hashes in parallel, so a salted algorithm with a tunable work factor makes each guess expensive. Unsalted SHA-256 is still fast, an encryption key stored beside the data offers little protection, and frequent changes do not slow the cracking of stolen hashes.

definition: An integrated approach organizations use to align IT and security activities with business goals, manage uncertainty and potential loss, and meet legal and regulatory obligations, often supported by dedicated GRC software platforms.
examContext: SY0-701 uses GRC as an umbrella concept tying together policy, risk management, and regulatory requirements; expect it in the context of security program oversight, where governance sets the rules, risk management evaluates exposure, and compliance verifies adherence.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya is tasked with building a single dashboard that tracks policy exceptions, open risk items, and upcoming audit deadlines for executive leadership. Priya implements a GRC platform that ties these three disciplines together, giving the board a unified view of the organization's overall risk and compliance posture.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's policies are written by one team, risk assessments are run by another, and compliance checks are done by a third, with no shared view of the results. Leadership wants these activities aligned with business goals. Which of the following approaches BEST achieves this?
quizOptions: A) A larger red team that tests the security controls of the whole company each quarter
B) A new SIEM that centralizes the logs collected from every system and application
C) A single, stricter acceptable use policy that applies to all employees
D) A governance, risk and compliance program that integrates all three activities
detail.explanation: GRC ties together governance (the rules), risk management (the exposure) and compliance (verifying adherence) so the three work from one picture. A red team, a stricter policy and a SIEM each address only one narrow area.

items.name: Fines
items.detail: Monetary penalties set by regulators (GDPR is the best-known example).

items.name: Sanctions
items.detail: Formal restrictions or penalties, including legal action or being barred from certain activity.

items.name: Reputational damage
items.detail: Loss of customer trust and negative press.

items.name: Loss of license
items.detail: Losing the right to operate, handle payment cards, or practice in a regulated field.

items.name: Contractual impacts
items.detail: Breach of contract, terminated agreements and lost business.

items.name: Boards
items.detail: Set strategy and oversee risk at the top of the organization.

items.name: Committees
items.detail: Cross-functional groups such as a security steering committee or a Change Advisory Board (CAB).

items.name: Government entities
items.detail: Regulators and agencies that set legal requirements at local, regional, national and global levels.

items.name: Centralized
items.detail: One authority sets policy for everyone. Consistent, but slower and less tailored.

items.name: Decentralized
items.detail: Business units set their own policy. Flexible, but risks inconsistency.

items.name: Monitoring and revision
items.detail: Policies must be reviewed regularly and updated when laws, threats or the business change.

definition: GRE is a tunneling protocol that encapsulates a wide variety of network layer protocols inside point-to-point links, often used to create VPN tunnels. On its own, GRE provides no encryption, so it's frequently paired with IPsec for confidentiality.
examContext: SY0-701 may test that GRE alone lacks encryption and authentication, making GRE-over-IPsec a common combination when a secure, encrypted tunnel is required.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam sets up a GRE tunnel between two routers to carry a non-IP routing protocol across the internet, but realizes the tunnel traffic is completely unencrypted and readable by anyone capturing it. He wraps the GRE tunnel inside IPsec to add the encryption GRE itself lacks.
detail.quizQuestion: Two offices use a GRE tunnel to carry routing protocols between their routers. A security review notes that the tunnel carries internal data across the internet in clear text. Which of the following BEST fixes this?
quizOptions: A) Use a stronger password on the routers' SSH management ports and enable login banners
B) Change the GRE tunnel to use a different tunnel interface number on both routers
C) Increase the MTU on the tunnel interface to reduce fragmentation of the routing updates
D) Run the GRE tunnel inside an IPsec tunnel so the encapsulated traffic is encrypted
detail.explanation: GRE only encapsulates traffic and provides no encryption, so it is commonly paired with IPsec for confidentiality. The tunnel number, MTU and management passwords have no effect on whether the tunneled data is encrypted.

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

definition: HA refers to system designs that minimize downtime through redundancy, failover mechanisms, and elimination of single points of failure, ensuring continuous operation. It's a core availability control supporting business continuity goals.
examContext: SY0-701 ties HA to redundancy concepts like clustering, load balancing, and failover; know HA specifically addresses the 'availability' leg of the CIA triad.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya designs a web application with HA in mind, deploying it across two data centers with automatic failover so that if one site loses power, traffic seamlessly shifts to the other. When a storm knocks out power at the primary site, customers never notice any interruption in service.
detail.quizQuestion: An e-commerce site must keep its web tier available even if one server fails, without manual intervention. Which of the following designs BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A single web server with a RAID 0 array for faster disk performance
B) A warm standby server that an administrator brings online manually after an outage
C) A single powerful web server with a full backup taken every night and tested weekly
D) Two or more web servers behind a load balancer with automatic failover
detail.explanation: High availability uses redundancy and automatic failover so no single failure stops the service. A single server, a manually activated standby, and RAID 0 (which has no redundancy) all leave the site down until someone intervenes or restores.

definition: An HDD is a traditional storage device that uses spinning magnetic platters to store data. Proper disposal or sanitization of HDDs, through degaussing, wiping, or physical destruction, is critical to prevent data recovery after decommissioning.
examContext: SY0-701 covers secure data destruction methods for HDDs, including degaussing and multi-pass wiping, which differ from the sanitization methods appropriate for SSD-based media.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's company retires a batch of old servers and uses a degaussing device to destroy the magnetic patterns on each HDD before recycling the hardware. An independent audit later confirms none of the drives contain any recoverable data, satisfying the company's data destruction policy.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is decommissioning 200 magnetic hard drives that held confidential data and plans to donate the computers. Which of the following methods BEST ensures the data cannot be recovered while still allowing the drives to be reused?
quizOptions: A) Delete the partitions and perform a quick format on each drive before donating it
B) Degauss each drive with a strong magnetic field before the computers are donated
C) Overwrite every sector of each drive with a wiping tool that verifies the passes
D) Shred the drives into small fragments before the computers are donated
detail.explanation: Overwriting every sector sanitizes the data and leaves a working drive. A quick format leaves the data recoverable, and shredding or degaussing destroys the drive so it cannot be reused.

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: A HIDS monitors a single host's system logs, file integrity, and activity to detect signs of a compromise, rather than monitoring network traffic. It complements network-based detection by catching threats that only become visible once they're already running on the endpoint.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to contrast HIDS with NIDS: HIDS watches one host's internal activity (file changes, logs, processes) while NIDS watches network traffic; know that HIDS can detect threats that encrypted traffic might hide from a network sensor.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria deploys a HIDS agent on the company's critical database server to monitor for unauthorized changes to system files and configuration, since encrypted application traffic would otherwise hide malicious activity from network sensors. When an attacker modifies a system binary after gaining a foothold, the HIDS immediately flags the file integrity violation.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst needs to detect a malicious script that modifies system files on a server whose traffic is entirely encrypted with TLS. A network sensor sees only encrypted packets. Which of the following controls would BEST provide visibility?
quizOptions: A) A web application firewall configured as a reverse proxy in front of the server
B) A network-based IDS on a SPAN port that sees the traffic in front of the server
C) A stateless packet filter on the switch port that the server is connected to
D) A host-based IDS that monitors file changes, logs and processes on the server
detail.explanation: A HIDS watches activity inside the host, such as file modifications and processes, so encrypted network traffic does not hide the attack. A network IDS and a packet filter see only packets, and a WAF inspects web requests rather than file changes on the server.

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

expansion: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
definition: A US federal law that establishes national standards for protecting sensitive patient health information, requiring healthcare providers, insurers, and their business associates to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to associate HIPAA with protecting PHI (protected health information) in the healthcare sector, and to know it mandates specific security controls and breach notification requirements distinct from general privacy laws like GDPR.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya works for a hospital IT department rolling out a new patient portal and must ensure all patient records are encrypted at rest and in transit, with access logs retained for audits. Priya configures role-based access so only treating physicians and billing staff can view relevant PHI, satisfying HIPAA's technical safeguard requirements.
detail.quizQuestion: A small medical billing company receives patient records from a clinic and stores them in the cloud. A breach exposes patient names and diagnoses. Which of the following BEST identifies the regulation the company must follow and the data involved?
quizOptions: A) SOX, because the company bills a clinic for the services that it provides
B) HIPAA, because the data is protected health information handled for a covered entity
C) PCI DSS, because the records contain patient names together with billing information
D) GDPR, because the records are stored in a cloud environment outside the clinic
detail.explanation: Patient names and diagnoses handled for a healthcare provider are protected health information, which HIPAA governs, including for business associates. PCI DSS covers payment card data, SOX covers public company financial reporting, and storing data in the cloud does not by itself trigger GDPR.

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: A HIPS actively monitors and can automatically block malicious activity detected on a single host, such as preventing a suspicious process from executing or modifying protected files. Unlike a HIDS, which only alerts, a HIPS takes real-time preventive action on the endpoint itself.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know the detect-versus-prevent distinction: HIDS detects and alerts, HIPS detects and actively blocks; this same detect/prevent pairing also applies to the NIDS/NIPS network-based equivalents.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures HIPS on the finance team's workstations so that any process attempting to inject code into another running process is automatically terminated rather than just logged. During a later malware outbreak, the HIPS blocks the payload's privilege-escalation attempt in real time, stopping the infection before it spreads.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants an endpoint control that not only detects a ransomware process encrypting files but also automatically stops the process and blocks changes to protected folders. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) A host-based intrusion prevention system that blocks malicious activity in real time
B) A file integrity monitor that reports changes to critical system files
C) A host-based intrusion detection system that alerts when suspicious activity occurs
D) A network-based IDS that analyzes a copy of the traffic on a mirrored port
detail.explanation: A HIPS detects and actively blocks malicious behavior on the host. A HIDS and a file integrity monitor only alert, and a network IDS sees traffic rather than what happens inside the endpoint.

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

definition: HMAC combines a cryptographic hash function with a secret key to verify both the integrity and authenticity of a message. Unlike a plain hash, HMAC ensures that only someone with the shared secret key could have generated a valid code for the message.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know HMAC provides authentication in addition to integrity, unlike a bare hash such as SHA alone, because it incorporates a secret key into the calculation.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen implements HMAC-SHA256 to sign API requests between two internal services, using a shared secret key known only to both systems. When a request arrives with a valid HMAC, the receiving service knows not just that the message is intact, but that it genuinely came from the trusted sender.
detail.quizQuestion: An API receives webhook messages from a partner. It must confirm that each message was not modified and truly came from the partner, using a secret the two parties already share. Which of the following BEST provides this?
quizOptions: A) A CRC-32 value appended to the end of each message
B) A plain SHA-256 hash of the message sent along with the message
C) Base64 encoding of the message body before it is sent
D) An HMAC calculated over the message using the shared secret key
detail.explanation: An HMAC mixes a secret key into the hash, so only a party holding the key can produce a valid code, proving both integrity and origin. A plain hash or CRC can be recomputed by an attacker, and Base64 is just an encoding.

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

definition: HOTP generates a one-time password using an HMAC function combined with a counter value that increments with each use. Unlike TOTP, the code remains valid until it is used, since it isn't tied to a time window.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts HOTP, which is counter-based and valid until used, with TOTP, which is time-based and expires after a short window; both are common hardware/software token mechanisms for MFA.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria issues hardware tokens using HOTP to field technicians who often work in areas with no reliable clock synchronization, since HOTP codes depend on a counter rather than the current time. Each code remains valid until used, avoiding failed logins caused by clock drift that a time-based token might suffer.
detail.quizQuestion: A hardware token shows a new six-digit code each time the user presses its button. The authentication server tracks a counter, and an unused code stays valid until it is used. Which of the following BEST describes this token?
quizOptions: A) An SMS code, which is delivered to the user's registered mobile number
B) HOTP, which is based on a counter that increments with each use
C) TOTP, which is based on the current time and expires after a short window
D) A push notification, which asks the user to approve a sign-in on a phone
detail.explanation: A counter-based code that remains valid until used is HOTP. TOTP codes derive from the clock and expire within seconds, while push approvals and SMS codes are delivered to a phone rather than generated by a token.

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

definition: An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant physical device that generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys, performing encryption operations without ever exposing the keys to the host system. It provides a higher level of key protection than software-based key storage.
examContext: SY0-701 references HSMs for secure key management and generation, often in the context of PKI and high-security environments requiring FIPS-validated hardware.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization stores its root CA's private signing key inside an HSM rather than on a general-purpose server's file system. Even if the server hosting the CA software is later compromised, the attacker cannot extract the private key itself because it never leaves the tamper-resistant hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: A certificate authority must protect its root private key so that it can never be exported to the host server, even by administrators, and wants tamper-resistant hardware that performs the signing operations internally. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) An encrypted USB drive that is kept in the administrator's desk drawer at night
B) A hardware security module that generates and uses the key in tamper-resistant hardware
C) A TPM chip on the host server's motherboard that stores the keys for disk encryption
D) A software key store on the server that is protected by a long passphrase
detail.explanation: An HSM keeps keys inside tamper-resistant hardware and performs cryptographic operations without exposing them. A TPM is tied to one device's platform integrity, and a software store or USB drive can be copied or removed by someone with access.

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: HTML is the standard markup language used to structure and display content on web pages. Improper handling of user-supplied input that gets reflected as HTML is the root cause of cross-site scripting vulnerabilities.
examContext: SY0-701 ties HTML to web application vulnerabilities like XSS, where unsanitized user input is rendered as executable HTML or JavaScript in a victim's browser.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's web application takes a comment field and renders it directly into the page's HTML without sanitizing special characters. An attacker submits a comment containing a script tag, and that malicious HTML executes in every other visitor's browser who views the comment section.
detail.quizQuestion: A comment form on a company's site displays whatever visitors type. A tester enters <script>alert(1)</script> and a pop-up appears for every visitor who later views the page. Which of the following defenses would BEST prevent this?
quizOptions: A) Limit the number of comments that a single visitor can post to the page each minute
B) Require TLS for the comment submission request that is sent from the visitor's browser
C) Validate input and encode output so user text is displayed as data, not as executable HTML
D) Use parameterized queries when the comments are saved to the database behind the form
detail.explanation: The script runs because the page renders user input as HTML, so input validation and output encoding are the defenses against this stored cross-site scripting. Parameterized queries stop SQL injection, TLS protects transport, and rate limits do not stop malicious content.
