items.name: ISO/IEC 27001
items.detail: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS). 27002 gives control guidance; 27701 extends it to privacy; 27017 and 27018 cover cloud security and cloud PII; ISO 31000 covers risk management.

items.name: CIS Controls / Benchmarks
items.detail: A prioritized set of safeguards (v8 has 18 controls), plus configuration benchmarks for hardening specific systems.

items.name: SOC 2
items.detail: An audit report on a service organization's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over a period.

items.name: OWASP
items.detail: Community resources for application security, best known for the OWASP Top 10 web risks.

definition: A P12 (or PFX) file is a password-protected archive format that bundles a private key together with its corresponding public key certificate (and any chain certificates) into a single portable file. It's commonly used to import or export a certificate and its private key together, such as when installing a certificate on a new server.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference P12/PFX files in the context of certificate management and PKI; know that because a P12 file contains the private key itself, it must be protected with a strong password and handled far more carefully than a public-only certificate file like a .cer or .pem containing no private key.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen needs to migrate a web server's TLS certificate to a new load balancer and exports it as a password-protected P12 file containing both the certificate and its private key. He transfers the file over an encrypted channel and immediately deletes the local copy afterward, since anyone who obtains that P12 file could impersonate the server.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator must move a TLS certificate and its private key from an old web server to a new one by using a single file. Because the file contains the private key, it must be protected with a password. Which of the following formats BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) DER (.cer), a binary file that holds the public certificate without the private key
B) PKCS #12 (.pfx), a password-protected bundle of the certificate and private key
C) PEM (.crt), a Base64 text file that holds only the public certificate and chain
D) CSR (.csr), a request that asks a certificate authority to issue a certificate
detail.explanation: PKCS #12 bundles the certificate, chain and private key in one password-protected file, which is why it is used to move a certificate between servers. The DER and PEM files described contain only public data, and a CSR is just a request for a certificate.

definition: P2P is a network architecture in which devices communicate and share resources directly with each other rather than through a centralized server, commonly seen in file-sharing applications and some blockchain/cryptocurrency networks. P2P traffic is a common vector for malware distribution and can also expose sensitive files if an employee misconfigures sharing software on a corporate machine.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference P2P applications as a security risk needing policy restriction (e.g., via an AUP or application whitelisting), since P2P software run on a corporate endpoint can both leak sensitive files and serve as a malware entry point.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's DLP alerts show a corporate laptop running a P2P file-sharing application that has inadvertently shared the entire "Documents" folder, including confidential contracts, with anyone on that P2P network. She has the software removed and updates the acceptable use policy to explicitly prohibit P2P applications on company devices.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst finds a BitTorrent client on a finance workstation. The client is sharing a folder of internal spreadsheets with outside peers, and it also downloaded a trojanized video player. Which of the following controls would BEST prevent a recurrence?
quizOptions: A) Daily backups of the finance share so that damaged spreadsheets can be restored
B) Full-disk encryption on every endpoint so that stolen drives cannot be read by others
C) Application allow listing, backed by an acceptable use policy that bans P2P software
D) A longer minimum password length for the accounts that sign in to the workstations
detail.explanation: Allow listing stops unapproved P2P clients from running, and the AUP sets the rule, which addresses both the data leak and the malware entry point. Encryption, longer passwords and backups do not stop a user from running software that shares files.

definition: A cloud service model that provides a managed runtime environment, including operating system, middleware, and development tools, so developers can build and deploy applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to distinguish PaaS from IaaS and SaaS on the shared responsibility model: in PaaS, the provider manages the OS and runtime while the customer is responsible for the application code and data.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's development team wants to deploy a web application without managing servers, patching operating systems, or configuring runtime environments. Maria selects a PaaS offering so developers can push code directly, while the cloud provider handles the underlying OS, patching, and infrastructure scaling.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants to deploy a web application without managing servers, operating system patching or the runtime. The team will manage only its own application code and data. Which of the following cloud service models BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) Software as a service, in which the provider manages the application and every layer below
B) An on-premises data center, in which the company manages every layer of the stack itself
C) Platform as a service, in which the provider manages the operating system and runtime
D) Infrastructure as a service, in which the customer installs and patches the operating system
detail.explanation: In PaaS the provider runs the operating system and runtime, leaving the customer responsible for its code and data. In IaaS the customer still patches the operating system, SaaS delivers a finished application, and an on-premises data center leaves every layer to the company.

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: A PAC file is a small script that tells a web browser which proxy server to use for a given URL, allowing automatic and centralized control of how web traffic is routed. Organizations use PAC files to force browsers through inspection proxies or content filters without manual configuration on each device.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference PAC files as a mechanism for transparently directing client web traffic to a secure web gateway or proxy for content filtering and monitoring; know it is distributed automatically rather than configured by hand on each machine.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya pushes a PAC file to every managed laptop through group policy so that all web requests are automatically routed through the company's secure web gateway, even when employees work from home, ensuring content filtering and malware scanning apply consistently.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants every employee's browser to send web requests through an inspection proxy automatically, without configuring each laptop by hand, while some internal sites bypass the proxy. Which of the following BEST accomplishes this?
quizOptions: A) Publish a proxy auto-configuration file that tells browsers which proxy to use
B) Configure a static route on each laptop that sends all web traffic to the proxy
C) Create DNS records that point every external website name to the proxy server
D) Deploy a captive portal that asks each employee to choose a proxy before browsing
detail.explanation: A PAC file is a small script that tells the browser which proxy to use for each URL, so it can be distributed centrally and can exempt internal sites. Routes and DNS changes cannot make a browser use a proxy selectively, and a captive portal is not per-URL proxy selection.

definition: A set of tools and policies for controlling, monitoring, and auditing accounts with elevated permissions, such as administrator or root accounts. PAM reduces the attack surface created by standing privileged access through techniques like credential vaulting and just-in-time elevation. (Note: PAM can also stand for Pluggable Authentication Modules — a Linux authentication framework — distinct from Privileged Access Management, which this card focuses on.)
examContext: SY0-701 covers PAM under privileged account management, including concepts like just-in-time access, password vaulting, and session recording; know PAM minimizes the time and scope of elevated privileges rather than eliminating them.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria deploys a PAM solution that vaults all domain administrator passwords and requires approval plus automatic password rotation after each checkout. When an admin account is checked out for a single maintenance task, its credentials are automatically rotated afterward so no standing privileged session remains.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's domain administrators currently hold permanent administrator rights. The security team wants those rights granted only when needed and for a limited time, with the session recorded and the password retrieved from a vault. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) Single sign-on that lets a user authenticate once to reach many different applications
B) Privileged access management that grants just-in-time elevation and records the session
C) Role-based access control that assigns permanent permissions based on the job function
D) Pluggable authentication modules, a Linux framework that configures how users sign in
detail.explanation: Privileged access management limits the time and scope of elevated rights through vaulting, just-in-time elevation and session recording. Pluggable authentication modules are a Linux authentication framework, RBAC grants standing permissions, and SSO simplifies sign-in without limiting privilege.

items.name: Privileged Access Management
items.detail: Controls, vaults, rotates and audits the credentials of administrator and other powerful accounts: password vaulting, just-in-time elevation, session recording and ephemeral credentials.

items.name: Pluggable Authentication Modules
items.detail: A Linux/Unix framework (configured in /etc/pam.d) that lets administrators plug different authentication methods (passwords, MFA, LDAP, smart cards) into services without changing the applications.

items.name: Just-in-time permissions
items.detail: Privilege is granted only when needed and removed automatically afterwards, so no one holds standing admin rights.

items.name: Password vaulting
items.detail: Privileged credentials are stored encrypted in a vault, checked out by approved users, and rotated after use.

items.name: Ephemeral credentials
items.detail: Short-lived credentials or tokens created on demand for a single task or session, so there is nothing long-lived to steal.

items.name: Session recording
items.detail: Privileged sessions are monitored and recorded for audit and forensics.

items.name: Least privilege / separation of duties
items.detail: Give only the access needed, and split sensitive tasks across people so no single person can complete fraud alone.

definition: A legacy authentication protocol that transmits usernames and passwords in plaintext over a point-to-point link, offering no encryption or protection against eavesdropping. It has largely been replaced by stronger protocols like CHAP and EAP.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize PAP as an insecure, cleartext authentication method often mentioned alongside CHAP as the secure alternative; if a scenario mentions passwords sent unencrypted during PPP authentication, think PAP.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam discovers during a network assessment that an old dial-up VPN concentrator is still configured to accept PAP authentication, exposing user passwords in cleartext on the wire. He reconfigures the device to require CHAP or a modern EAP method instead, eliminating the plaintext exposure.
detail.quizQuestion: During an audit of a legacy dial-in service, an analyst captures PPP authentication traffic and finds that the usernames and passwords are readable. Which of the following authentication protocols is MOST likely in use?
quizOptions: A) MS-CHAPv2, which performs mutual authentication using hashed responses
B) EAP-TLS, which authenticates both sides with digital certificates
C) CHAP, which answers a server challenge with a hashed response
D) PAP, which sends the username and password across the link in clear text
detail.explanation: PAP sends credentials unprotected, so a capture shows them directly. CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 use hashed challenge-response exchanges, and EAP-TLS uses certificates, so none of them exposes a readable password.

definition: A form of network address translation that maps many internal private IP addresses to a single public IP address by distinguishing connections using different port numbers. It conserves public IPv4 addresses and hides internal network topology.
examContext: SY0-701 may test PAT as a variant of NAT where one public address is shared among many internal hosts via port mapping; distinguish it from static NAT (DNAT), which maps one-to-one.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures the branch office firewall to use PAT so that all 200 internal workstations share the single public IP address assigned by the ISP, with the firewall tracking each session by source port. This conserves the limited public IPv4 allocation while still letting every workstation reach the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: An enterprise router performs PAT for 5,000 users behind one public IP address. During a large event, users report that new connections fail even though the router's CPU and bandwidth are normal. The translation table shows roughly 64,000 active entries for the public address. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?
quizOptions: A) The upstream DNS server has stopped resolving the names in the users' web requests
B) The router has run out of available source ports for the single public address
C) The router has run out of private addresses to assign to the connecting users
D) The router's ARP cache is full, so it cannot learn the MAC addresses of new users
detail.explanation: PAT tells connections apart by port number, and one public address offers roughly 65,000 ports, so heavy use can exhaust them. Private addresses are not handed out by the translation process, and DNS or ARP problems would not line up with a nearly full translation table.

items.name: Static NAT
items.detail: One-to-one fixed mapping between a private and a public address. Used to publish an internal server.

items.name: Dynamic NAT
items.detail: Private addresses are mapped to a pool of public addresses on demand.

items.name: PAT (NAT overload)
items.detail: Many private hosts share ONE public IP, distinguished by port numbers. What home routers do.

items.name: DNAT / port forwarding
items.detail: Destination NAT: rewrites the destination of inbound traffic so an outside client can reach an internal service.

items.name: Security note
items.detail: NAT hides internal addressing but is NOT a firewall; it provides no real protection by itself.

definition: PBKDF2 is a key derivation function that repeatedly hashes a password together with a random salt thousands or millions of times to produce a cryptographic key, deliberately slowing down the process to resist brute-force and rainbow table attacks. It is widely used for securely storing password hashes and deriving encryption keys from passphrases.
examContext: Exam questions test recognition of PBKDF2 as a key-stretching algorithm alongside bcrypt and Argon2; remember it combines salting with a configurable iteration count to increase computational cost for attackers.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen updates the user authentication service to store password hashes using PBKDF2 with a unique salt per account and 600,000 iterations, so that even if the password database is stolen, attackers cannot feasibly brute-force the original passwords.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's password database uses a single round of SHA-256 with a unique salt for each user. A security assessment shows that attackers with GPUs can test billions of guesses per second. Which of the following changes would BEST slow these attacks?
quizOptions: A) Encrypt each stored hash with AES so that attackers cannot read the hash values directly
B) Increase the salt length to 64 bytes so that each guess takes much longer to compute
C) Switch to SHA-512 with the same unique salt, since a longer hash resists brute force
D) Switch to PBKDF2 with a high iteration count so that each guess takes far longer to compute
detail.explanation: PBKDF2 repeats the hash thousands of times (key stretching), making every guess expensive for attackers with fast hardware. A longer hash or salt adds no meaningful work per guess, and encrypting the hashes only moves the problem to protecting the encryption key.

definition: A PBX is a private telephone switching system that routes calls within an organization and connects internal extensions to outside phone lines. Unsecured or misconfigured PBX systems can be exploited for toll fraud, eavesdropping, or as a pivot point into the corporate network.
examContext: SY0-701 covers PBX under physical and communications security; know that default credentials and remote administration features on a PBX are common attack vectors for toll fraud and voicemail hacking.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan audits the company's PBX and finds the remote administration portal still using the factory default password, which could let an outsider reroute calls or rack up charges through expensive international lines; he changes the credentials and disables remote access from the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's phone bill shows thousands of international calls placed overnight. A review finds that the on-premises PBX still has its default administrator password and exposes its remote management interface to the internet. Which of the following BEST describes the attack and the BEST immediate fix?
quizOptions: A) Smishing, fixed by blocking text messages that contain links on the company phones
B) Vishing, fixed by training receptionists to verify callers before transferring calls
C) Bluejacking, fixed by disabling Bluetooth discovery on the desk phones in the office
D) Toll fraud, fixed by changing the default credentials and restricting remote management
detail.explanation: A PBX with default credentials and an exposed management interface lets attackers place calls at the company's expense, which is toll fraud. Changing credentials and restricting remote administration closes the hole. Smishing, vishing and bluejacking do not match the facts.

definition: A file format and method for recording the full contents of network traffic as it crosses an interface, capturing complete packet data, including headers and payloads, for detailed forensic analysis and troubleshooting.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know PCAP files preserve full packet content, unlike NetFlow which only captures metadata, making them essential for deep forensic investigation but costly to store at scale; tools like Wireshark read and analyze PCAP files.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria is investigating a suspected data exfiltration incident and needs to see the exact contents of the suspicious traffic, not just summary statistics. Maria pulls the PCAP captured by a network tap at the time of the incident and opens it in Wireshark, confirming that sensitive customer data was sent unencrypted to an external IP address.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst must determine exactly which files an attacker downloaded over an unencrypted HTTP session two days ago. NetFlow records show that the connection occurred but not what it contained. Which of the following data sources would BEST allow the analyst to reconstruct the transferred files?
quizOptions: A) Firewall logs, which record the allowed and denied connections and their ports
B) Vulnerability scan reports, which list known weaknesses on the web server
C) Packet captures, which preserve the full headers and payloads of the traffic
D) DNS logs, which list the host names that internal systems asked to resolve
detail.explanation: Only a full packet capture stores payloads, so the downloaded files can be carved out of it. Firewall logs and DNS logs keep metadata, and vulnerability reports describe weaknesses rather than traffic.

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

definition: Refers to the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a set of security requirements that organizations handling credit card data must follow to protect cardholder information. Non-compliance can result in fines, increased transaction fees, or loss of card processing privileges.
examContext: SY0-701 treats PCI DSS as a key example of an industry-specific regulatory framework (as opposed to a government law); remember it applies to any organization that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, regardless of size.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's e-commerce company undergoes an annual PCI DSS assessment, which requires her to segment the cardholder data environment onto its own VLAN and encrypt stored card numbers. Passing the assessment keeps the company's merchant account with its payment processor in good standing.
detail.quizQuestion: A small online florist stores customers' card numbers in its own database and processes only a few hundred orders per month. The owner asks whether PCI requirements apply to the business. Which of the following statements is correct?
quizOptions: A) They apply only to merchants that process more than a million card transactions a year
B) They apply only to banks and card processors, so a small online florist is exempt
C) They apply only to businesses that are located in the same country as the card brands
D) They apply to any organization that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data
detail.explanation: PCI DSS is an industry standard that applies to every organization that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data, whatever its size. Smaller merchants may validate compliance differently, but they are not exempt.

expansion: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
definition: PCI DSS is a contractual security standard created by major card brands that defines requirements for protecting cardholder data, including network segmentation, encryption, access control, and regular testing. Any organization that stores, processes, or transmits credit card data must comply, regardless of size or industry.
examContext: Know PCI DSS as an industry-mandated contractual standard rather than a government law, and that it specifically targets payment card data; expect it in scenario questions about e-commerce or retail environments handling card transactions.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's online retail company fails its annual PCI DSS assessment because customer card numbers are stored unencrypted on an internal reporting server; the team segments that server off the main network and encrypts the stored data before the next audit cycle.
detail.quizQuestion: A retailer's cardholder data environment shares a flat network with the corporate office, and the assessor says that far more systems are in scope for PCI DSS than necessary. Which of the following would BEST reduce the scope of the assessment?
quizOptions: A) Segment the cardholder data environment from the rest of the network with firewalls
B) Add more wireless access points in the corporate office to improve its coverage
C) Encrypt all of the email messages that employees in the corporate office send
D) Require annual security awareness training for all of the corporate employees
detail.explanation: Segmentation isolates the systems that store, process or transmit card data, so only those systems fall within the PCI DSS scope. Email encryption, extra access points and awareness training do not change which systems are in scope.

items.name: GDPR
items.detail: EU law protecting the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is. Consent, right to be forgotten, 72-hour breach notification; fines up to the higher of EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover.

items.name: HIPAA
items.detail: US healthcare privacy and security rules protecting PHI. Applies to covered entities and their business associates.

items.name: PCI DSS
items.detail: Industry (contractual, not a law) standard for organizations that handle payment-card data.

items.name: SOX
items.detail: US law for public companies on accurate financial reporting and internal controls; aimed at accounting fraud.

items.name: CCPA
items.detail: California consumer privacy law: the right to know, delete and opt out of the sale of personal data.

items.name: FISMA
items.detail: US law requiring federal agencies to secure their information systems using NIST standards.

items.name: FedRAMP
items.detail: A standardized security authorization program for cloud services used by US federal agencies.

items.name: Law vs standard
items.detail: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, CCPA and FISMA are laws; PCI DSS and ISO/NIST frameworks are standards, which may become binding through contracts or regulators.

definition: A PDU is a device that distributes electrical power from a single source to multiple pieces of equipment in a server rack or data center, often with remote monitoring and outlet-level switching. PDUs are a key part of availability planning alongside UPS systems and backup generators.
examContext: Exam scenarios about resiliency and redundancy may reference dual PDUs fed from separate circuits as a control against a single power failure taking down an entire rack.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam installs two PDUs in each server rack, each fed from a different electrical circuit, so that servers with redundant power supplies stay online automatically if one circuit or PDU fails during maintenance.
detail.quizQuestion: A data center hosts a critical rack with a single power feed and a single PDU. A fuse failure in that PDU would take down every server in the rack. Which of the following is the BEST way to eliminate this single point of failure?
quizOptions: A) Add a larger UPS to the rack so that the single PDU can run longer on battery power
B) Install dual PDUs fed from separate circuits and use servers with dual power supplies
C) Move the servers to a different rack that is closer to the room's cooling units
D) Replace the PDU with a surge protector rated for a much higher number of joules
detail.explanation: Two PDUs on separate circuits, with dual-supply servers, mean that one failed PDU or circuit does not stop the rack. A bigger UPS, a surge protector or better cooling all leave the single PDU as a point of failure.

definition: A version of EAP that wraps the authentication exchange in an encrypted TLS tunnel before credentials are transmitted, commonly used to secure wireless network authentication in WPA2 and WPA3 Enterprise deployments.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know PEAP protects user credentials during 802.1X wireless authentication by establishing a TLS tunnel first, similar to how HTTPS protects HTTP, preventing credentials from being exposed in plaintext over the air.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen is configuring enterprise Wi-Fi authentication and wants to ensure employee usernames and passwords are never exposed in plaintext over the air. Chen configures PEAP so the authentication server establishes an encrypted TLS tunnel before the client's credentials are ever transmitted across the wireless network.
detail.quizQuestion: A company deploys WPA2-Enterprise Wi-Fi and wants users to authenticate with the usernames and passwords stored in Active Directory, without installing client certificates on every device. The credentials must travel inside a TLS tunnel. Which of the following authentication methods BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) WPA2-Personal, which gives every user the same shared passphrase instead of individual logins
B) EAP-TLS, which requires a certificate on the server and on every client device
C) LEAP, which uses a legacy exchange that attackers can crack with offline dictionary attacks
D) PEAP, which protects user credentials inside a TLS tunnel set up by the server certificate
detail.explanation: PEAP builds a TLS tunnel with only the server's certificate and carries the username and password inside it, so no client certificates are needed. EAP-TLS requires client certificates, LEAP can be cracked offline, and WPA2-Personal has no per-user credentials.

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

definition: A PED is any personally owned portable device, such as a smartphone, tablet, or smartwatch, that an employee or visitor might bring into a secure facility. Unrestricted PEDs create risks of unauthorized photography, audio recording, data exfiltration, and introduction of malware through unmanaged devices.
examContext: SY0-701 may test PED restrictions as a physical security control in sensitive areas like data centers or SCIFs, often alongside clean desk and visitor logging policies.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's organization requires visitors and even employees to leave personal phones and tablets in lockers before entering the data center floor, reducing the risk that a PED could be used to photograph sensitive rack labeling or cabling diagrams.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is building a facility where employees handle classified design data. The security officer wants to reduce the risk of unauthorized photography, audio recording and data exfiltration by staff and visitors. Which of the following controls is the BEST fit?
quizOptions: A) Require a visitor log that records each visitor's name, arrival time and host
B) Prohibit personal electronic devices in the secure area and offer entrance lockers
C) Install a wireless intrusion prevention system to detect rogue access points nearby
D) Allow personal devices in the area but require a mobile device manager on each of them
detail.explanation: Banning personal electronic devices and providing lockers keeps cameras, microphones and storage out of the area. MDM on personal devices still lets them in, a WIPS only detects rogue Wi-Fi, and a visitor log records who entered but does not prevent recording.

definition: A Base64 ASCII text format for encoding and storing X.509 certificates, private keys, and certificate chains, delimited by header and footer lines such as '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----'. It is the most common certificate container format used across web servers and PKI tooling.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to recognize PEM as a Base64-encoded certificate file format (readable as plain text) as opposed to binary formats like DER or PKCS#12; know that a .pem file can contain a certificate, a private key, or both.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex exports a web server's certificate and private key into a single PEM file so the Nginx configuration can reference one plain-text file for TLS termination. Because PEM is Base64 text, Alex can also open the file in a text editor to confirm the certificate boundaries before deployment.
detail.quizQuestion: A web server administrator opens a certificate file in a text editor and sees a block of Base64 text that begins with the line -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. Which of the following BEST describes the file?
quizOptions: A) A PEM file, a Base64 text encoding that can hold certificates, chains and keys
B) A DER file, a binary encoding that cannot be read in a plain text editor
C) A CRL file, a signed list of the certificates that a CA has revoked
D) A PFX file, a password-protected binary bundle of a certificate and its private key
detail.explanation: PEM files are Base64 text with BEGIN and END lines and can contain certificates, keys or both. DER and PFX are binary formats, and a CRL lists revoked certificates rather than being a certificate itself.

definition: PFS is a property of certain key exchange methods ensuring that each session uses a unique, temporary key that is not derived from a long-term private key. This means that even if an attacker later steals the server's private key, previously captured encrypted sessions cannot be decrypted.
examContext: Exam questions link PFS to ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (DHE or ECDHE) in TLS cipher suites, and may ask why these are preferred over static RSA key exchange for protecting past traffic.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya reconfigures the organization's web servers to prioritize ECDHE-based cipher suites instead of static RSA key exchange, enabling perfect forward secrecy so that a future compromise of the server's private key cannot be used to decrypt previously recorded HTTPS sessions.
detail.quizQuestion: A security engineer is concerned that an attacker who records encrypted web traffic today could decrypt it years from now if the web server's private key is ever stolen. Which of the following BEST addresses this concern?
quizOptions: A) Configure the web server to encrypt its stored private key with a stronger passphrase
B) Configure TLS to use ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange for perfect forward secrecy
C) Configure TLS to use static RSA key exchange with a longer 4096-bit private key on the server
D) Configure the web server to use a certificate with a much longer validity period
detail.explanation: With ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE) every session uses a temporary key, so a later theft of the server's private key cannot decrypt recorded sessions. Static RSA key exchange still depends on the long-term key, and a longer certificate life or stronger passphrase does not change that.

definition: An encryption application that provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for emails and files using a combination of symmetric and asymmetric cryptography and a decentralized web-of-trust model. It is a common alternative to S/MIME for securing email content.
examContext: SY0-701 may contrast PGP's web-of-trust key validation model with S/MIME's hierarchical CA-based trust model; both provide email encryption and digital signatures but manage trust differently.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria encrypts a sensitive contract using the recipient's PGP public key before emailing it, and digitally signs the message with her own private key so the recipient can verify both confidentiality and authenticity. Neither party needs to trust a centralized certificate authority because they exchanged public keys directly.
detail.quizQuestion: Two researchers at different organizations want to exchange encrypted and digitally signed email without relying on a certificate authority. Each wants to decide for themselves whose public keys to trust, based on endorsements from people they know. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) DKIM, which signs outgoing messages at the domain level to show where they came from
B) PGP, which uses a decentralized web of trust to validate the public keys of other users
C) TLS, which protects the connection between mail servers but not the stored messages
D) S/MIME, which uses certificates issued through a hierarchy of certificate authorities
detail.explanation: PGP relies on a web of trust in which users vouch for each other's keys, with no central CA. S/MIME depends on a CA hierarchy, TLS protects only the server connection, and DKIM authenticates a sending domain rather than encrypting content or validating personal keys.

items.name: SPF
items.detail: A DNS TXT record listing which servers and IPs may send mail for the domain. The receiver checks the sending server's IP against it. Stops simple sender forgery, but can break when mail is forwarded.

items.name: DKIM
items.detail: The sending server adds a digital signature to the message; the receiver checks it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message came from the domain and was not altered in transit.

items.name: DMARC
items.detail: The policy layer on top of SPF and DKIM: tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), requires the visible From domain to align, and sends reports to the domain owner.

items.name: S/MIME and PGP
items.detail: Different job: end-to-end signing and encryption of the message CONTENT, not domain-level sender checks.

items.name: Secure email gateway
items.detail: A filter in front of the mail server that scans for spam, phishing links and malicious attachments.

definition: Any individually identifiable health information, such as medical records, diagnoses, or treatment history, that is created, received, or maintained by a healthcare provider and protected under regulations like HIPAA. Breaches of PHI carry specific legal reporting and penalty requirements.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize PHI as a regulated data type under HIPAA, distinct from PII; a scenario describing a hospital or clinic data breach usually signals PHI-specific compliance obligations.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's hospital encrypts all patient records containing PHI both at rest in the database and in transit to the billing vendor, and logs every access to satisfy HIPAA's audit requirements. When a laptop containing unencrypted PHI is later reported stolen, the breach must be reported within the regulation's required timeframe.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital suffers a breach that affects several databases. Which of the following exposed data sets is the BEST example of protected health information that triggers HIPAA breach obligations?
quizOptions: A) A donor's name and credit card number from the foundation's online giving page
B) A staff member's name, home address and Social Security number from the HR system
C) A patient's name together with the diagnosis and treatment dates from a clinic record
D) The hospital's published visiting hours, main phone number and department directory
detail.explanation: PHI is individually identifiable health information that a provider creates or holds, such as a diagnosis tied to a patient's name. Employment records, card numbers and public directory information may be sensitive or covered by other rules, but they are not PHI.

items.name: Public
items.detail: Safe to disclose; no harm.

items.name: Private / internal
items.detail: For internal use only.

items.name: Sensitive
items.detail: Disclosure could cause harm or embarrassment.

items.name: Confidential
items.detail: Disclosure would cause serious harm; protected by contract or law.

items.name: Restricted
items.detail: The most tightly controlled, with very limited access.

items.name: Critical
items.detail: Essential to operations; loss or alteration would be severe.

items.name: Government scheme
items.detail: Unclassified, then Confidential, Secret and Top Secret, in rising order of damage if disclosed.

items.name: Data types
items.detail: Regulated (PII, PHI, payment data), trade secrets, intellectual property, legal information and financial information. Data may be human-readable or non-human-readable (binary, encoded).

definition: Any data that can be used on its own or combined with other information to identify a specific individual, such as a name, Social Security number, or email address. Protecting PII is a core driver of data classification, privacy law, and data loss prevention programs.
examContext: SY0-701 treats PII as a foundational data classification category tested alongside PHI and data privacy concepts; expect scenario questions about labeling, handling, or a breach involving customer PII.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the company's DLP solution to automatically detect and block emails containing unmasked Social Security numbers and credit card numbers from leaving the network. This prevents accidental PII exposure when employees mistakenly attach the wrong spreadsheet to an external email.
detail.quizQuestion: A researcher plans to publish a dataset after removing names and Social Security numbers. The dataset keeps each person's full birth date, gender and 5-digit ZIP code. Which of the following BEST describes the privacy risk?
quizOptions: A) There is no risk because PII consists only of direct identifiers such as names and SSNs
B) The fields can be combined to identify individuals, so the dataset still contains PII
C) The risk exists only if the dataset is shared with people outside the researcher's country
D) There is no risk because ZIP codes are public and birth dates are not sensitive alone
detail.explanation: PII includes data that identifies a person alone or when combined with other data, and birth date, gender and ZIP code together can single out most people. Removing direct identifiers does not make a dataset anonymous, and the risk does not depend on the country.

definition: A PIV card is a government-issued smart card that cryptographically proves an employee's or contractor's identity for both physical building access and logical access to computer systems. It typically combines a certificate-holding chip with a PIN, providing multifactor authentication in a single credential.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs PIV with CAC (Common Access Card) as examples of smart-card-based authentication; remember it combines something you have (the card) with something you know (the PIN) to satisfy MFA.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's federal agency issues PIV cards containing an embedded certificate, requiring employees to insert the card into a reader and enter a PIN before they can log into any workstation, satisfying multifactor authentication with a single physical credential.
detail.quizQuestion: A civilian federal agency issues smart cards to its employees and contractors. Each card holds a certificate, and users must enter a PIN to use it for both building access and computer sign-in. Which of the following BEST describes this credential?
quizOptions: A) A proximity badge that provides one factor and holds no digital certificate
B) A PIV card that provides multifactor authentication through the card and the PIN
C) A software token that stores the user's certificate in an encrypted mobile app
D) A hardware OTP token that provides a code which changes every thirty seconds
detail.explanation: A PIV card is a smart card with a certificate-bearing chip plus a PIN, combining something you have with something you know for physical and logical access. A proximity badge has no certificate, an OTP token only displays codes, and a software token is not a card.

definition: A set of numbered specifications (PKCS#1 through PKCS#15) published by RSA Security that define standard formats and procedures for implementing public-key cryptography, such as PKCS#12 for bundling a certificate with its private key. They promote interoperability between cryptographic software and hardware.
examContext: SY0-701 may reference PKCS#12 specifically as a password-protected file format (.p12/.pfx) used to export a certificate and its private key together; know it differs from the plain-text PEM format.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen exports a code-signing certificate along with its private key into a password-protected PKCS#12 file so the build server can sign application releases without storing the key in plain text. The .p12 file is then stored in a hardware security module rather than on the build server's disk.
detail.quizQuestion: A server administrator generates a key pair and creates a signed file containing the public key and the server's identity details, to submit to a certificate authority. Which of the following PKCS standards defines this request format?
quizOptions: A) PKCS #1, the standard that defines how RSA keys and signatures are encoded
B) PKCS #7, the standard for signed and encrypted messages and certificate chains
C) PKCS #12, the password-protected bundle of a certificate and its private key
D) PKCS #10, the standard that defines the certificate signing request format
detail.explanation: PKCS #10 defines the certificate signing request that is sent to a CA. PKCS #12 bundles a certificate with its private key, PKCS #1 covers RSA, and PKCS #7 covers signed and encrypted messages and certificate chains.

definition: The complete framework of policies, roles, hardware, and software used to create, manage, distribute, store, and revoke digital certificates and public keys. It underpins trust for TLS, email encryption, code signing, and more.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily tests PKI components, including certificate authorities, registration authorities, CRLs, OCSP, and certificate chains of trust; expect scenario questions about certificate issuance, revocation, and trust validation.
relatedAcronyms: CA, CRL, OCSP, RSA, PEM, PKCS

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan builds out a two-tier PKI with an offline root CA and an online issuing CA, so the organization can issue, renew, and revoke employee and server certificates without ever exposing the root key to the network. If the issuing CA is ever compromised, the offline root remains safe and can issue a replacement.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants users to verify a vendor's website certificate without contacting the vendor directly. A trusted third party signs the certificate, and clients check it against a chain that ends at a root they already trust. Which of the following components provides this trust?
quizOptions: A) A registration authority that verifies identities but does not sign certificates
B) A certificate revocation list that names certificates which are no longer trusted
C) A certificate authority that signs certificates and anchors the chain of trust
D) A key escrow service that stores copies of private keys for later recovery
detail.explanation: In a PKI the CA signs certificates, and the chain of trust leads back to a root that the client already trusts. An RA only verifies requesters, a CRL reports revoked certificates, and key escrow stores keys for recovery.

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: An email retrieval protocol (commonly POP3) that downloads messages from a mail server to a single client, typically deleting them from the server afterward. It lacks native encryption, so it is normally run over an encrypted tunnel or replaced with IMAP.
examContext: SY0-701 may ask you to identify POP3's default port (110, or 995 for POP3S) and recognize it as an email retrieval protocol that, unlike IMAP, does not keep mail synchronized across multiple devices.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex notices that sales staff using POP3 on their laptops lose access to old emails once they're downloaded and removed from the server, causing confusion when switching between a phone and a laptop. He migrates the team to IMAP so messages stay synchronized across every device.
detail.quizQuestion: A user's email client retrieves messages with POP3 on port 110 and sends the username and password in clear text. The user wants to read the same mailbox from a phone and a laptop, with messages staying synchronized and the credentials protected. Which of the following is the BEST solution?
quizOptions: A) Use IMAP on port 143 without encryption, which synchronizes messages across the devices
B) Use SMTP with STARTTLS on port 587, which encrypts the mail that the client sends
C) Use POP3S on port 995, which encrypts the session but downloads messages to one device
D) Use IMAP over TLS on port 993 to keep the mailbox on the server and encrypt the session
detail.explanation: IMAPS on port 993 keeps messages on the server so every device sees the same mailbox, and TLS protects the credentials. POP3S encrypts but is designed to download mail to one client, SMTP submission is for sending, and plain IMAP syncs without encryption.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: POTS refers to the traditional analog landline telephone network, which carries voice calls without the encryption, authentication, or modern signaling features found in digital or VoIP systems. Legacy POTS lines left in place for fax machines or alarm systems can become an overlooked and unmonitored path into a facility's communications.
examContext: Exam scenarios may reference a forgotten POTS line, such as one used for a fax machine or alarm dialer, as a legacy communication path that bypasses network security monitoring entirely.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen discovers an old POTS line still active for a fax machine in the finance department that bypasses the corporate firewall and network monitoring entirely; he has it disconnected since it could serve as an unmonitored channel for data exfiltration.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester finds a forgotten analog phone line in a server room that is connected to a fax machine with a built-in modem. The line is outside the scope of the firewall and the IDS. Which of the following is the BEST action to reduce the risk?
quizOptions: A) Change the telephone number of the line so that attackers cannot find it easily
B) Enable full-disk encryption on the fax machine so that stored documents are protected
C) Deploy an inline IPS on the data network to block malicious traffic from the fax machine
D) Inventory the analog lines, disconnect unused ones and monitor the ones that remain
detail.explanation: A POTS line with a modem bypasses the firewall and IDS entirely, so the fix is to inventory analog lines, remove those that are unnecessary and monitor the rest. An IPS on the data network never sees the dial-in traffic, and encryption or a new number does not close the path.

definition: PPP is a data link layer protocol that establishes a direct connection between two network nodes, commonly used for dial-up, DSL, and some WAN links. It supports authentication methods such as PAP and CHAP to verify the identity of the connecting party before allowing traffic.
examContext: Exam may ask you to distinguish PPP, a general point-to-point link protocol, from PPTP, which tunnels PPP traffic over an IP network for VPN use; know PAP sends credentials in clear text while CHAP uses a challenge-response.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex configures a legacy WAN link between two branch offices to use PPP with challenge-response authentication instead of the older plain-text method, preventing credentials from being captured by anyone monitoring the link.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineer is documenting a legacy WAN link. The protocol in use establishes a direct connection between two nodes at the data link layer and supports PAP and CHAP to authenticate the remote end. Which of the following BEST identifies it?
quizOptions: A) PPTP, a VPN protocol that tunnels PPP frames across an IP network
B) L2TP, a tunneling protocol that depends on IPsec to provide encryption
C) PPP, a data link protocol that creates a direct link between two nodes
D) SSH, a protocol for encrypted remote shell sessions over TCP port 22
detail.explanation: PPP creates a direct data link connection and authenticates the peer with PAP or CHAP. PPTP and L2TP tunnel traffic over IP for VPNs, and SSH provides encrypted remote shell sessions.

definition: PPTP is an early VPN tunneling protocol that wraps PPP packets for transmission across an IP network to create a private tunnel. It is now considered insecure because of weaknesses in its MS-CHAPv2 authentication and encryption, and modern VPNs use stronger alternatives.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to identify PPTP as a deprecated, insecure VPN protocol and choose a stronger replacement such as an IPSec-based VPN when asked to remediate a weak remote access solution.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria discovers that a remote branch office still connects to headquarters using a PPTP VPN tunnel; she migrates the connection to an IPSec-based VPN after learning that PPTP's authentication can be cracked, exposing the tunnel's traffic.
detail.quizQuestion: A security assessment finds that a company's remote access VPN uses PPTP with MS-CHAPv2 authentication. Which of the following is the BEST recommendation?
quizOptions: A) Replace it with an IPsec or TLS VPN, because PPTP and MS-CHAPv2 are both weak
B) Keep PPTP but change it to a non-standard port so that scanners cannot find it
C) Keep PPTP but require longer passwords, since the encryption is still considered strong
D) Keep PPTP but switch to PAP, which avoids the weaknesses in MS-CHAPv2
detail.explanation: PPTP's encryption and MS-CHAPv2 authentication are both considered broken, so the VPN should be replaced with IPsec or TLS. Longer passwords do not fix the MS-CHAPv2 flaw, PAP is worse, and changing the port is only obscurity.

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

definition: A PSK is a secret value shared in advance between two parties and used to authenticate or derive encryption keys for their communication, commonly seen in WPA2/WPA3-Personal Wi-Fi and some site-to-site VPN configurations. Because everyone uses the same key, PSKs scale poorly and are hard to revoke for a single user in a large organization.
examContext: Exam distinguishes WPA2-PSK (Personal mode, a single shared passphrase) from WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X with individual RADIUS credentials); know that PSK cannot selectively revoke access for one user without changing the key for everyone.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya sets up a small branch office Wi-Fi network with WPA2-PSK and a strong shared passphrase since only five employees use it, but she recommends headquarters move to 802.1X enterprise authentication so each of its two hundred employees can have individually revocable credentials.
detail.quizQuestion: A 60-employee company uses WPA2-Personal with one shared passphrase. Each time an employee leaves, management must change the passphrase on every device to keep that person off the network. Which of the following BEST solves this problem going forward?
quizOptions: A) Move to WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X so that each user has individual credentials
B) Move to WPA3-Personal, which keeps one passphrase but resists offline guessing
C) Use a longer passphrase and change it every month so that the old one expires quickly
D) Hide the SSID so that former employees cannot see the name of the network
detail.explanation: A PSK is shared by everyone, so revoking one person means changing it for all. WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X gives each user credentials that can be disabled individually. A longer passphrase or WPA3-Personal still shares one secret, and hiding the SSID is not a control.

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: PTZ describes a security camera that can be remotely panned, tilted, and zoomed to actively track activity across a wide area, rather than only covering a single fixed field of view. PTZ cameras let a smaller security staff monitor larger areas as a detective physical security control.
examContext: SY0-701 covers PTZ cameras under physical security and surveillance controls; know they are a detective control and are often combined with motion detection to automatically track movement.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's security team installs a PTZ camera above the loading dock so a single guard can remotely follow a delivery vehicle and zoom in to verify a driver's badge, replacing four fixed cameras that previously left blind spots between their fields of view.
detail.quizQuestion: A warehouse has one guard on the night shift but needs to monitor a large yard with several loading docks. Management wants cameras that the guard can redirect remotely to follow movement across the whole area. Which of the following BEST meets this need?
quizOptions: A) A perimeter fence with a locked gate, which blocks entry but does not monitor activity
B) PTZ cameras that can pan, tilt and zoom to follow activity, as a detective control
C) Motion-activated floodlights, which deter intruders but cannot record or track activity
D) Fixed cameras at each loading dock, which can record only a single field of view
detail.explanation: PTZ cameras can be steered remotely to track activity across a wide area, giving a small team detective coverage. Fixed cameras see one view, floodlights deter, and fences prevent entry without detecting anything.

definition: A PUP is software bundled with a legitimate application installer that gets installed with minimal or deceptive user consent. While not always outright malicious, PUPs commonly display intrusive ads, change browser settings, or track user activity, and can weaken overall system security.
examContext: Exam questions may ask you to classify an unwanted toolbar or bundled adware as a PUP rather than a virus or trojan, since it typically arrives through a legitimate-looking installation rather than direct exploitation.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's help desk receives a complaint about a new toolbar and a changed default search engine after a user installed a free file-conversion tool; endpoint protection flags the bundled software as a PUP, and Alex removes it before it can collect more browsing data.
detail.quizQuestion: After installing a free PDF converter, a user's browser has a new toolbar and search engine, and pop-up ads appear constantly. Antivirus finds no virus or trojan, and the installer's terms listed the extra software. How should this software be classified?
quizOptions: A) A rootkit that hides its presence from the operating system and from security tools
B) A worm that spreads to other hosts through network vulnerabilities on its own
C) A logic bomb that executes its payload when a specific date or condition is met
D) A potentially unwanted program that arrived bundled with a legitimate installer
detail.explanation: Adware and toolbars bundled with an installer and accepted with minimal or deceptive consent are classified as PUPs: not truly malicious, but unwanted. A rootkit hides itself, a logic bomb waits for a condition, and a worm spreads on its own.

definition: RA can refer to either a Recovery Agent, a trusted role or entity holding special keys or credentials that can recover encrypted data if the original key is lost, forgotten, or unavailable, or a Registration Authority, the PKI component that verifies a requester's identity before a Certificate Authority issues a certificate. Context determines which meaning applies.
examContext: SY0-701 most often tests the Recovery Agent meaning in key-escrow scenarios, where a designated role can decrypt data such as EFS-protected files using an escrowed key when the original user's key is lost; separately, remember a Registration Authority offloads identity verification from the CA in a PKI hierarchy.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization designates a Recovery Agent role holding an escrowed key for EFS-encrypted files; when an employee departs unexpectedly without decrypting files needed for a legal hold, the recovery agent uses the escrowed key to restore access without ever needing the former employee's password.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee who encrypted files with EFS leaves the company, and the private key was lost along with the employee's profile. The files must be recovered. Which of the following roles or components BEST allows this?
quizOptions: A) An OCSP responder that reports whether a certificate has been revoked
B) A registration authority that verifies identities before a CA issues a certificate
C) A certificate revocation list that publishes the keys that are no longer valid
D) A recovery agent whose designated key can decrypt the EFS-protected files
detail.explanation: A recovery agent is a designated role with a key that can decrypt data when the user's own key is lost, which is why it appears in key escrow planning. A registration authority only verifies identities for a CA, and a CRL or OCSP responder reports revocation status.

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

items.name: Recovery Agent
items.detail: A designated person or role allowed to recover encrypted data when a user's own key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example EFS or BitLocker recovery).

items.name: Registration Authority
items.detail: A PKI component that verifies a requester's identity on the certificate authority's behalf before the CA issues a certificate. It does not sign certificates.

expansion: Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe
definition: RACE was a European research program that funded advanced communications and cryptography research, including the work that led to the RIPEMD family of hash functions. On the exam, it appears mainly as background explaining where RIPEMD originated.
examContext: You are unlikely to be tested on RACE in isolation; its exam relevance is almost entirely as the origin of RIPEMD, so remember the link between the two rather than details of the program itself.

detail.practicalScenario: While reviewing cryptographic hash history, Alex learns that RACE was the European research initiative that sponsored the work leading to the RIPEMD hash function, explaining why RIPEMD's name traces back to a European research effort.
detail.quizQuestion: A European research program called RACE funded cryptographic work in the late 1980s. Which of the following hash function families is the best known product of that work?
quizOptions: A) MD5, a 128-bit hash that Ronald Rivest designed in the United States
B) The LM hash, a legacy password hash that Microsoft created for Windows
C) RIPEMD, a hash family that includes 128-bit, 160-bit and longer variants
D) SHA-256, a hash that the U.S. National Security Agency designed and NIST published
detail.explanation: The RACE program's integrity primitives project produced RIPEMD, so that is the link to remember. SHA-256 came from the NSA and NIST, MD5 from Ronald Rivest, and the LM hash from Microsoft.

definition: RAD is a software development methodology that emphasizes quick iterative prototyping and continuous user feedback over extensive upfront planning, allowing functional software to be delivered faster than traditional waterfall approaches. Security teams must adapt their review and testing processes to keep pace with RAD's fast release cycles.
examContext: Exam questions may contrast RAD's rapid, prototype-driven cycles with the more rigid phases of a traditional SDLC, and ask how security testing (such as automated scanning in CI/CD) should be integrated to keep up.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's development team adopts RAD to deliver a customer-facing feature in weekly prototype cycles, so she integrates automated security scanning directly into their CI/CD pipeline rather than relying on a single lengthy review at the end, keeping pace with the accelerated release schedule.
detail.quizQuestion: A team uses rapid application development and releases a new prototype every two weeks. The security team finds that annual penetration tests cannot keep pace with the release cycle. Which of the following is the BEST way to integrate security testing?
quizOptions: A) Delay each release until a manual code review of the whole application is completed
B) Move the security testing to a quarterly schedule that covers all of the releases at once
C) Automate static and dynamic scans in the CI/CD pipeline so that each build is tested
D) Skip testing of the early prototypes and test only the final version before launch
detail.explanation: Automated scanning in the CI/CD pipeline gives fast, repeatable feedback on every build, which matches RAD's pace. Full manual reviews and quarterly testing slow or skip releases, and testing only the final version finds problems too late.

definition: A centralized client/server protocol that provides authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) for users connecting to a network, such as through VPN or 802.1X-secured Wi-Fi. It encrypts only the password field within an otherwise unencrypted packet, using a shared secret between the client and server.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know RADIUS is a widely used AAA protocol for network access control (e.g., tying into 802.1X), and that it uses UDP and encrypts only the password, unlike protocols that encrypt the entire payload.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the corporate wireless controllers to authenticate every Wi-Fi connection against a central RADIUS server tied to Active Directory, so employees use their domain credentials instead of a shared pre-shared key. This also lets her instantly revoke a single terminated employee's network access without changing the Wi-Fi password for everyone else.
detail.quizQuestion: A network team needs a centralized AAA protocol for Wi-Fi and VPN user authentication. Separately, the team needs per-command authorization for administrators on switches and routers, with the entire payload encrypted. Which of the following pairs BEST matches the two requirements?
quizOptions: A) RADIUS for the network access users and TACACS+ for the device administrators
B) TACACS+ for the network access users and RADIUS for the device administrators
C) Kerberos for the network access users and LDAP for the device administrators
D) RADIUS for the network access users and Kerberos for the device administrators
detail.explanation: RADIUS is the common AAA protocol for network access such as VPN and 802.1X, while TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the whole payload, which suits per-command control of device administrators. The other pairings reverse or misuse the protocols.

items.name: EAP
items.detail: A framework, not a single protocol. Carried over 802.1X between the supplicant (client), authenticator (AP or switch) and the authentication server (RADIUS).

items.name: EAP-TLS
items.detail: Mutual certificate authentication: BOTH the server and every client present certificates. The strongest option, but it needs a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

items.name: PEAP
items.detail: Protected EAP: only the SERVER needs a certificate; it builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's credentials (usually MS-CHAPv2) travel inside it. Very common on Windows networks.

items.name: EAP-TTLS
items.detail: Like PEAP, with a server certificate and a TLS tunnel, but allows many inner methods (PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP).

items.name: EAP-FAST
items.detail: Cisco method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates to build the tunnel; created to replace LEAP.

items.name: LEAP
items.detail: Old Cisco proprietary method built on MS-CHAP; crackable and deprecated.

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

definition: A storage technology that combines multiple physical disks into a single logical unit to improve performance, provide fault tolerance, or both, depending on the RAID level chosen. It supports the availability leg of the CIA triad by letting a system survive one or more disk failures without data loss.
examContext: SY0-701 ties RAID to availability and fault tolerance planning; know common levels conceptually (RAID 1 mirroring, RAID 5/6 striping with parity) and that RAID is not a backup substitute since it doesn't protect against accidental deletion or ransomware.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures the file server's storage array as RAID 6 so that up to two simultaneous disk failures can occur without any data loss or downtime, while a hot-spare drive rebuilds automatically. He still maintains separate offsite backups, since he knows RAID does not protect against accidental file deletion.
detail.quizQuestion: A database server must survive the failure of any two disks in the same array without data loss. Cost is less important than availability. Which of the following RAID levels BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) RAID 6, which stripes data and stores two independent sets of parity
B) RAID 0, which stripes data across disks for speed with no redundancy
C) RAID 1, which mirrors the data onto a second disk
D) RAID 5, which stripes data and stores a single set of parity
