items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: SRTP is an extension of RTP that adds encryption, message authentication, and replay protection to real-time audio and video streams, commonly used to secure VoIP and video conferencing traffic. It protects call content from eavesdropping while preserving the low-latency delivery RTP provides.
examContext: Exam pairs SRTP with RTP, expecting you to know SRTP is the encrypted version used when confidentiality of voice or video calls is required, similar to how HTTPS relates to HTTP.

detail.practicalScenario: After discovering that call audio could be captured in clear text on the network, Chen reconfigures the organization's VoIP platform to use SRTP instead of plain RTP, encrypting all call media so that anyone capturing network traffic cannot reconstruct the conversations.
detail.quizQuestion: A video conferencing system must protect its media streams from eavesdropping, tampering and replayed packets while keeping the low delay that real-time delivery requires. Which of the following protocols BEST meets this need?
quizOptions: A) SRTP, which adds encryption, authentication and replay protection to RTP
B) RTCP, which reports quality statistics about the media streams to the endpoints
C) SIP over TLS, which encrypts the call signaling but not the media streams
D) TCP, which retransmits lost packets so that every packet is delivered in order
detail.explanation: SRTP secures RTP media with encryption, message authentication and replay protection without sacrificing real-time delivery. RTCP only reports quality, SIP over TLS protects signaling rather than media, and TCP adds delay without any security.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: An SSD is a storage device that uses flash memory instead of spinning magnetic platters to store data, offering faster performance but presenting different secure-erasure challenges than traditional hard drives. Because SSDs use wear-leveling, standard overwrite-based wiping methods may not reliably erase all copies of data, making full-disk encryption and vendor-specific secure erase commands important.
examContext: Exam may test that traditional degaussing and simple overwrite wiping, effective on HDDs, are unreliable on SSDs due to wear-leveling, and that full-disk encryption or the drive's built-in secure erase command should be used instead.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization retires a batch of laptops and learns that the standard disk-wiping tool used for old HDDs does not reliably erase data on the new SSDs due to wear-leveling; the team switches to each drive's built-in ATA secure erase command and verifies that full-disk encryption had been enabled from day one as a backup safeguard.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is retiring laptops that contain sensitive data on solid state drives. The IT team has used a three-pass overwrite and a degausser on its old hard disk drives. Which of the following is the BEST approach for the SSDs?
quizOptions: A) Delete the partitions and format the drives, because formatting removes the data
B) Run the same three-pass overwrite on each drive, because flash memory works like a disk
C) Use the drive's secure erase or cryptographic erase command, or destroy the drive
D) Degauss the drives, because the flash cells store their data in a magnetic field
detail.explanation: Wear leveling means overwrites can miss copies of data on an SSD, and flash is not magnetic, so degaussing does nothing. Secure or cryptographic erase, or physical destruction, are reliable, while formatting leaves data recoverable.

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: An encrypted network protocol used to securely access and manage remote systems via command line, replacing insecure legacy protocols like Telnet. It supports both password and public-key authentication and also tunnels other protocols like SFTP.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SSH (port 22) as the secure, encrypted replacement for Telnet for remote administration, and that key-based authentication is generally preferred over passwords for SSH access.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam disables Telnet on every network switch and requires SSH with public-key authentication for all administrative access instead. A subsequent audit confirms no administrative credentials are ever transmitted in cleartext across the management VLAN.
detail.quizQuestion: Administrators manage Linux servers through Telnet. The security team wants encrypted sessions and stronger authentication than passwords, without distributing shared passwords. Which of the following is the BEST solution?
quizOptions: A) Replace Telnet with SSH on TCP port 22 and use public key authentication
B) Replace Telnet with HTTP on TCP port 80 and use a web-based management console
C) Keep Telnet but restrict it to the management VLAN and require a complex password
D) Replace Telnet with SNMPv3 on UDP port 161 and use the community string for login
detail.explanation: SSH encrypts the session and supports public key authentication, replacing Telnet's clear text. Restricting Telnet to a VLAN still exposes credentials on that network, HTTP is unencrypted, and SNMP is for monitoring rather than remote shell access.

items.name: Telnet (23) → SSH (22)
items.detail: Remote administration: Telnet sends everything in clear text; SSH encrypts the session and supports key-based authentication.

items.name: HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)
items.detail: Web traffic wrapped in TLS.

items.name: FTP (20/21) → SFTP or FTPS
items.detail: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol (a single port, 22). FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS (needs certificates and extra data ports). They are different protocols despite similar names.

items.name: SNMP v1/v2c → SNMPv3 (161/162)
items.detail: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. v3 adds authentication and encryption.

items.name: LDAP (389) → LDAPS (636)
items.detail: Directory queries over TLS.

items.name: POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) → POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993)
items.detail: Mailbox retrieval over TLS.

items.name: SMTP (25) → SMTPS / STARTTLS (465 / 587)
items.detail: Mail submission and relay with TLS.

items.name: DNS (53) → DNSSEC, DoH, DoT
items.detail: DNSSEC adds signatures for authenticity and integrity; DoH/DoT encrypt queries for privacy.

items.name: RTP → SRTP
items.detail: Voice/video streams encrypted and authenticated.

definition: The human-readable name broadcast by a wireless access point to identify a Wi-Fi network, used by devices to locate and connect to it. Hiding an SSID provides little real security since it can still be discovered through passive wireless monitoring, and attackers can also set up rogue APs that spoof a legitimate SSID.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know that SSID hiding or disabling broadcast is a weak security-through-obscurity control, not a real protection; also recognize evil twin attacks where a rogue AP broadcasts a legitimate-looking SSID to lure victims.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's wireless security assessment finds an evil twin access point broadcasting the same SSID as the corporate Wi-Fi network in the parking lot, attempting to capture employee credentials. The deployed WIDS detects the duplicate SSID with a mismatched hardware address and alerts the security team to the rogue device.
detail.quizQuestion: A company hides its corporate SSID to protect its Wi-Fi, but a consultant discovers the network name within minutes using a passive wireless monitor. Which of the following BEST explains how?
quizOptions: A) The name is stored in the access point's MAC address, which every nearby device can see
B) The name still appears in probe requests and association frames sent by real clients
C) The name is derived from the WPA2 passphrase, so capturing a handshake reveals it
D) The name is published in public DNS records, which any host on the internet can query
detail.explanation: Hiding the SSID only removes it from beacon frames. Legitimate clients still send it in probe requests and association frames, so a passive monitor sees it, and hiding does not stop an evil twin. The name is not derived from the passphrase, the MAC address or DNS.

items.name: Evil twin
items.detail: A rogue access point that copies a legitimate SSID so victims connect to it and can be eavesdropped on or phished.

items.name: Rogue access point
items.detail: ANY unauthorized AP plugged into your network, often by an employee, which creates a back door around your perimeter.

items.name: Deauthentication
items.detail: Forged deauth frames knock clients off the Wi-Fi (denial of service, or to force a reconnect so a handshake can be captured). Defeated by 802.11w protected management frames (mandatory in WPA3).

items.name: Jamming
items.detail: Transmitting noise on the same frequency to block wireless communication. A radio-frequency denial of service.

items.name: Bluejacking
items.detail: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices. An annoyance rather than data theft.

items.name: Bluesnarfing
items.detail: Stealing data (contacts, email) from a Bluetooth device without permission. Far more serious than bluejacking.

items.name: War driving
items.detail: Driving around with a laptop or phone mapping and probing Wi-Fi networks. War chalking (marking them) is the older sibling.

items.name: Wi-Fi Protected Setup
items.detail: The WPS PIN can be brute-forced quickly, so disable WPS.

definition: The predecessor encryption protocol to TLS for securing network communications, now considered obsolete and insecure due to multiple known vulnerabilities such as POODLE. The term SSL is still used colloquially even though modern deployments actually use TLS.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know SSL is deprecated and broken and should be disabled in favor of TLS 1.2 or 1.3; a scenario describing a server still accepting SSL connections is a finding that should be remediated.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's vulnerability scan flags a legacy application server that still accepts SSL 3.0 connections, exposing it to the POODLE downgrade attack. She disables SSL entirely on the server and enforces TLS 1.2 as the minimum supported protocol version.
detail.quizQuestion: A scan of the company's older load balancer shows that it still accepts SSL 3.0 connections, which are vulnerable to the POODLE attack. The load balancer also supports TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Which of the following is the BEST remediation?
quizOptions: A) Disable SSL 3.0 on the load balancer and allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3
B) Replace the load balancer's certificate with one that has a longer key length
C) Enable SSL 2.0 as a fallback so that older clients have a stronger option
D) Keep SSL 3.0 enabled but restrict it to cipher suites that use 3DES encryption
detail.explanation: SSL 3.0 is obsolete and vulnerable to POODLE, so it should be disabled in favor of TLS 1.2 and 1.3. A longer certificate key does not fix the protocol, SSL 2.0 is even weaker, and POODLE affects SSL 3.0 regardless of the cipher suite.

items.name: SSL 2.0 / 3.0
items.detail: Broken (SSL 3.0 fell to POODLE) and prohibited. SSL as a name survives only in casual speech; it is TLS now.

items.name: TLS 1.0 / 1.1
items.detail: Deprecated by the IETF in 2021; vulnerable to attacks such as BEAST. Disable them.

items.name: TLS 1.2
items.detail: Still widely deployed and secure when configured with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM.

items.name: TLS 1.3
items.detail: Current version: faster 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy mandatory, and weak options (RC4, 3DES, SHA-1, static-RSA key exchange, CBC) removed.

definition: An authentication capability that lets a user log in once and gain access to multiple independent applications or systems without re-entering credentials for each one. It improves user convenience and centralizes authentication, though a compromised SSO credential can grant access to everything downstream.
examContext: SY0-701 tests SSO as both a convenience and a risk concentration point; expect scenarios about using SAML or OAuth to implement SSO, as well as the mitigation of pairing SSO with strong MFA since a single compromised credential now unlocks multiple systems.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan rolls out SSO across the organization's cloud applications so employees authenticate once each morning instead of managing a dozen separate passwords. Recognizing that SSO concentrates risk into a single credential, Jordan also mandates MFA on the SSO portal itself to offset that risk.
detail.quizQuestion: A company implements single sign-on for 30 cloud applications. After a phishing attack steals one employee's SSO password, the attacker accesses several applications at once. Which of the following BEST reduces this risk without removing the convenience of SSO?
quizOptions: A) Extend the SSO session lifetime so that users sign in less often during the week
B) Require users to change the SSO password every 30 days using a shorter minimum length
C) Remove SSO and require a separate password for each application the user needs
D) Require multifactor authentication at the SSO sign-in and monitor for unusual activity
detail.explanation: SSO concentrates risk in one credential, so adding MFA and monitoring protects every downstream application while keeping the convenience. Removing SSO loses the benefit, longer sessions add exposure, and frequent changes to a shorter password weaken security.

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: A configuration standard published by the U.S. Defense Information Systems Agency that provides detailed, prescriptive hardening instructions for specific operating systems, applications, and network devices. Organizations use STIGs as an authoritative baseline for secure configuration, especially in government and defense environments.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs STIG with SCAP-based compliance scanning as a prescriptive hardening baseline commonly used for government systems; know it provides specific, actionable configuration settings rather than general policy guidance.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex hardens a new batch of government-issued laptops by applying the relevant STIG for the operating system, disabling unnecessary services and enforcing the prescribed password and audit settings. An SCAP-compliant scan afterward confirms each laptop meets the STIG baseline before deployment.
detail.quizQuestion: A defense contractor must harden its Windows servers by using detailed, prescriptive settings published by the Defense Information Systems Agency, and then verify compliance with SCAP-based scans. Which of the following BEST describes the document it should use?
quizOptions: A) NIST SP 800-53, which catalogs security controls but not product-specific settings
B) A security technical implementation guide with prescriptive settings for each product
C) A CIS Benchmark, which is a consensus-based configuration guide from a nonprofit
D) ISO/IEC 27001, which sets requirements for an information security management system
detail.explanation: STIGs are DISA's prescriptive hardening guides for specific operating systems, applications and devices, and SCAP tools can check them. A CIS Benchmark comes from a nonprofit, SP 800-53 is a control catalog, and ISO 27001 is a management system standard.

definition: A standardized language and format for representing and sharing cyber threat intelligence, including indicators, threat actors, and attack patterns, in a structured, machine-readable way so organizations can exchange threat data consistently.
examContext: SY0-701 commonly pairs STIX with TAXII; remember STIX defines the structured format and language for describing threat intelligence, while TAXII defines the transport protocol used to share STIX data between organizations.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's threat intelligence team wants to share indicators of a new phishing campaign with an industry information-sharing group in a format every member's tools can automatically parse. Sam structures the threat data using STIX, ensuring threat actors, indicators, and attack patterns are described consistently across all participating organizations.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to receive threat intelligence from an industry partner automatically, in a standardized machine-readable format. Which of the following BEST describes the roles of the two standards that make this possible?
quizOptions: A) STIX defines the structured format of the intelligence, and OVAL defines how it is exchanged
B) TAXII defines the structured format of the intelligence, and STIX defines how it is exchanged
C) STIX defines the structured format of the intelligence, and TAXII defines how it is exchanged
D) SCAP defines the structured format of the intelligence, and TAXII defines how it is exchanged
detail.explanation: STIX is the language and format for describing threat intelligence, while TAXII is the protocol that transports it between organizations. OVAL and SCAP relate to configuration and vulnerability checks rather than threat intelligence.

items.name: Open-source (OSINT)
items.detail: Freely available: government advisories, vendor blogs, social media, paste sites, public feeds.

items.name: Proprietary / third-party
items.detail: Paid commercial feeds and research services, often more curated and timely.

items.name: Information-sharing organizations
items.detail: Industry communities such as ISACs and the Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) service, which share indicators among members.

items.name: Dark web
items.detail: Hidden forums and markets where stolen credentials and exploits are traded; monitoring them gives early warning of leaks.

items.name: Responsible disclosure program
items.detail: A published, safe way for researchers to report a vulnerability privately so it can be fixed before it is public.

items.name: Bug bounty program
items.detail: A responsible-disclosure program that PAYS researchers for valid findings.

definition: A SWG is a security appliance or cloud service that sits between users and the internet to enforce acceptable use policy, filter malicious or inappropriate content, and inspect web traffic for threats such as malware downloads. It gives organizations centralized visibility and control over outbound web browsing regardless of where users connect from.
examContext: SY0-701 may group SWG with CASB and SASE as modern approaches to inspecting and controlling user traffic to the internet and cloud services; know its core function is web traffic filtering and threat inspection.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya deploys a cloud-based SWG so that remote employees' web traffic is filtered and inspected for malware the same way it would be if they were sitting in the office, even though they now connect from home networks outside the corporate perimeter.
detail.quizQuestion: A company with employees working from home wants every user's web traffic inspected for malware downloads and filtered by category, enforcing the acceptable use policy wherever the user connects from, without backhauling traffic to headquarters. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) A reverse proxy that sits in front of the company's public web servers and caches pages
B) A hardware load balancer that distributes requests across the application servers
C) A host-based intrusion detection system that monitors changes to local system files
D) A cloud-delivered secure web gateway that inspects and filters outbound web traffic
detail.explanation: A SWG, often delivered from the cloud, enforces policy and inspects web traffic for threats wherever users are. A reverse proxy protects servers, a load balancer distributes requests, and a HIDS monitors one host's files.

items.name: Forward proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of CLIENTS. Users' outbound requests go through it for content filtering, caching, logging and anonymity. Clients are configured to use it.

items.name: Reverse proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of SERVERS. Outside clients talk to the proxy, which forwards to the back end. Used for load balancing, TLS offloading, caching and hiding server details.

items.name: Transparent proxy
items.detail: Intercepts traffic inline without any client configuration, so users do not know it is there.

items.name: Caching proxy
items.detail: Stores copies of frequently requested content to save bandwidth and speed responses.

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

expansion: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
definition: A Cisco-developed AAA protocol that encrypts the entire authentication packet and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct processes, giving administrators granular control over which commands a user can run on network devices.
examContext: SY0-701 candidates should know TACACS+ uses TCP port 49 and encrypts the full packet (unlike RADIUS, which only encrypts the password), and that it is commonly used for device administration AAA on routers and switches.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex manages a fleet of core routers and switches and needs per-command authorization so junior technicians can run show commands but not configuration changes. Alex deploys TACACS+ on the network devices, pointing them at a centralized AAA server, so every command a technician types is individually authorized and logged for audit purposes.
detail.quizQuestion: A network team wants administrators to log in to routers and switches with centralized authentication, with authorization that restricts which commands each administrator may run, and with all of it logged. The entire authentication packet should be encrypted. Which of the following BEST meets these requirements?
quizOptions: A) TACACS+, which separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the packet
B) LDAP, which queries a directory of user accounts but does not authorize device commands itself
C) Kerberos, which issues time-limited tickets to authenticated clients inside a single realm
D) RADIUS, which combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password field
detail.explanation: TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet and separates the AAA functions, allowing per-command authorization for device administration. RADIUS encrypts only the password and combines authentication with authorization, Kerberos issues tickets, and LDAP is a directory protocol.

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

expansion: Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information
definition: An application protocol used to transport cyber threat intelligence, typically formatted in STIX, between organizations and security platforms in a standardized, automated way. It lets threat intel feeds be shared and consumed programmatically rather than manually.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs TAXII with STIX as the mechanism for transporting standardized threat intelligence data between organizations and tools; know TAXII as the transport/protocol layer, not the data format itself.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's threat intelligence platform automatically pulls indicator feeds from an information-sharing community over TAXII every hour, ingesting new malicious IP addresses and file hashes without any manual download. This automated feed lets her firewall block newly reported command-and-control servers within minutes of public disclosure.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's threat intelligence platform needs to subscribe to an industry partner's feed and receive new indicators automatically every few minutes over HTTPS. Which of the following protocols is designed to transport this intelligence?
quizOptions: A) SNMP, a protocol that monitors and manages routers, switches and servers
B) TAXII, a protocol that exchanges STIX-formatted intelligence between organizations
C) SFTP, a protocol that transfers files over an encrypted SSH connection
D) STIX, a language that structures the description of indicators and threat actors
detail.explanation: TAXII is the transport protocol that exchanges threat intelligence, typically in STIX format, between organizations and platforms. STIX is the data format rather than the transport, SNMP manages devices, and SFTP transfers files without any intelligence-sharing model.

items.name: Open-source (OSINT)
items.detail: Freely available: government advisories, vendor blogs, social media, paste sites, public feeds.

items.name: Proprietary / third-party
items.detail: Paid commercial feeds and research services, often more curated and timely.

items.name: Information-sharing organizations
items.detail: Industry communities such as ISACs and the Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) service, which share indicators among members.

items.name: Dark web
items.detail: Hidden forums and markets where stolen credentials and exploits are traded; monitoring them gives early warning of leaks.

items.name: Responsible disclosure program
items.detail: A published, safe way for researchers to report a vulnerability privately so it can be fixed before it is public.

items.name: Bug bounty program
items.detail: A responsible-disclosure program that PAYS researchers for valid findings.

definition: A connection-oriented transport layer protocol that establishes a reliable session through a three-way handshake and guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery of data between applications, forming the basis for protocols like HTTP and SSH.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know TCP's three-way handshake, consisting of SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK, as the basis for understanding SYN flood attacks, and to contrast TCP's reliable, connection-oriented delivery with UDP's connectionless, best-effort delivery.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam notices a server becoming unresponsive and traffic captures show thousands of incomplete connection attempts stuck after the initial SYN packet. Sam recognizes this as a SYN flood attack exploiting the TCP three-way handshake, and enables SYN cookies on the server to mitigate the resource exhaustion.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst sees a flood of packets with the SYN flag set from many spoofed addresses, and the server's connection table fills with half-open connections. Which of the following BEST explains why the attack works?
quizOptions: A) The server reserves resources while it waits for the final ACK of the three-way handshake
B) The server answers every SYN with an RST packet, which saturates its outbound bandwidth
C) The server skips the handshake for spoofed sources, which lets the packets bypass the firewall
D) The server must complete a reverse DNS lookup on each source address before replying
detail.explanation: In a SYN flood the attacker never sends the final ACK, so the server keeps half-open connections in its table until they time out and eventually has no room for legitimate clients. The server does not reply with resets, perform reverse lookups or skip the handshake.

definition: TCP/IP is the foundational suite of protocols that governs how data is addressed, transmitted, routed, and received across the internet and most modern networks. Understanding TCP/IP's layered structure is essential for troubleshooting connectivity and recognizing where different security controls, such as firewalls and IDS/IPS, operate.
examContext: Exam expects general familiarity with TCP/IP as the underlying model for network communication, including how it maps loosely to the OSI model's layers, and recognition of common protocols (HTTP, DNS, FTP) that run on top of it.

detail.practicalScenario: When troubleshooting why a new server cannot reach the internet, Jordan walks through the TCP/IP stack layer by layer, confirming the IP address and subnet mask first, then checking routing, before finally discovering a misconfigured firewall rule blocking the specific port.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer is documenting where controls operate in the TCP/IP model. Which of the following correctly matches a function with the layer where it primarily operates?
quizOptions: A) A router makes forwarding decisions using IP addresses at the internet layer
B) An Ethernet MAC address is used for routing between networks at the internet layer
C) A web application firewall filters on TCP port numbers at the application layer
D) A switch makes forwarding decisions using IP addresses at the transport layer
detail.explanation: Routers forward packets by IP address at the internet layer. Switches use MAC addresses at the link layer, TCP port numbers are a transport layer concept, and MAC addresses are not used for routing between networks.

definition: A TGT is a credential issued by the Key Distribution Center in Kerberos after a user successfully authenticates, allowing the user to request access tickets for specific services without re-entering their password each time. It is time-limited and reduces how often credentials must be transmitted across the network.
examContext: Exam ties TGT directly to the Kerberos authentication flow: the KDC's Authentication Service issues the TGT, which is then presented to the Ticket Granting Service to obtain service tickets for individual resources; know this sequence for scenario questions about Kerberos.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria explains to a new hire that after logging into the domain in the morning, their workstation receives a TGT from the KDC, which is then used throughout the day to silently request individual service tickets for file shares and applications without prompting for a password again.
detail.quizQuestion: A user signs in to a Windows domain at 8:00 a.m. and then opens a file share, a database and an intranet site over the next hour without entering the password again. Which of the following Kerberos components allows the user to request access to each service without re-authenticating?
quizOptions: A) The ticket-granting ticket that the KDC issued after the initial authentication
B) The user's password hash, which the client presents again to each server it visits
C) A service ticket that is valid for every server and application in the domain
D) A SAML assertion that the identity provider issues to each service provider
detail.explanation: After the initial authentication the KDC issues a TGT, which the client presents to the ticket-granting service to obtain a service ticket for each resource without re-entering the password. Service tickets are specific to one service, Kerberos does not resend the password hash, and SAML is a different federation protocol.

variants.title: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Kerberos vs LDAP

items.name: RADIUS
items.detail: Open standard, UDP 1812/1813. Combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password in the packet. Typical use: network ACCESS (VPN, Wi-Fi 802.1X).

items.name: TACACS+
items.detail: TCP 49. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the ENTIRE payload. Typical use: administrator access to network DEVICES, with per-command authorization.

items.name: Diameter
items.detail: RADIUS's successor: more reliable transport, better roaming support; found in 4G/5G carrier networks.

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based single sign-on for Windows domains (port 88). The KDC issues a TGT, then service tickets; supports mutual authentication and is sensitive to clock skew (5 minutes).

items.name: LDAP / LDAPS
items.detail: Directory protocol for looking up users, groups and attributes (TCP 389; 636 with TLS). Often the backend that the others query.

items.name: Exam shortcut
items.detail: Network access = RADIUS. Device administration with command control = TACACS+. Windows domain SSO = Kerberos. Directory lookup = LDAP.

definition: An encryption protocol introduced to fix WEP's weaknesses by generating a unique per-packet key, used as part of the original WPA. TKIP is itself now considered deprecated and insecure, having been replaced by the stronger CCMP/AES encryption used in WPA2 and WPA3.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to recognize TKIP as the encryption method used in original WPA, an interim fix for WEP, now deprecated in favor of AES-CCMP in WPA2/WPA3; a scenario describing a network still allowing TKIP is a finding to remediate.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's wireless audit finds several access points still configured to allow legacy WPA/TKIP connections for compatibility with old devices. He disables TKIP entirely and requires WPA2/WPA3 with AES-CCMP, retiring the last of the incompatible legacy hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: A wireless survey finds an access point configured for WPA2 that still allows TKIP as an encryption option for compatibility with some old devices. Which of the following is the BEST recommendation?
quizOptions: A) Keep TKIP because it generates a unique key for every packet, which makes it secure
B) Keep TKIP but increase the passphrase length to at least 20 characters
C) Replace TKIP with WEP because WEP is the more recent encryption protocol
D) Disable TKIP and require AES-CCMP for WPA2, or move the network to WPA3
detail.explanation: TKIP was an interim fix for WEP and is now deprecated, so networks should use AES-CCMP in WPA2 or WPA3. Per-packet keys did not make TKIP secure, WEP is older and broken, and a longer passphrase does not remove TKIP's weaknesses.

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: The modern cryptographic protocol that secures network communications in transit, providing confidentiality, integrity, and server (and optionally client) authentication. It is the successor to SSL and underlies HTTPS, secure email, and countless other encrypted connections.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are the currently recommended versions, that TLS replaced SSL, and that the TLS handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to establish a shared symmetric session key.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the company's web servers to support only TLS 1.2 and 1.3, disabling all older protocol versions and weak cipher suites. A follow-up scan confirms every client connection now negotiates a strong, modern cipher suite.
detail.quizQuestion: A security assessment of a payment portal finds that the web server supports TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.2. The security team wants to follow current best practice for the protocol versions it allows. Which of the following is the BEST configuration?
quizOptions: A) Allow only SSL 3.0, because it was the original standard for encrypted web traffic
B) Allow TLS 1.0 and 1.1 for older clients, and require TLS 1.3 only for the payment pages
C) Allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, and disable TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and all SSL versions
D) Allow TLS 1.0 through 1.2 and rely on a longer certificate key to protect older clients
detail.explanation: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are the currently recommended versions, and TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and all SSL versions are deprecated. A longer certificate key does not fix weak protocol versions, and leaving old versions enabled lets clients downgrade.

items.name: SSL 2.0 / 3.0
items.detail: Broken (SSL 3.0 fell to POODLE) and prohibited. SSL as a name survives only in casual speech; it is TLS now.

items.name: TLS 1.0 / 1.1
items.detail: Deprecated by the IETF in 2021; vulnerable to attacks such as BEAST. Disable them.

items.name: TLS 1.2
items.detail: Still widely deployed and secure when configured with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM.

items.name: TLS 1.3
items.detail: Current version: faster 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy mandatory, and weak options (RC4, 3DES, SHA-1, static-RSA key exchange, CBC) removed.

definition: TOC refers to the moment a program checks a condition, such as verifying a file's permissions or state, before acting on it. TOC is the first half of the TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) race condition, where an attacker exploits the gap between the check and the later use of that resource.
examContext: Exam pairs TOC with TOU as a classic race condition vulnerability; know that the risk comes from an attacker changing the resource's state in the gap between the check and the subsequent use.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam reviews a script that checks whether a file is a safe, non-symbolic regular file and then opens it moments later; because an attacker could swap the file for a symlink to a sensitive file in that gap, Sam rewrites the code to perform the check and the open as a single atomic operation.
detail.quizQuestion: A program checks that a file belongs to the current user and then, a moment later, opens the file to write to it. An attacker replaces the file with a link to a protected system file between those two steps. In this attack, what does the time of check refer to?
quizOptions: A) The moment the program writes data to the file after it has been opened
B) The moment the operating system closes the file and releases the lock on it
C) The moment the program verifies the file's ownership, before it acts on the file
D) The moment the attacker swaps the file for a link to a protected system file
detail.explanation: Time of check is when the program verifies a condition, such as ownership. The attacker exploits the gap before the time of use, when the program writes to the file. The swap is the exploit, not the check.

definition: An algorithm that generates a temporary numeric passcode derived from a shared secret and the current time, typically valid for only 30-60 seconds, commonly used as a second authentication factor via an authenticator app. Because the code depends on time synchronization rather than a server-issued counter, it works even without network connectivity to the authentication server.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts TOTP with HOTP: TOTP codes are time-based and expire quickly, while HOTP codes are counter-based and remain valid until used; both are common 'something you have' MFA factor implementations via an authenticator app.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan requires all employees to pair an authenticator app generating TOTP codes with their account password, so logging in requires both the password and a code that changes every 30 seconds. Even if an attacker steals a password in a data breach, the stolen credential alone is useless without the synchronized TOTP code.
detail.quizQuestion: A company deploys authenticator apps that display a six-digit code which changes every 30 seconds. The app and the server share a secret key but do not need to communicate when a code is generated. Which of the following BEST describes this method?
quizOptions: A) A push notification, which asks the user to approve a sign-in request on the phone
B) TOTP, which derives each code from a shared secret and the current time of day
C) An SMS code, which the server generates and sends to the phone number on file
D) HOTP, which derives each code from a shared secret and an incrementing counter
detail.explanation: TOTP uses a shared secret and the current time, so codes expire quickly and can be generated offline. HOTP is counter based and stays valid until used, push notifications require a connection, and SMS codes are generated and sent by the server.

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

definition: TOU refers to the moment a program actually uses or acts on a resource after previously checking it. Paired with TOC, it forms the TOCTOU race condition, where an attacker swaps or modifies the resource during the window between the check and the use, causing the program to act on something different than what it validated.
examContext: Exam expects you to recognize TOU as the second half of a TOCTOU race condition; the fix is typically to eliminate the time gap by making the check-and-use sequence atomic or by using file handles instead of re-resolving paths.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan discovers that a privileged helper program checks a temporary file's ownership and then, moments later, uses that same file path to write sensitive output; an attacker could replace the file with a symlink in between, so Jordan changes the program to retain the original file handle from the check through the use step.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer wants to eliminate a time-of-check to time-of-use vulnerability in code that verifies a temporary file's permissions and then opens the file in a separate step. Which of the following is the BEST fix?
quizOptions: A) Open the file once and run the checks on the open handle instead of the path
B) Add a delay after the check so that the file system has time to settle
C) Encrypt the temporary file so that an attacker cannot replace its contents
D) Run the check twice and open the file only if both checks give the same result
detail.explanation: A TOCTOU flaw exists because the resource can change between the check and the use. Checking through an already open handle makes the check and the use one atomic step. Delays and repeated checks leave a window, and encryption does not prevent the swap.

definition: A dedicated hardware chip embedded in a device's motherboard that securely generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys, and can attest to the integrity of the boot process. It underpins features like full-disk encryption key storage and measured or secure boot.
examContext: SY0-701 ties TPM to hardware-based key storage and secure/measured boot alongside UEFI Secure Boot; know that full-disk encryption can store its key sealed inside a TPM so the key is unavailable if the boot process is tampered with.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen enables full-disk encryption on all company laptops, storing the encryption key sealed inside each laptop's TPM chip rather than in software. If an attacker tries to boot the stolen laptop's drive in a different machine, the TPM refuses to release the key because the boot environment doesn't match.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants full-disk encryption keys to be released only if the laptop boots with unmodified firmware and bootloader, so that tampering with the boot process leaves the disk locked. The key must not be stored on the disk itself. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A TPM that seals the key and releases it only when the boot measurements are correct
B) An HSM in the data center that holds the keys for every server in the company
C) A USB drive that holds a copy of the key and stays plugged into the laptop
D) A KMS in the cloud that stores the key and sends it to any device that asks for it
detail.explanation: A TPM is a chip on the device that generates and stores keys and can seal them to the boot measurements, so a modified boot process cannot unlock the disk. An HSM or KMS is a network resource not tied to the laptop's boot state, and a key left on a USB drive can be stolen with the laptop.

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: TSIG is a mechanism that uses a shared secret key and HMAC to cryptographically authenticate DNS messages, most commonly used to secure dynamic DNS updates and zone transfers between servers. It ensures that only a server possessing the correct shared key can submit changes to a DNS zone.
examContext: Exam may pair TSIG with DNSSEC; know the distinction that DNSSEC authenticates DNS responses to clients using public-key signatures, while TSIG authenticates server-to-server transactions like zone transfers and dynamic updates using a shared secret.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures TSIG with a shared secret key between the primary and secondary DNS servers so that zone transfer requests are cryptographically authenticated, preventing an attacker from impersonating a secondary server and pulling a full copy of the internal DNS zone.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's primary DNS server must be configured so that only its secondary server can request zone transfers, and the secondary must be sure that updates really come from the primary. Both servers share a secret key. Which of the following BEST provides this authentication?
quizOptions: A) DNSSEC, which uses public key signatures to let resolvers validate DNS answers
B) DNS over HTTPS, which encrypts client queries to a resolver inside an HTTPS session
C) A split-horizon design, which returns different answers to internal and external clients
D) TSIG, which uses a shared key and HMAC to authenticate server-to-server DNS messages
detail.explanation: TSIG authenticates DNS transactions between servers, such as zone transfers and dynamic updates, using a shared secret and HMAC. DNSSEC signs answers for resolvers using public keys, DoH encrypts client queries, and split-horizon DNS separates internal from external views.

items.name: A / AAAA
items.detail: Map a hostname to an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.

items.name: CNAME
items.detail: An alias that points one name at another name.

items.name: MX
items.detail: Names the mail servers for a domain, with priorities.

items.name: NS
items.detail: Names the authoritative name servers for the zone.

items.name: PTR
items.detail: Reverse lookup: IP address to hostname.

items.name: TXT
items.detail: Free-form text. Used for domain verification and for email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).

items.name: SOA
items.detail: Start of authority: zone metadata such as the serial number and refresh timers.

items.name: SRV
items.detail: Locates a service, giving host and port.

items.name: DNSSEC
items.detail: Signs records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity (defeats cache poisoning). It does NOT encrypt queries.

items.name: DoH / DoT
items.detail: DNS over HTTPS / TLS: encrypt DNS queries for privacy.

definition: TTP describes the behavior patterns of a threat actor, including their high-level strategies (tactics), the specific methods used to execute them (techniques), and the detailed step-by-step actions taken (procedures). Security teams use TTP analysis, often mapped to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK, to profile adversaries and anticipate their next moves.
examContext: Exam expects you to recognize TTP as the framework for describing adversary behavior, commonly referenced alongside threat intelligence and the MITRE ATT&CK framework; know the three terms build from general strategy down to specific implementation detail.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's threat intelligence team documents the TTPs of a ransomware group targeting their industry, mapping each phishing lure, lateral movement technique, and data staging procedure to MITRE ATT&CK, which helps the SOC build detections tuned to that specific group's known behavior.
detail.quizQuestion: A threat intelligence report states that an adversary group typically gains initial access through spearphishing, uses a specific PowerShell script to move laterally, and compresses data with a particular tool before uploading it. The team wants to map these behaviors to a common framework. Which of the following terms BEST describes this information?
quizOptions: A) The group's vulnerabilities, such as the unpatched software that the group has exploited
B) The group's indicators of compromise, such as file hashes and malicious IP addresses
C) The group's attack surface, such as the exposed services of its target organizations
D) The group's tactics, techniques and procedures, which can be mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
detail.explanation: TTPs describe how an adversary behaves: tactics are the goals, techniques the methods and procedures the specific implementations, and they map to MITRE ATT&CK. IoCs are artifacts such as hashes and IP addresses, and vulnerabilities and attack surface describe the target rather than the attacker.

variants.title: MITRE ATT&CK vs Kill Chain vs Diamond Model

items.name: MITRE ATT&CK
items.detail: A knowledge base of real-world adversary TACTICS (the goal, such as persistence) and TECHNIQUES (how they do it), arranged as a matrix. Used for detection engineering and red/purple teaming.

items.name: Cyber Kill Chain
items.detail: Lockheed Martin's seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stop the attacker at ANY stage to break the chain.

items.name: Diamond Model
items.detail: Analyzes an intrusion through four linked features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure and Victim.

items.name: TTPs / IoCs
items.detail: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures describe HOW an adversary behaves. Indicators of Compromise are the artifacts they leave (hashes, IPs, domains).

definition: A framework for describing the behavior of threat actors: the overall strategies (tactics), the specific methods (techniques), and the detailed implementation steps (procedures) they use during an attack. Security teams use TTPs, often mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, to profile adversaries and build targeted detections.
examContext: SY0-701 ties TTPs directly to threat intelligence and the MITRE ATT&CK framework; know that TTPs describe adversary behavior patterns used for attribution and detection engineering, rather than a single indicator like an IP address.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's threat intel team maps a recent intrusion's observed behaviors to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, documenting the attacker's TTPs from initial phishing access through lateral movement and data exfiltration. Comparing these TTPs to previous incidents lets the team attribute the intrusion to a known APT group with similar historical behavior.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst documents that an actor wanted to steal credentials, did so by dumping the memory of the LSASS process, and used a specific tool with particular command-line flags. Which of the following BEST maps this behavior onto tactics, techniques and procedures?
quizOptions: A) Tactic: dumping LSASS memory. Technique: stealing credentials. Procedure: the specific tool and flags
B) Tactic: the specific tool and flags. Technique: stealing credentials. Procedure: dumping LSASS memory
C) Tactic: stealing credentials. Technique: dumping LSASS memory. Procedure: the specific tool and flags
D) Tactic: stealing credentials. Technique: the specific tool and flags. Procedure: dumping LSASS memory
detail.explanation: Tactics are the adversary's goals, techniques are the general methods used to reach them, and procedures are the specific implementations, such as an exact tool and command line. The other mappings put the levels in the wrong order.

variants.title: MITRE ATT&CK vs Kill Chain vs Diamond Model

items.name: MITRE ATT&CK
items.detail: A knowledge base of real-world adversary TACTICS (the goal, such as persistence) and TECHNIQUES (how they do it), arranged as a matrix. Used for detection engineering and red/purple teaming.

items.name: Cyber Kill Chain
items.detail: Lockheed Martin's seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stop the attacker at ANY stage to break the chain.

items.name: Diamond Model
items.detail: Analyzes an intrusion through four linked features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure and Victim.

items.name: TTPs / IoCs
items.detail: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures describe HOW an adversary behaves. Indicators of Compromise are the artifacts they leave (hashes, IPs, domains).

definition: The final phase of software testing where actual end users validate that an application meets business requirements and works correctly in realistic scenarios, performed before production release. Security issues can still surface during UAT, so it should include realistic data handling and permission scenarios rather than only functional checks.
examContext: SY0-701 places UAT at the end of the SDLC and change management process, just before production deployment; know it's where business stakeholders validate behavior, and skipping it is a cited root cause for post-deployment incidents.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's team conducts UAT on a new expense-reporting feature using a sanitized copy of real workflows, and a finance user discovers during testing that a report inadvertently exposes other employees' salary data. Catching this during UAT prevents the sensitive data exposure from ever reaching the production release.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team finishes its testing and is ready to deploy a new HR application on Friday. The business owner has not yet confirmed that the application meets the HR department's requirements with realistic data and permissions. Which of the following should occur BEFORE the production release?
quizOptions: A) A peer code review of the application's source code by the developers who wrote it
B) User acceptance testing, in which HR staff validate it with realistic scenarios
C) A penetration test of the production environment after the application is released
D) A load test that measures how many concurrent users the application can support
detail.explanation: UAT is the final stage before production, where real users confirm that the application meets business requirements, including data handling and permissions. Penetration testing in production comes too late, code review happens during development, and load testing measures performance.

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: A UAV, or drone, is a remotely piloted or autonomous aircraft that can be used for legitimate purposes like facility inspection and perimeter surveillance, but also poses a security risk when used by attackers for unauthorized surveillance, signal jamming, or even physically delivering a rogue wireless access point near a target building.
examContext: SY0-701 covers UAVs under physical security threats; know that drones can be used offensively to capture images of badge codes or screens, or to place a rogue access point within range of a target's Wi-Fi network from outside normal perimeter security.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's physical security assessment flags that a UAV could hover near the building's upper floors and photograph whiteboards or badge entry codes through windows, bypassing fences and guards entirely; he recommends window film and policies restricting drone flight over the property.
detail.quizQuestion: Security staff observe a drone hovering outside the conference room windows of the executive floor during board meetings. Which of the following controls would BEST reduce the risk that the drone captures sensitive information shown on screens and whiteboards?
quizOptions: A) Install a host-based firewall on each of the computers in the conference room
B) Install privacy film on the windows and orient sensitive displays away from them
C) Add a mantrap at the entrance of the executive floor to control tailgating
D) Require WPA3 encryption and 802.1X authentication on the conference room wireless network
detail.explanation: A drone can photograph screens or whiteboards through windows, so physical measures such as privacy film and display placement address the risk. Wireless encryption, host firewalls and a mantrap protect against network and entry threats, not observation from outside.

definition: A connectionless transport layer protocol that sends data without establishing a session or guaranteeing delivery, order, or error correction, trading reliability for speed and lower overhead; used by applications like DNS, DHCP, and streaming media.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know UDP's lack of a handshake makes it the protocol of choice for amplification and reflection DDoS attacks, such as DNS or NTP amplification, since the source IP can be spoofed with no connection verification.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's organization experiences a massive volume of unsolicited DNS responses flooding its network from servers it never queried. Priya identifies this as a UDP-based amplification DDoS attack, where attackers spoofed the victim's IP address in DNS queries sent to open resolvers, since UDP requires no connection setup to verify the source.
detail.quizQuestion: A DNS server is flooding a victim with traffic. Analysis shows that attackers send small DNS queries with the victim's IP address as the source, and the server's much larger responses go to the victim. Which characteristic of UDP makes this attack possible?
quizOptions: A) UDP is connectionless, so the source address can be spoofed because there is no handshake
B) UDP is connection-oriented, so each query holds resources until the response is acknowledged
C) UDP guarantees ordered delivery, so the server retransmits responses until they are received
D) UDP encrypts the query payload, so the server cannot inspect the request before replying
detail.explanation: UDP has no handshake to verify the sender, so attackers can spoof the victim's address and have DNS servers send large responses to it (reflection and amplification). UDP is not connection-oriented, does not retransmit, and does not encrypt.

definition: A security technology that uses machine learning and statistical analysis to establish a baseline of normal user and device behavior, then flags anomalies that may indicate compromised credentials or insider threats. It can detect subtle attacks that signature-based tools miss, such as a legitimate account suddenly accessing unusual resources.
examContext: SY0-701 ties UEBA to behavioral and anomaly-based detection as opposed to signature-based detection, often integrated with or feeding into a SIEM; know it's particularly effective for detecting insider threats and compromised account misuse.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's UEBA platform flags an accountant's user account for suddenly downloading gigabytes of files from the HR system at 3 a.m., a sharp deviation from that user's established behavioral baseline. Investigation reveals the account's credentials were stolen and are being used by an attacker rather than the legitimate employee.
detail.quizQuestion: A finance employee's account normally uses five applications during business hours from the headquarters office. At 2 a.m., the account downloads 20 GB from the file server and signs in from a country where the company has no presence. No signature or known malware is detected. Which of the following technologies is MOST likely to flag this activity?
quizOptions: A) UEBA, which compares current activity with a learned baseline of normal behavior
B) A vulnerability scanner that checks the file server for missing patches
C) A signature-based antivirus engine that matches files against a list of known malware
D) A stateless packet filter that permits or denies traffic based on ports
detail.explanation: UEBA builds baselines of normal user and entity behavior and flags deviations such as unusual volumes, times and locations, which catches compromised accounts without signatures. Antivirus, packet filters and vulnerability scanners do not analyze behavior.

definition: The modern firmware interface that replaces the legacy BIOS, responsible for initializing hardware and loading the operating system, with support for Secure Boot, larger drives, and a richer pre-boot environment. Secure Boot within UEFI cryptographically verifies that only trusted, signed bootloaders and OS components run during startup.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts UEFI's Secure Boot capability with legacy BIOS, which has no such protection; know that Secure Boot helps prevent bootkits and rootkits from loading unsigned code before the operating system starts.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam enables UEFI Secure Boot on all new company laptops, which cryptographically verifies every bootloader component against a trusted signature list before allowing startup to proceed. When malware later attempts to install a bootkit on a test machine, Secure Boot refuses to load the unsigned, tampered bootloader.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to stop a bootkit from loading before the operating system starts on new laptops. The firmware should verify digital signatures on the bootloader and refuse to run anything that is unsigned or altered. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) UEFI Secure Boot, which verifies signed bootloaders before the operating system loads
B) A network intrusion prevention system that inspects traffic from the laptops
C) Legacy BIOS with a boot password, which prevents the boot order from being changed
D) A host-based antivirus agent that starts after the operating system has loaded
detail.explanation: UEFI Secure Boot checks that bootloaders and early operating system components are signed by a trusted authority, which prevents bootkits and rootkits from loading. A BIOS password does not verify code, antivirus starts after the OS, and a network IPS cannot see what happens during boot.

definition: UEM is a management platform that combines mobile device management, application management, and traditional desktop and laptop management into a single console, allowing administrators to enforce consistent security policies across every type of endpoint an organization supports. It consolidates what were once separate MDM and EMM tools into one unified approach.
examContext: Exam may present UEM as the evolution of MDM/EMM, covering phones, tablets, laptops, and desktops from one console; know it is used to push patches, enforce encryption, and remotely wipe lost or stolen devices across all device types.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's IT team replaces separate mobile device and desktop management tools with a single UEM platform, letting them push the same encryption and patch compliance policies to every laptop, tablet, and phone in the company from one console instead of juggling multiple systems.
detail.quizQuestion: A company has 800 corporate laptops, 1,200 smartphones and 300 tablets, each group managed with a different tool. The security team wants one console that enforces encryption, pushes patches and can remotely wipe any lost device, regardless of type. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) Unified endpoint management, which manages every endpoint type from a single console
B) Network access control, which checks devices when they connect to the network
C) A virtual desktop infrastructure, which hosts desktops on centralized servers
D) Mobile application management, which controls only specific apps on mobile devices
detail.explanation: UEM combines mobile device management, application management and traditional PC management in one console, so policy can be applied to all endpoints. MAM covers apps only, NAC controls network admission, and VDI centralizes desktops rather than managing devices.

items.name: BYOD
items.detail: Bring Your Own Device: the employee's personal device. Cheapest, but hardest to control and mixes personal and work data.

items.name: COPE
items.detail: Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the company buys the device and allows personal use; the company keeps control.

items.name: CYOD
items.detail: Choose Your Own Device: the employee picks from an approved list of company devices.

items.name: Corporate-owned (COBO)
items.detail: Company-owned and for business use only. Maximum control.

items.name: Management tools
items.detail: MDM, UEM and MAM: remote wipe, encryption, passcode rules, application control, containerization and geofencing.

definition: A battery-backed device that provides short-term emergency power to connected equipment during a utility power outage, giving systems time to gracefully shut down or switch to a generator. It supports the availability objective of the CIA triad by protecting against abrupt power loss.
examContext: SY0-701 lists UPS among physical and environmental security and resiliency controls alongside generators and HVAC, supporting availability during short power disruptions; know a UPS is a short-term bridge, not a replacement for a generator during extended outages.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's data center installs UPS units on every server rack so that a brief utility power flicker doesn't cause an abrupt, disk-corrupting shutdown. When a storm later causes a sustained outage, the UPS bridges power long enough for the backup generator to start and take over seamlessly.
detail.quizQuestion: A server room has a UPS rated for 15 minutes of runtime and no generator. A utility outage in the area is expected to last several hours. Which of the following is the BEST way to keep the critical servers available throughout the outage?
quizOptions: A) Move the servers to a second circuit that is fed by the same utility provider
B) Add a generator that starts automatically and use the UPS to bridge the startup
C) Replace the UPS with a larger one that provides about 30 minutes of runtime
D) Install a surge protector between the UPS and the power supplies of the servers
detail.explanation: A UPS only bridges short interruptions, so a multi-hour outage needs a generator, with the UPS covering the seconds before it takes over. A slightly bigger UPS still runs out, surge protectors do not supply power, and a second circuit from the same utility fails too.

definition: A URI is a string of characters that uniquely identifies a resource, such as a web page, file, or API endpoint; a URL is the most common type of URI that also specifies how to access the resource's location. Attackers sometimes manipulate URIs to perform directory traversal or injection attacks by embedding malicious characters or encoded sequences.
examContext: Exam may test that a URL is a specific type of URI that includes a retrieval method (like https://), while a URI can also simply name a resource without specifying how to fetch it; watch for questions about malicious or encoded characters hidden in a URI during input validation scenarios.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex reviews a web application's logs and notices a URI containing encoded directory traversal sequences attempting to escape the web root and read a system password file; the web application firewall blocks the request and Alex tightens input validation on all URI parameters.
detail.quizQuestion: A web server logs the request GET /download?file=..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd and returns a file that contains user account names. Which of the following BEST describes how the attacker abused the URI, and the best defense?
quizOptions: A) SQL injection using encoded characters, mitigated by parameterized queries and escaping
B) Session fixation using encoded characters, mitigated by regenerating session identifiers
C) Directory traversal using encoded sequences, mitigated by input validation of the path
D) Cross-site scripting using encoded characters, mitigated by output encoding and CSP
detail.explanation: The ..%2f sequences are encoded parent-directory references, so the attacker walks out of the web root to read system files, and validating and canonicalizing the input stops it. The other attacks target databases, browsers or sessions.

definition: The text address used to locate a specific resource on the internet, such as a web page, specifying the protocol, domain, and path. Attackers frequently manipulate or disguise URLs, through typosquatting, shorteners, and homograph characters, to trick victims into visiting malicious sites during phishing campaigns.
examContext: SY0-701 ties URLs to phishing indicators such as typosquatting, URL shorteners hiding a malicious destination, and homograph attacks using look-alike characters; expect scenario questions about identifying a suspicious URL in an email or message.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan trains employees to hover over hyperlinks before clicking, after a phishing simulation shows that a URL displaying a trusted brand name in the link text actually points to a lookalike domain with a swapped character. The training reduces the click-through rate on the next simulated phishing test significantly.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees receive an email saying their account is locked, with a link displayed as https://www.examp1e-bank.com/login. In the link, the letter l of the real bank's domain has been replaced by the digit 1. Which of the following BEST describes the technique used in the URL?
quizOptions: A) Typosquatting with look-alike characters that imitate the legitimate bank's domain
B) Domain hijacking that transfers the real domain to the attacker through fraud
C) Pharming that redirects the legitimate domain to the attacker's server through DNS
D) URL shortening that hides the final destination behind an unrelated short link
detail.explanation: Registering a domain that differs by a look-alike character is typosquatting (a homograph-style trick), meant to fool victims in phishing. A shortener hides a destination, pharming poisons name resolution, and hijacking takes over the real domain, none of which is described.

definition: A standard interface for connecting peripherals and storage devices to a computer. USB ports and removable drives are a common vector for both data exfiltration and malware introduction, such as via an infected flash drive, which is why many organizations restrict or disable USB storage through endpoint policy.
