examContext: SY0-701 ties USB to removable media risks, including data exfiltration and malware delivery such as a dropped malicious USB drive in a parking lot, and the mitigation of disabling USB mass storage or using DLP/endpoint controls to restrict it.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's security team disables USB mass storage on all workstations through group policy after an employee plugged in an unknown flash drive found in the parking lot, which turned out to be loaded with malware. Endpoint DLP logs now also flag any attempt to copy sensitive files to removable media.
detail.quizQuestion: A security awareness exercise leaves USB flash drives labeled Payroll in the parking lot, and 40 percent of them are plugged into corporate computers. Which of the following controls would BEST reduce the risk of this attack in practice?
quizOptions: A) Disable USB mass storage with endpoint policy and train staff to report found drives
B) Require a complex password on every computer that has an available USB port
C) Enable full-disk encryption on all of the corporate laptops and desktops it owns
D) Place a stronger firewall at the perimeter to filter inbound internet traffic
detail.explanation: A dropped USB drive delivers malware when someone plugs it in, so blocking USB storage through endpoint controls and training users to report found devices addresses the vector. Complex passwords, disk encryption and a perimeter firewall do not stop a local device from running code.

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: USB OTG is a specification that allows a mobile device, such as a smartphone, to act as a USB host and directly connect to peripherals like flash drives, keyboards, or other phones without needing a computer in between. This capability can be exploited to exfiltrate data directly from a managed mobile device to removable media, bypassing cloud-based data loss prevention controls.
examContext: Exam may test USB OTG as a data exfiltration risk on mobile devices, since it lets a phone read or write directly to a USB flash drive, which some MDM/UEM policies specifically disable to enforce data loss prevention.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's UEM policy review finds that corporate phones can still use USB OTG adapters to copy files directly to a USB flash drive, completely bypassing the cloud-based DLP controls monitoring email and app data; she pushes a policy disabling USB OTG peripheral access on managed devices.
detail.quizQuestion: A company uses a UEM platform to enforce data loss prevention on managed smartphones, blocking uploads to personal cloud storage. An investigation finds that an employee copied a large customer file to a flash drive plugged directly into the phone. Which feature allowed this, and what is the BEST control?
quizOptions: A) USB OTG, which lets the phone host removable drives and can be disabled by policy
B) Wi-Fi Direct, which links two devices without an access point and can be blocked by policy
C) Bluetooth tethering, which shares a connection and can be blocked by disabling the radio
D) NFC beaming, which passes small data items by tapping and can be limited with a PIN
detail.explanation: USB OTG lets a phone act as a USB host and read or write removable storage directly, bypassing cloud-based DLP, so MDM or UEM policy should disable it. Bluetooth tethering, Wi-Fi Direct and NFC beaming are not how a drive plugged into the phone works.

items.name: Cellular
items.detail: Carrier network. Risks: interception, rogue base stations (IMSI catchers), SIM swapping.

items.name: Wi-Fi
items.detail: Use WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise; avoid open hotspots.

items.name: Bluetooth
items.detail: Short range; risks are bluejacking, bluesnarfing and weak pairing. Turn it off when unused.

items.name: NFC
items.detail: Very short range (about 4 cm); used for contactless payment. Risks: eavesdropping and relay attacks.

items.name: RFID
items.detail: Tags read at a distance; cheap tags are easy to clone or skim.

items.name: GPS
items.detail: Location. A privacy concern and the basis of geofencing.

items.name: USB
items.detail: Charging and data. Risks: juice jacking and malicious cables or drives.

definition: A single security appliance or platform that consolidates multiple protective functions, such as firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus, content filtering, and VPN, into one integrated solution. It simplifies management for smaller organizations compared to deploying and maintaining separate point solutions.
examContext: SY0-701 presents UTM as an all-in-one network security appliance combining several functions such as firewall, IPS, antimalware, and content filtering; know the trade-off is a single point of failure/bottleneck versus the simplicity of consolidated management.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's small business deploys a single UTM appliance at the network edge that handles firewalling, intrusion prevention, web content filtering, and the site-to-site VPN, replacing five separate devices the company previously struggled to manage. The consolidated dashboard lets Sam's small IT team monitor every security function from one interface.
detail.quizQuestion: A 25-person company has one IT administrator and wants a single appliance that provides a firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus scanning, content filtering and VPN termination, managed from one console. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) A unified threat management appliance that consolidates several security functions
B) A network tap that copies traffic to a separate monitoring tool for analysis
C) A web application firewall that protects the company's public web applications
D) A load balancer that distributes incoming requests across several web servers
detail.explanation: A UTM combines firewall, IPS, antimalware, content filtering and VPN in one appliance, which suits a small company, though it is also a single point of failure. A WAF protects web applications, a tap only copies traffic, and a load balancer distributes requests.

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

definition: UTP is a common type of copper network cabling, such as Cat5e or Cat6, that twists pairs of wires together to reduce electromagnetic interference without an additional shielding layer. It is inexpensive and widely used for standard Ethernet connections, but is more susceptible to eavesdropping and interference than shielded or fiber alternatives in high-interference or high-security environments.
examContext: Exam may contrast UTP with shielded twisted pair (STP) or fiber optic cabling when discussing susceptibility to electromagnetic interference and ease of physical tapping in a wiring closet.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's facilities team runs new network drops through an area near heavy manufacturing equipment and chooses shielded cabling instead of standard UTP specifically to reduce electromagnetic interference from the nearby machinery, after noticing intermittent packet loss on the existing UTP runs.
detail.quizQuestion: A high-security lab uses unshielded twisted pair Ethernet cabling in a shared ceiling space. A consultant warns that the cabling is easy to tap physically and is susceptible to electromagnetic interference. Which of the following BEST addresses both concerns?
quizOptions: A) Replace it with coaxial cable, which was the standard medium for early Ethernet
B) Replace it with Cat6 UTP, which uses the same unshielded design at higher speeds
C) Replace it with fiber optic cabling, which resists tapping and electromagnetic interference
D) Replace it with shielded twisted pair, which reduces interference but is still a copper cable
detail.explanation: Fiber carries light rather than electrical signals, so it does not radiate or pick up electromagnetic interference and is much harder to tap. STP reduces interference but is still copper, Cat6 UTP is still unshielded, and coaxial cable is also a tappable copper medium.

definition: A scripting language built into Microsoft Office applications that automates tasks through macros. Attackers frequently abuse VBA macros embedded in Word or Excel documents to execute malicious code when a victim opens the file and enables macros.
examContext: SY0-701 ties VBA macros to a common malware delivery vector in phishing attachments; know that disabling macros by default, or allowing only signed macros, is the standard mitigation for this attack vector.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's organization blocks all VBA macros from running in documents downloaded from the internet, after a phishing campaign tried to deliver ransomware through a malicious invoice spreadsheet with an embedded macro. Employees who need legitimate macros must have them digitally signed and explicitly approved by IT.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees receive an invoice as a Word document. When it is opened, it asks them to click Enable Content, and afterward a script downloads malware from the internet. Which of the following is the BEST preventive control?
quizOptions: A) Enable full-disk encryption so that the downloaded malware cannot read the user's files
B) Add the sender's domain to the mail filter's blocklist after the first employee reports it
C) Disable macros by default in documents from the internet, and allow only signed macros
D) Deploy a host-based firewall rule that blocks all inbound connections to the workstations
detail.explanation: The attack depends on a VBA macro running when the user enables content, so disabling macros by default and permitting only signed ones removes the vector. An inbound firewall rule does not stop outbound downloads, disk encryption does not stop malware from running, and blocklisting a sender is reactive.

definition: A VDE is the individual virtual desktop session a user interacts with, running on a server and streamed to the user's endpoint device, as opposed to the backend infrastructure that hosts it. Centralizing the actual desktop environment on a server lets administrators keep sensitive data off endpoint devices and apply consistent security controls to every session.
examContext: Exam may use VDE alongside VDI, where VDI is the overall infrastructure and a VDE is the individual desktop session a specific user experiences; know that data stays on the server rather than the local endpoint in both cases.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex provisions a standardized VDE for each contractor so that regardless of what personal laptop they connect from, they see the same locked-down desktop with no ability to copy files to their local machine, keeping sensitive project data entirely on company servers.
detail.quizQuestion: A company deploys a platform of servers that hosts hundreds of virtual desktops for contractors, who see a full Windows desktop streamed to their personal laptops. Which of the following correctly identifies the platform and the individual desktop session each contractor uses?
quizOptions: A) The platform is a VPN, and each contractor's session is a virtual desktop environment
B) The platform is a VDE, and each contractor's session is a virtual desktop infrastructure
C) The platform is VDI, and each contractor's session is a virtual desktop environment
D) The platform is VDI, and each contractor's session is a virtual private network
detail.explanation: VDI is the backend infrastructure that hosts the virtual desktops, while a VDE is the individual desktop session a user experiences. A VPN extends a network rather than hosting desktops, and the two desktop terms are not reversed.

definition: VDI is the backend infrastructure that hosts and manages virtual desktops on centralized servers, delivering a consistent desktop experience to users on a wide variety of endpoint devices, including thin clients, personal laptops, or tablets. Because the actual computing and data storage happen in the data center, VDI can reduce the impact of a lost or stolen endpoint device, since little or no sensitive data is stored locally on it.
examContext: Exam expects you to know VDI centralizes desktop computing and data storage in the data center rather than on the endpoint, making it a strong control for BYOD scenarios where endpoint devices are not fully trusted or managed.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's company deploys VDI for all remote call-center staff using personal computers at home, so that even if an employee's home PC is compromised or stolen, no customer data was ever actually stored on that device, since every session runs on servers back at the data center.
detail.quizQuestion: A company allows contractors to use their own laptops. It wants no sensitive data stored on those devices and wants to limit the damage if a laptop is lost or infected. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) Provide virtual desktops hosted in the data center so that the data stays off the endpoint
B) Install a mobile device manager that backs up the data to the contractor's laptop
C) Require full-disk encryption and a local copy of the data on each personal laptop
D) Issue each contractor a USB drive that stores the project files in an encrypted container
detail.explanation: With VDI the desktop and data live on servers in the data center, so a lost or untrusted endpoint holds little or no sensitive data. Encryption helps but still leaves local copies, and local backups or USB drives put data on the very devices that are not trusted.

definition: A logical segmentation of a physical network into multiple separate broadcast domains, allowing administrators to isolate groups of devices for security or organizational purposes without requiring separate physical switches or cabling.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know VLANs provide network segmentation, a key defense-in-depth control, and that inter-VLAN traffic must pass through a router or Layer 3 device; also be aware of VLAN hopping attacks that exploit misconfigured trunk ports.

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan wants to isolate IoT devices on the corporate network from sensitive finance workstations without installing new physical switches. Jordan creates separate VLANs for IoT devices and finance systems, configuring the switch to prevent any direct Layer 2 communication between them.
detail.quizQuestion: Guest laptops and the accounting servers are connected to the same switch. The security team must prevent guests from reaching the accounting servers while avoiding the cost of separate hardware. Which of the following is the BEST solution?
quizOptions: A) Place them in the same VLAN with different IP subnets, because subnets alone isolate traffic
B) Place them in separate VLANs and route and filter traffic between them at Layer 3
C) Place them in separate VLANs and switch the traffic between them directly at Layer 2
D) Place them in separate VLANs and trunk every port so that all VLAN tags are visible
detail.explanation: VLANs create separate broadcast domains on the same hardware, and traffic between them must pass through a router or Layer 3 device where ACLs or firewall rules can filter it. Different subnets in one VLAN do not isolate, Layer 2 switching between VLANs defeats the purpose, and trunking every port invites VLAN hopping.

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.

items.name: ARP poisoning
items.detail: Forged ARP replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP, putting the attacker on-path. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries.

items.name: DNS poisoning
items.detail: Forged records are injected into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker sites. Fix: DNSSEC, patched resolvers.

items.name: MAC flooding
items.detail: Fills a switch's CAM table so it floods traffic out of every port, letting the attacker sniff. Fix: port security.

items.name: MAC spoofing
items.detail: Adopting another device's MAC address to evade filtering or impersonate it. Fix: 802.1X, port security.

items.name: VLAN hopping
items.detail: Switch spoofing or double tagging to reach other VLANs. Fix: disable trunk negotiation, change the native VLAN, prune unused ports.

items.name: On-path (MITM)
items.detail: The attacker sits between two parties to read or alter traffic. Fix: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, mutual authentication.

items.name: Session hijacking
items.detail: Stealing or guessing a session token to impersonate a logged-in user. Fix: TLS, secure and HttpOnly cookies, short sessions.

items.name: SSL stripping
items.detail: Downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to HTTP. Fix: HSTS.

items.name: Replay
items.detail: Captured valid data is re-sent later. Fix: nonces, timestamps and expiring tokens.

items.name: Spoofing
items.detail: Forging an address or identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID). Fix: ingress/egress filtering, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication.

definition: VLSM is a technique for subnetting a network into subnets of different sizes, rather than dividing it into equally sized blocks, allowing more efficient use of available IP address space. Proper VLSM design supports network segmentation, which is itself a key security control for isolating systems with different trust levels.
examContext: Exam may test VLSM as the method enabling efficient, differently-sized subnets in support of network segmentation; know that it reduces wasted IP addresses compared to fixed-size classful subnetting.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam redesigns the company's IP addressing scheme using VLSM so that a small subnet of eight addresses is allocated for the point-to-point link between routers, while a larger subnet of 500 addresses is allocated for the main office network, avoiding the massive address waste a fixed-size subnetting scheme would have caused.
detail.quizQuestion: A company has been assigned 192.168.10.0/24 and needs one subnet for 100 hosts, one for 50 hosts and two point-to-point links with two hosts each. The network engineer wants to avoid wasting addresses. Which of the following techniques BEST accomplishes this?
quizOptions: A) DHCP reservations, which assign a specific address to a specific device each time
B) VLSM, which allows subnets of different sizes to be carved from the same block
C) NAT overload, which maps many private addresses to a single public address
D) Fixed-length subnetting, which divides the block into equal subnets of the same size
detail.explanation: VLSM lets an engineer use different prefix lengths so each subnet fits its host count, wasting fewer addresses, and smaller subnets also support segmentation. Equal-size subnets waste space, NAT conserves public addresses rather than dividing a block, and DHCP reservations assign individual addresses.

definition: A VM is a software-based emulation of a physical computer, running its own operating system on top of a hypervisor that shares the underlying hardware with other VMs. Virtualization enables workload isolation and rapid provisioning, but a vulnerability in the hypervisor could potentially allow an attacker to escape one VM and access others on the same host.
examContext: Exam may reference VM escape as a key virtualization risk, where an attacker breaks out of a guest VM's isolation to access the hypervisor or other VMs on the same physical host; know that keeping hypervisors patched is the primary defense.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's cloud security review flags an outdated hypervisor version known to be vulnerable to a VM escape exploit, where a compromised VM on the shared host could potentially break out and access other customers' virtual machines running on the same physical server; she schedules immediate patching.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud administrator learns of a vulnerability that allows code in one guest virtual machine to break out and access the hypervisor, and through it other guests on the same host. Which of the following BEST describes this attack and the primary defense?
quizOptions: A) Resource exhaustion, in which one guest starves the others, mitigated by setting limits
B) VM escape, in which a guest breaks out to the host, mitigated by patching the hypervisor
C) VM sprawl, in which unused guests pile up unmanaged, mitigated by decommissioning them
D) Snapshot tampering, in which a saved state is altered, mitigated by controlling restores
detail.explanation: Breaking out of a guest into the hypervisor or other guests is VM escape, and prompt hypervisor patching is the primary defense. VM sprawl is unmanaged growth, resource exhaustion is a denial of service among guests, and snapshot tampering alters saved states.

definition: VoIP is technology that transmits voice calls as digital data over IP networks rather than traditional analog phone lines, typically using RTP for media transport and SIP or similar protocols for call signaling. Because it runs over the same network as other data, VoIP traffic needs its own security considerations like VLAN segmentation and encrypted media to prevent eavesdropping or toll fraud.
examContext: Exam may ask you to recommend placing VoIP phones on a separate VLAN from general data traffic and using SRTP for encryption; know that VoIP traffic shares infrastructure with other IP traffic unless segmented.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen segments the office's VoIP phones onto their own dedicated VLAN separate from employee workstations, so that a compromised computer on the data VLAN cannot easily eavesdrop on or disrupt voice traffic traveling across the phone VLAN.
detail.quizQuestion: A company deploys VoIP phones on the same network segment as employee workstations. During an assessment, a tester on a workstation captures calls and finds that the phones can be enumerated and called directly from the workstation. Which of the following BEST reduces both risks?
quizOptions: A) Keep the phones on the workstation VLAN and use TLS only for the web management portal
B) Place the phones on a separate VLAN and use SRTP to encrypt the voice media streams
C) Place the phones on a separate VLAN but leave the voice media streams unencrypted
D) Place the phones in the DMZ and allow inbound SIP traffic from any internet address
detail.explanation: A separate voice VLAN limits who can reach and enumerate the phones, and SRTP encrypts the media so captured calls cannot be heard. Leaving media unencrypted fixes only half of it, and TLS on a portal or exposing SIP to the internet does not address either risk.

definition: An isolated, logically segmented section of a public cloud provider's infrastructure where an organization can deploy resources with its own private IP addressing, subnets, and network controls. It lets a cloud tenant apply network segmentation and security controls similar to a traditional private data center network.
examContext: SY0-701 ties VPC to cloud network segmentation and isolation; know that a VPC lets an organization control subnetting, routing, and security groups or ACLs within a cloud provider's shared infrastructure, isolating their resources from other tenants.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex designs the company's cloud environment with a VPC split into public and private subnets, placing database servers in the private subnet with no direct internet route and only the web tier in the public subnet. This segmentation ensures that even if the web tier is compromised, the database servers aren't directly reachable from the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A company moves a three-tier application to a public cloud and wants an isolated section of the provider's network with its own private IP ranges, subnets, route tables and security groups, separated from other customers' resources. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A site-to-site VPN, which connects the on-premises network to the cloud provider
B) A content delivery network, which caches static content on servers close to the end users
C) A virtual private cloud, a logically isolated network section within the public cloud
D) A dedicated physical server, which the provider places in the shared data center
detail.explanation: A VPC gives a tenant its own isolated address space, subnets, routing and security controls inside the provider's infrastructure. A CDN accelerates content, a VPN connects networks, and a dedicated server is a hardware option rather than a logical network.

definition: A technology that creates an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet, allowing remote users or sites to securely access private network resources as if directly connected. It protects data confidentiality and integrity in transit and can mask the user's originating IP address and location.
examContext: SY0-701 tests VPN in both remote-access and site-to-site forms, often alongside IPsec and TLS as the underlying encryption protocols; also know split-tunnel versus full-tunnel VPN configurations as exam-relevant distinctions.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures a full-tunnel VPN for remote employees so that all of their internet traffic, not just traffic destined for the corporate network, routes through and is inspected by the company's security stack. This prevents remote workers from bypassing content filtering and DLP controls by browsing directly out to the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: Remote employees connect to the corporate VPN with split tunneling enabled, so only traffic for corporate subnets goes through the tunnel while other internet traffic leaves directly from their home connection. The security team wants all web traffic inspected by the corporate proxy. Which of the following changes BEST achieves this?
quizOptions: A) Keep the split tunnel and add a firewall rule that blocks all personal web browsing by users
B) Configure a full tunnel so that all client traffic is routed through the corporate network
C) Switch from an IPsec VPN to an SSL VPN, which encrypts web traffic more strongly
D) Keep the split tunnel and require longer passwords for all of the VPN accounts
detail.explanation: A full tunnel sends all client traffic through the corporate network, where the proxy and other controls can inspect it, while a split tunnel lets non-corporate traffic bypass them. Blocking browsing locally is not enforceable, changing the VPN type does not change routing, and longer passwords do not affect inspection.

items.name: Remote access (client-to-site)
items.detail: One user's device connects to the corporate network across the internet. The standard remote-worker VPN.

items.name: Site-to-site
items.detail: Two networks (for example two offices) are joined through VPN gateways. Always on and invisible to users.

items.name: Full tunnel
items.detail: ALL of the client's traffic, including web browsing, goes through the VPN, so corporate inspection and filtering still apply. Uses more bandwidth.

items.name: Split tunnel
items.detail: Only traffic for corporate resources uses the VPN; everything else goes straight to the internet. Saves bandwidth, but that traffic bypasses corporate security controls.

items.name: SSL/TLS VPN
items.detail: Runs over TLS (usually port 443) so it passes through most firewalls, often via a browser portal with no client software.

items.name: IPsec VPN
items.detail: Works at the network layer using IKE, ESP and/or AH; usually needs client software or a gateway.

items.name: L2TP / PPTP
items.detail: L2TP provides the tunnel but NO encryption of its own, so it is paired with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP is obsolete and insecure.

items.name: Always-on
items.detail: The VPN connects automatically at startup or network change without the user doing anything.

items.name: AH
items.detail: Authentication Header: integrity and authentication of the whole packet but NO encryption. IP protocol 51, and it breaks when NAT rewrites the header.

items.name: ESP
items.detail: Encapsulating Security Payload: encryption plus (optional) integrity and authentication. IP protocol 50. This is what provides confidentiality.

items.name: Transport mode
items.detail: Encrypts only the payload and keeps the original IP header; typically host-to-host.

items.name: Tunnel mode
items.detail: Encrypts the entire original packet and wraps it in a new IP header; typically gateway-to-gateway (site-to-site VPN).

items.name: IKE
items.detail: Internet Key Exchange: negotiates the security associations and keys (UDP 500; UDP 4500 for NAT traversal).

definition: VTC refers to systems and services that allow participants in different locations to communicate using real-time video and audio. Unsecured VTC sessions can be joined by unauthorized participants (sometimes called meeting bombing) or intercepted if the stream is not properly encrypted, risking exposure of sensitive discussions.
examContext: Exam may reference VTC alongside VoIP as collaboration technology that needs strong access controls, such as meeting passwords and waiting rooms, and encryption to prevent eavesdropping or unauthorized participants.

detail.practicalScenario: After an uninvited participant joins a confidential executive VTC meeting by guessing a predictable meeting link, Sam enables mandatory meeting passwords and a waiting room feature requiring host approval before anyone can join future video conferences.
detail.quizQuestion: Uninvited participants keep joining the company's video conferences and displaying offensive content. Meetings use a public link that anyone can open, and no password is required. Which of the following controls would BEST prevent this?
quizOptions: A) Increase the video bitrate so that the meeting is harder for outsiders to intercept
B) Move the meetings to a different port number so that outsiders cannot find them
C) Record every meeting so that outsiders can be identified after the session ends
D) Require meeting passwords, use a waiting room and let only the host admit attendees
detail.explanation: Passwords, a waiting room and host admission are access controls that stop unauthorized participants from joining. Bitrate and port changes do not control entry, and recording is detective rather than preventive.

definition: A security appliance or service that filters, monitors, and blocks malicious HTTP/HTTPS traffic to and from a web application, defending against attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It operates at the application layer, inspecting request content rather than just IP addresses and ports like a traditional network firewall.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes a WAF's application-layer content inspection from a traditional network firewall's lower-layer filtering; expect scenarios where a WAF blocks a specific attack pattern, like a SQL injection payload, targeting a public web application.

detail.practicalScenario: Chen deploys a WAF in front of the company's public-facing e-commerce site, configuring rules that block requests containing common SQL injection and XSS payload patterns. When an automated scanner later probes the site with injection attempts, the WAF blocks every malicious request before it reaches the application server.
detail.quizQuestion: A public e-commerce site is attacked with requests that contain SQL injection payloads in a search parameter. The development team needs several weeks to fix the code. Which of the following would BEST provide immediate protection?
quizOptions: A) Deploy a stateless packet filter that blocks traffic from the attackers' source ports
B) Deploy a network tap that copies the traffic to a protocol analyzer for review
C) Deploy a load balancer that distributes the search requests across more servers
D) Deploy a web application firewall with rules that block SQL injection patterns
detail.explanation: A WAF inspects HTTP requests at the application layer and can block SQL injection patterns as a compensating control while the code is fixed. A packet filter sees only addresses and ports, a tap only observes, and a load balancer spreads the attack across more servers.

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

items.name: Forward proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of CLIENTS. Users' outbound requests go through it for content filtering, caching, logging and anonymity. Clients are configured to use it.

items.name: Reverse proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of SERVERS. Outside clients talk to the proxy, which forwards to the back end. Used for load balancing, TLS offloading, caching and hiding server details.

items.name: Transparent proxy
items.detail: Intercepts traffic inline without any client configuration, so users do not know it is there.

items.name: Caching proxy
items.detail: Stores copies of frequently requested content to save bandwidth and speed responses.

definition: A WAP is a networking device that allows wireless client devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi. Misconfigured or rogue WAPs, including ones secretly connected by an employee or physically placed by an attacker, can bypass perimeter security controls entirely and provide a direct wireless path into the internal network.
examContext: Exam may test rogue access point scenarios, where an unauthorized WAP plugged into a network jack creates a backdoor; know that wireless intrusion prevention systems (WIPS) and port security help detect and prevent this.

detail.practicalScenario: During a routine sweep, Maria's WIPS detects a cheap consumer-grade WAP that an employee quietly plugged into a conference room network jack to get better Wi-Fi reception for personal devices, completely bypassing the corporate wireless security policies; she removes it and reports the incident.
detail.quizQuestion: A technician finds a small, unmanaged wireless access point plugged into a wall jack in a meeting room. An employee installed it for convenience, and it still has its default password. Which of the following controls would BEST prevent this kind of unauthorized access point from providing a path into the network?
quizOptions: A) Disable DHCP on the wired network so that new devices cannot obtain addresses
B) Enable 802.1X or port security on the switch ports and monitor with a wireless IPS
C) Require WPA3 on the company's approved access points and keep the network name hidden
D) Ask employees to report any wireless network names that they do not recognize
detail.explanation: A rogue AP on a network jack bypasses the perimeter, so wired-side controls such as 802.1X or port security, plus a wireless IPS to detect and contain rogue radios, address it. WPA3 on approved APs does not affect an unapproved one, static addressing defeats disabling DHCP, and relying on reports is weak.

definition: An early, now completely broken Wi-Fi encryption standard that used a static, weak implementation of the RC4 cipher, making it crackable within minutes using widely available tools. It has been entirely superseded by WPA2 and WPA3.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to immediately recognize WEP as deprecated and insecure and never an acceptable answer for securing a wireless network; it's a classic wrong-answer option alongside correct choices like WPA2/WPA3.

detail.practicalScenario: Sam discovers a forgotten guest wireless network in a warehouse still configured with WEP encryption from over a decade ago. He immediately reconfigures the access point to WPA2, or WPA3 if supported, since WEP can be cracked in minutes with freely available tools.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester recovers a Wi-Fi network key within minutes by collecting packets and analyzing repeated initialization vectors, without any knowledge of the passphrase. Which of the following wireless security standards is MOST likely in use?
quizOptions: A) WPA2-Enterprise, which uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server to authenticate each user
B) WEP, which uses the RC4 cipher with a short, frequently repeated initialization vector
C) WPA2-Personal, which uses AES with CCMP and a four-way handshake to derive session keys
D) WPA3-Personal, which uses SAE to resist offline dictionary attacks against the passphrase
detail.explanation: Repeated initialization vectors let attackers recover a WEP key from captured packets within minutes. WPA2, WPA3 and WPA2-Enterprise use AES-based encryption and stronger key handling and do not have this weakness.

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: A system that monitors radio-frequency spectrum and wireless traffic to detect unauthorized access points, rogue devices, and wireless attack patterns such as deauthentication floods or evil twin APs. Unlike a wireless intrusion prevention system, a WIDS only alerts on suspicious activity rather than automatically blocking it.
examContext: SY0-701 contrasts a detection-only WIDS with a prevention-capable WIPS; know both monitor wireless-specific threats like rogue APs and deauth attacks that a wired IDS/IPS wouldn't see.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's WIDS sensors detect a rogue access point broadcasting from an unrecognized device in the building's parking lot, alerting the SOC before any employee connects to it. Because the system is a WIDS rather than a WIPS, security staff must manually locate and remove the rogue device rather than having it automatically blocked.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital wants to be alerted when someone sets up an unauthorized access point or launches a deauthentication flood in the building, but it does not want a system that takes automated action which could disrupt neighboring networks. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) A wireless intrusion prevention system that automatically disconnects the offending devices
B) A wired network intrusion detection system on a SPAN port of the core switch
C) A wireless intrusion detection system that monitors the spectrum and only generates alerts
D) A host-based firewall on each wireless client that blocks inbound connections
detail.explanation: A WIDS watches the wireless spectrum for rogue access points and attacks such as deauthentication floods, and it only alerts. A WIPS takes automated action, which the hospital wants to avoid, and wired IDS or host firewalls cannot see these radio-level events.

variants.title: IDS vs IPS and detection methods

items.name: IDS
items.detail: Intrusion DETECTION: passive and out-of-band, fed a copy of traffic. It alerts but cannot block, and if it fails the network keeps running.

items.name: IPS
items.detail: Intrusion PREVENTION: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop, block or reset malicious traffic in real time. A failure or false positive can disrupt legitimate traffic.

items.name: Host-based (HIDS / HIPS)
items.detail: Software on an endpoint. Sees local file changes, logs and processes, and can read traffic after decryption. Must be deployed and managed per host.

items.name: Network-based (NIDS / NIPS)
items.detail: Sensors on a network segment inspect all traffic crossing it. One sensor covers many hosts but cannot see inside encrypted payloads.

items.name: Signature-based
items.detail: Matches known attack patterns. Accurate for known threats and low on false positives, but blind to zero-days and needs constant signature updates.

items.name: Anomaly / behavior-based
items.detail: Compares activity to a learned baseline. Can catch zero-days and novel attacks, but produces more false positives and needs a training period.

items.name: Wireless (WIDS / WIPS)
items.detail: Monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins and deauthentication floods; WIPS can also actively contain them.

items.name: Evil twin
items.detail: A rogue access point that copies a legitimate SSID so victims connect to it and can be eavesdropped on or phished.

items.name: Rogue access point
items.detail: ANY unauthorized AP plugged into your network, often by an employee, which creates a back door around your perimeter.

items.name: Deauthentication
items.detail: Forged deauth frames knock clients off the Wi-Fi (denial of service, or to force a reconnect so a handshake can be captured). Defeated by 802.11w protected management frames (mandatory in WPA3).

items.name: Jamming
items.detail: Transmitting noise on the same frequency to block wireless communication. A radio-frequency denial of service.

items.name: Bluejacking
items.detail: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices. An annoyance rather than data theft.

items.name: Bluesnarfing
items.detail: Stealing data (contacts, email) from a Bluetooth device without permission. Far more serious than bluejacking.

items.name: War driving
items.detail: Driving around with a laptop or phone mapping and probing Wi-Fi networks. War chalking (marking them) is the older sibling.

items.name: Wi-Fi Protected Setup
items.detail: The WPS PIN can be brute-forced quickly, so disable WPS.

definition: A WIPS monitors the wireless spectrum to detect and automatically respond to threats such as rogue access points, evil twin networks, and wireless denial-of-service attacks. Unlike a standard WIDS, which only detects and alerts, a WIPS can take active measures, such as disconnecting unauthorized devices from the network.
examContext: Exam may distinguish WIPS from WIDS the same way IPS is distinguished from IDS: WIPS can actively block or disconnect a detected wireless threat, while a detection-only system simply generates an alert.

detail.practicalScenario: When an evil twin access point mimicking the corporate SSID appears near the building, Jordan's WIPS automatically sends deauthentication frames to disconnect any clients that attempt to associate with the rogue network, without requiring a security analyst to manually intervene.
detail.quizQuestion: A retailer finds that employees' phones keep connecting to an unauthorized access point broadcasting the store's SSID from the parking lot. The retailer wants a system that detects rogue and evil twin access points and automatically disconnects clients that associate with them. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) A captive portal that requires guests to accept terms before they can use the network
B) A wireless intrusion detection system that detects the rogue access point and alerts only
C) A MAC address filter on the store's approved access points for the employee phones
D) A wireless intrusion prevention system that detects the rogue access point and contains it
detail.explanation: A WIPS detects rogue and evil twin access points and can take active measures, such as disconnecting affected clients. A WIDS only alerts, a captive portal handles guest onboarding, and MAC filtering on approved APs does nothing about an unauthorized one.

definition: A WO is a formal document that authorizes and records a specific task to be performed, such as a maintenance activity, change, or repair, including what work is needed, who approved it, and who performed it. In security and change management, work orders provide an auditable trail connecting approved changes to the technicians who carried them out.
examContext: Exam may reference WO alongside change management documentation; know it supports accountability and non-repudiation by formally recording who authorized and who executed a given task.

detail.practicalScenario: Priya requires every firewall rule change to be tied to an approved WO documenting the business justification, the approver, and the technician who implemented it, so that during a later audit, every configuration change can be traced back to a formal, authorized request.
detail.quizQuestion: An auditor asks the IT department to show who approved a firewall rule change last month, what the change was, and which technician carried it out. Which of the following records BEST provides this information?
quizOptions: A) The business impact analysis, which ranks the firewall among the critical systems
B) The work order, which records the approved task, the approver and the technician
C) The service level agreement, which defines the firewall service's uptime targets
D) The disaster recovery plan, which lists the steps to restore the firewall
detail.explanation: A work order formally authorizes and records a task, including what was done, who approved it and who did it, which provides an auditable trail and supports accountability. An SLA, a BIA and a DR plan serve other purposes.

items.name: SLA
items.detail: Service Level Agreement: measurable performance commitments (uptime, response time) between provider and customer, usually with penalties.

items.name: MOU
items.detail: Memorandum of Understanding: a general, usually NON-binding statement of shared intent.

items.name: MOA
items.detail: Memorandum of Agreement: more formal than an MOU, with specific responsibilities and commitments.

items.name: MSA
items.detail: Master Service Agreement: the umbrella contract with general terms; later SOWs and work orders fall under it.

items.name: SOW
items.detail: Statement of Work: the specifics of one project (deliverables, schedule, cost).

items.name: WO
items.detail: Work Order: authorization for a specific task, often under an MSA.

items.name: NDA
items.detail: Non-Disclosure Agreement: legally binds the parties to keep information confidential.

items.name: BPA
items.detail: Business Partners Agreement: how partner firms share responsibilities, profits and losses.

definition: WPA is a wireless security standard introduced to replace the deeply flawed WEP protocol, providing improved authentication and encryption for Wi-Fi networks. WPA itself was an interim improvement, using TKIP, before being superseded by the stronger WPA2 and WPA3 standards.
examContext: Exam expects you to place WPA in the evolution WEP to WPA to WPA2 to WPA3, recognizing that each generation addressed weaknesses in the one before it; know WPA used TKIP as a stopgap before WPA2 introduced AES-based CCMP.

detail.practicalScenario: While decommissioning old equipment, Sam finds a warehouse Wi-Fi network still configured for original WPA with TKIP; he upgrades the access points to support WPA2 with AES encryption, closing the gap left by TKIP's known weaknesses.
detail.quizQuestion: A small office still has older access points that cannot support WPA2. They currently use WEP, and the vendor offers a firmware update that adds WPA with TKIP. Which of the following BEST describes the update?
quizOptions: A) It is an interim improvement over WEP, but WPA2 or WPA3 hardware should replace it
B) It makes the network as secure as WPA3 because TKIP uses the same AES encryption
C) It is unnecessary because WEP remains an acceptable standard for a small office
D) It is a downgrade because WPA sends passwords in clear text, which WEP does not do
detail.explanation: WPA with TKIP was a stopgap that fixed WEP's worst flaws on old hardware, but TKIP is itself deprecated, so the long-term fix is WPA2 or WPA3. TKIP does not use AES, WEP is not acceptable, and WPA does not send passwords in clear text.

items.name: WEP
items.detail: RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV. Can be cracked in minutes; obsolete and never acceptable.

items.name: WPA
items.detail: Interim patch for WEP hardware using TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys and an integrity check). Deprecated.

items.name: WPA2
items.detail: AES-CCMP: strong encryption. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with a dictionary; Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS.

items.name: WPA3
items.detail: Replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy. Adds OWE (encryption on open hotspots), mandatory protected management frames, and 192-bit Enterprise mode.

items.name: Personal vs Enterprise
items.detail: Personal: one shared passphrase for everybody. Enterprise: 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user or device has individual credentials and can be revoked individually.

items.name: WPS
items.detail: Push-button/PIN setup whose 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly. Disable it.

definition: A wireless security standard that replaced WPA, using the AES-based CCMP encryption protocol to provide strong confidentiality and integrity for Wi-Fi traffic. It remained the dominant wireless security standard for over a decade before being succeeded by WPA3, though its personal mode is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know WPA2 uses AES/CCMP, replacing WPA's TKIP, and that WPA2-Personal handshakes can be captured and attacked offline with a dictionary or brute-force attack, which WPA3 addresses with SAE.

detail.practicalScenario: Alex captures a WPA2 four-way handshake during an authorized wireless penetration test and runs it through a password-cracking tool against a common password list, successfully recovering the weak pre-shared key. He recommends the client migrate to WPA3, whose SAE handshake resists this exact offline attack.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer must choose the encryption protocol for a new WPA2 deployment. The security team requires strong confidentiality and integrity and does not want to use any deprecated option. Which of the following should be selected?
quizOptions: A) RC4 with WEP, which relies on a static key and a short initialization vector
B) RC4 with TKIP, which provides per-packet keys and was designed for older hardware
C) SAE with the Dragonfly handshake, which is the key exchange that WPA3 uses
D) AES with CCMP, which provides strong confidentiality and integrity for WPA2 networks
detail.explanation: WPA2 uses AES with CCMP for strong confidentiality and integrity. TKIP and WEP rely on RC4 and are deprecated, and SAE is the WPA3 handshake rather than a WPA2 encryption protocol.

definition: The current generation Wi-Fi security standard that replaces WPA2's pre-shared key handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), resisting offline dictionary attacks even against weak passwords, and mandates stronger encryption. It also adds individualized data encryption on open networks through Opportunistic Wireless Encryption.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know WPA3 improves on WPA2 primarily through SAE, replacing the four-way handshake vulnerable to offline attacks, and stronger mandatory encryption; it's generally the best-practice answer when securing new wireless deployments.

detail.practicalScenario: Maria upgrades the office's wireless infrastructure to WPA3, which replaces the legacy handshake with SAE so that even a captured authentication exchange can't be feasibly cracked offline. Guest visitors connecting to the open guest network also benefit from WPA3's opportunistic encryption, which protects their traffic from casual eavesdropping even without a password.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is deploying Wi-Fi for a new office. Employees will use a shared passphrase, and the security team is worried that attackers could capture a handshake and run offline dictionary attacks against weak passphrases. Which of the following BEST addresses this concern?
quizOptions: A) WPA3-Personal, which uses SAE so that a captured handshake cannot be attacked offline
B) WPA2-Personal with AES, which resists offline attacks when the passphrase is short
C) WPA with TKIP, which generates a new key for every packet that is transmitted
D) WEP with a 128-bit key, which provides stronger encryption than the 64-bit version
detail.explanation: WPA3-Personal replaces the WPA2 handshake with SAE, which defeats offline dictionary attacks even against weak passphrases. WPA2-Personal handshakes can be captured and cracked, TKIP is deprecated, and WEP remains broken at any key length.

definition: WPS is a feature that lets users connect devices to a Wi-Fi network easily, often using a PIN or a physical button press instead of typing a complex passphrase. The PIN-based method has a well-known brute-force vulnerability that can expose the network's actual passphrase, so security guidance generally recommends disabling WPS.
examContext: Exam may test that WPS's PIN method is vulnerable to brute-force attacks that can recover the Wi-Fi passphrase, making it a recommended setting to disable on both home and enterprise access points.

detail.practicalScenario: During a home office security review, Priya discovers the router's WPS PIN feature is still enabled and demonstrates how a free tool can brute-force the eight-digit PIN in a few hours to recover the actual Wi-Fi password; she disables WPS entirely on the router's settings page.
detail.quizQuestion: A router's WPS feature is enabled so that guests can join by pressing a button or entering an eight-digit PIN. A tester recovers the network's WPA2 passphrase by trying PIN combinations against the router. Which of the following is the BEST remediation?
quizOptions: A) Replace the passphrase with a longer one, because that blocks the PIN attack
B) Hide the SSID so that the tester can no longer find the router to target it
C) Disable WPS on the access point and share the passphrase through a controlled process
D) Make the WPS PIN longer than eight digits so that guessing it takes much more time
detail.explanation: The WPS PIN method can be brute-forced and reveals the real passphrase regardless of its length, so WPS should be disabled. The PIN length is fixed by the standard, hiding the SSID is obscurity, and a longer passphrase is still exposed through WPS.
